target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Hungary of Article 5 (Right to liberty and security) concerning Length of pre-trial detention; Reasonableness of pre-trial detention in this case

case_name: CASE OF DACI v. ALBANIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF DACI v. ALBANIA

(Application no. 5232/24)







JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

6 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Daci v. Albania,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Ioannis Ktistakis, President,
Peeter Roosma,
Darian Pavli,
Diana Kovatcheva,
Úna Ní Raifeartaigh,
Mateja Đurović,
Vasilka Sancin, judges,
and Milan Blaško, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 5232/24) against the Republic of Albania lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Albanian national, Mr Luan Daci (“the applicant”), on 13 February 2024;

the decision to give notice to the Albanian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint under Article 7 of the Convention concerning the applicant’s conviction for falsifying a document and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;

the decision to grant the applicant leave to represent himself before the Court (Rule 36 § 2 in fine of the Rules of Court);

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 8 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The case concerns the alleged lack of foreseeability of the legal basis for the criminal conviction of the applicant on charges of falsification of a document. He relied on Article 7 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Tirana.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr O. Moçka, General State Advocate.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

Background information

5.  The applicant was a judge at the Tirana District Court. On 24 December 1997, following disciplinary proceedings, he was dismissed by a decision of the High Council of Justice on the grounds of breaches of the law and incompetence (“shkelje të ligjës dhe paaftësi në detyrë”).

6.  In 2014 an ad hoc parliamentary committee for reform of the justice system was set up. It subsequently approved a report assessing the legal system in Albania (“the Assessment Report”), which led to the adoption of a strategy on reform of the justice system (“the Reform Strategy”). As a result of the proposed Reform Strategy, the Constitution was amended in 2016 and a number of essential statutes were enacted, one of which was the Transitional Re-evaluation of Judges and Prosecutors Act (Law no. 84/2016, hereinafter referred to as “the Vetting Act”). The vetting process to which all serving judges and prosecutors would be subject would be carried out by an Independent Qualification Commission (the “IQC) at first instance and, on appeal, by a Special Appeal Chamber (“the SAC”) attached to the Constitutional Court (jointly referred to hereinafter as “the vetting bodies”).

7.  Also, an International Monitoring Operation (“IMO”), led by the European Commission, was established, to support, monitor and supervise the re-evaluation process (for further role of IMO see Xhoxhaj v. Albania, no. 15227/19, § 105, 9 February 2021).

8.  The applicant responded to an open call for the recruitment of five judges to the District Court of Tirana, but on 5 November 2016 the High Council of Justice decided to disqualify him from the competition on the grounds that he had been dismissed from the same position on 24 December 1997.

9.  On 3 February 2017 the applicant applied to become a member of one of the vetting bodies by way of an application to the Albanian Ombudsperson (Avokati i Popullit), as was the prescribed procedure. In his application the applicant stated, inter alia, the following:

“... I have never been subject to a disciplinary measure of dismissal from office or any other disciplinary measure that is still in force, pursuant to the law applicable at the time of [my] application [for the position of SAC judge].”

In the attached curriculum vitae he did not mention that he had served as a judge at the Tirana District Court.

10.  Following the establishment by the Ombudsperson of an ad hoc commission that would review all applications received for positions in the vetting bodies, on 13 February 2017 the said commission and the IMO adopted a protocol on the method by which the compliance of candidates with the statutory eligibility criteria would be evaluated (“protokoll për metodën, sipas së cilës do të vlerësohej përmbushja e kritereve statutore për përzgjedhshmërinë nga kandidatët”). The protocol provided, among other things, that a self-declaration from the candidates would be sufficient to presume that a candidate had not been “subjected to a disciplinary measure of dismissal from office or any another disciplinary measure that had been still in force at the time of applying” for a position on one of the vetting bodies, as required by section 6(1)(dh) of the Vetting Act.

11.  On 2 June 2017 a hearing was held before a parliamentary selection committee. In response to a question by an MP as to whether he had worked before the year 2000, the applicant answered that he had been a judge at the Tirana District Court between 1993 and 1997. When asked whether he had left of his own initiative or had been removed, the applicant answered that he had resigned.

12.  The applicant’s application was successful and he was appointed a judge at the SAC by Parliament on 17 June 2017.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant

13.  In 2020 the Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organised Crime (“the Special Prosecution Office”), upon a criminal complaint lodged by B.C. (see Besnik Cani v. Albania, no. 37474/20, § 15, 4 October 2022), opened a criminal investigation against the applicant on charges of falsifying a “form” (formular), a criminal offence under Article 190 of the Criminal Code, and an investigation was opened in respect of the applicant. In the course of the investigation the offence was reclassified as the criminal offence of falsifying a document under Article 186 of the Criminal Code.

14.  On 1 December 2020 the Special Court of First Instance against Corruption and Organised Crime (hereinafter referred to as “the Special Court of First Instance”) found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to six months’ imprisonment, suspended for one year. It held that in an affidavit (self-declaration) included in his application for a position on the vetting bodies, the applicant had failed to disclose the fact that his previous employment as a district court judge had been terminated as a result of a disciplinary measure against him (see paragraph 5 above). That failure by the applicant had amounted to “intellectual falsification” as he had knowingly presented false relevant information in his application for a senior position in the justice system. The first-instance court held that, even though there had been no particular form prescribed for the affidavit and applicants had been free to draft it how they chose, it nevertheless constituted an official document capable of producing legal effects and had been required by law for the selection procedure to be initiated. The first-instance court stated that the applicant’s application had taken the form of a written letter which had served to attest and prove the information it contained, namely that the applicant met the criteria for applying for a position on the vetting bodies under section 6 of the Vetting Act. Therefore, the applicant’s application amounted to a “document” within the meaning of Article 186 of the Criminal Code. The applicant had been obliged to include in it information on any disciplinary measures that had been taken against him, which he had failed to do. His failure to include the disciplinary measure imposed on him meant that the document contained false information which had brought about legal consequences, including the appointment of the applicant to the SAC on the basis of that false information.

The court noted the applicant’s argument that the measure against him had been expunged from his record. It referred in that connection to section 32(1) of the 2008 Judiciary Act, which stated that disciplinary violations by judges were to be divided into levels of seriousness, namely: (i) minor, (ii) serious and (iii) very serious. In the court’s view, section 33(6) of the 2008 Judiciary Act should be construed in the sense that all disciplinary measures relating to minor and serious violations were to be removed from the record of the judge concerned upon the expiry of the relevant time-limits; however, it did not provide for the removal from the record of disciplinary measures relating to very serious violations, such as dismissal from office. The court also cited section 150(3) of the Status of Judges and Prosecutors Act, which governed the matter after the repeal of the 2008 Judiciary Act and which provided that the disciplinary measure of dismissal from office could not be removed from a judge’s record. The court therefore concluded that the 1997 disciplinary measure against the applicant had not been removed from his record.

The first-instance court concluded that the applicant had intentionally presented false information in his application with the aim of hiding a fact which disqualified him as a candidate for judge at the vetting bodies.

15.  The applicant lodged an appeal against that decision. He argued that the criminal offence of document falsification had not been committed in his case as his application had not been a “document” that could be falsified within the meaning of Article 186 of the Criminal Code. The application had merely been an expression of interest made in the context of an administrative procedure governed by the Code of Administrative Procedure and the relevant provisions of the Vetting Act. It was neither an official document nor a document containing altered or fabricated information. The applicant argued that the object of Article 186 of the Criminal Code could only be an official document, issued by State bodies, “enterprises or social institutions”. The courts had wrongly treated that unilateral administrative document as if it were a formal self‑declaration or an official record, thereby expanding the scope of criminal liability beyond what the law provided. Furthermore, had he made a false or inaccurate statement in a self‑declaration form, the appropriate offence would have been the one under the first paragraph of Article 190 of the Criminal Code, which concerned false declarations in an official “form” (formular). He argued that the courts had effectively recharacterised his application as a self‑declaration form, contrary to the law, and had thereby relied on an expansive interpretation by analogy which was prohibited in criminal matters. An important element of the applicant’s defence concerned the disciplinary measure imposed on him in 1997, which the prosecution and courts had considered to be a fact that he had concealed. He argued that that measure had expired. As more than two decades had passed, the measure no longer had any legal effect and, legally, was treated as if it had never existed. Any assessment of whether a disciplinary measure had remained in force was a matter of legal interpretation, not falsification, and could not give rise to criminal liability. There had been no direct intent to alter an official document, nor had any such alteration in fact occurred. He argued that “intellectual falsification”, as relied upon by the prosecution, was not a recognised offense in Albanian criminal law or jurisprudence, but derived instead from Italian doctrine, and contended that it could not be imported into domestic criminal law without a proper legal basis.

16.  On 8 March 2021 the Special Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, endorsing its reasoning. It stressed that the purpose of the applicant’s application for a position on the vetting bodies had not only been to express his intention to apply for that position, but also to serve as proof that he fulfilled all of the conditions required by law to apply. One such condition was not to have been, at the time of application, subject to disciplinary sanctions or a prior removal from office. The failure of the applicant to declare in his application that he had been a judge of the Tirana District Court and that he had been dismissed due to a disciplinary sanction, as well as his false statement at the parliamentary hearing that he had resigned from that position, were assessed as intentional concealment of a fact and false presentation of facts in an official document.

The appeal court concluded that the applicant had acted with direct intent to conceal a piece of information required by law to be disclosed in order to avoid being disqualified from the competition at issue. He had thus committed the criminal offence of falsifying a document under Article 186 of the Criminal Code.

The appeal court also held as follows:

“The content of the application/request [submitted by the applicant for a position on the SAC] in this case is important and carries consequences, as the non-fulfilment of the formal criteria provided [in section 6(1) of the Vetting Act] leads to the disqualification of the candidate. That rule demonstrates the importance that the lawmaker attached to those criteria, which relate to the personal qualities that an candidate must possess in order to be appointed to the institutions [overseeing the] transitional re-evaluation of judges and prosecutors. These qualities/criteria, [which are] required by law, are important when cited before a public institution – all the more so in the case at hand, where the whole process of the transitional re-evaluation of judges and prosecutors is directly related to public trust in the justice [system] ([the protection of] which is the purpose of the creation of these institutions).

...

... the fact that the bodies empowered by law for the verification of candidates to the [vetting bodies] have not performed the relevant verifications in accordance with the legal requirements ..., does not exclude the liability of the defendant, who, intentionally and in full awareness, has presented in his application a false circumstance, [thereby] concealing a disqualifying condition related to the existence of a disciplinary measure of removal/dismissal from office imposed on him.”

17.  On 20 April 2021 the applicant lodged an appeal against that decision with the Supreme Court, reiterating the arguments he had made in his appeal against the first-instance judgment (see paragraph 15 above).

18.  On 26 October 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the lower courts’ judgments. It held that for the criminal offence under Article 186 of the Criminal Code to have been committed there had to be a document which was falsified and the falsification had to be intentional and committed by a person subject to criminal liability.

As to the applicant’s application for a position on the vetting bodies, the Supreme Court held that it was a formal act required by law, namely section 7 of Law no. 84/2016 (the Vetting Act), necessary for inclusion in the selection procedure, and that the accuracy of the information provided therein was also a legal requirement. In the Supreme Court’s view that sufficed for it to be seen as a “document” within the meaning of Article 186 of the Criminal Code. In essence, it was a letter meant to testify to something in writing, namely that the candidate concerned satisfied all requirements under section 6 of the Vetting Act. From the moment the applicant had chosen to apply for a position on the vetting bodies, he had had an obligation to submit an application with the Ombudsperson, and that application was capable of producing legal effects. However, the applicant’s application had contained false information to the effect that he had not been subjected to the disciplinary measure of removal from office, or to any other disciplinary measure.

The Supreme Court stressed that the Criminal Code did not contain a definition of the word “document”, so it was to be interpreted according to the definition in the Dictionary of the Albanian Language. In that dictionary the word “falsify” meant to represent as truth something that was a lie. Falsification was not only a falsified signature or a forged document, but also presenting or describing untrue facts as truthful. In the courts’ case-law, that form of falsification was known as “intellectual falsification”.

The Supreme Court relied on its previous judgment no. 00-2017-581 (111) of 12 July 2017, in which it had held that:

“intellectual falsification is committed by creating an act or document, in its entirety, through which a physical or legal person, whether public or private, expresses their will or assumes rights and obligations which, in reality, were not expressed. The criminal offense of falsifying documents ... may be committed in two ways, either directly in the document, by inserting false additions or other alterations, or with any other intervention to an existing document ... or in the other way that consists in falsifying the content of a document, without affecting its form ... That is the case of an ‘intellectual’ falsification that affects the descriptive and declaratory part of the document.”

The Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s argument that that form of falsification did not exist in Albanian law and that he had been punished without law.

As to the element of the criminal offence under Article 186 of the Criminal Code that required that the action have consequences, the Supreme Court held that, when it came to a private document, that element would be satisfied when the author of the document concerned had obtained unfair benefits or caused harm to third parties. Therefore, for the criminal offence in question to have been committed, it was not enough that a document had been falsified: there also had to have been consequences flowing from that act.

As to the applicant, the Supreme Court found that he had benefited from providing untrue information in his application, namely by being appointed a SAC judge. Not only had he submitted false information in his application, but he had also misled the parliamentary selection committee for the verification of candidates. At a hearing before that committee, he had confirmed that he had been a district court judge, but had falsely stated that he had resigned from that position, whereas he had actually been dismissed because of a disciplinary sanction against him. Given those circumstances, the Supreme Court concluded that, at the time of his application, the applicant had been aware of the disciplinary measure “dismissal from the post of judge” imposed on him by the former High Council of Justice.

The Supreme Court stated that a previous dismissal from office disqualified a candidate from holding certain public functions and confirmed that disciplinary measures for very serious violations were not removed from a judge’s record with the passage of time. The court further found that:

“69. ... [the applicant] deliberately provided false information in his application for the position of judge with the [SAC], for which position he [was deemed] qualified and [to which he was later] appointed precisely because of the untrue information that he had provided in the application form. If [the applicant] had disclosed in his application his dismissal from his post in 1997 he would have risked being disqualified under law [from being considered] for a position [on the vetting bodies].

70. The failure of the relevant bodies under [the Vetting Act] ... to verify the conditions that must be met by candidates for positions [on] the [vetting bodies] does not absolve the applicant of responsibility for declaring false information in his application.”

19.  One of the Supreme Court judges dissented from the majority decision, considering that the application for a position on the vetting bodies could not be treated as a “document” for the purposes of the criminal offence at issue. He argued that not all private submissions to a State body could be considered “documents” within the meaning of Article 186 of the Criminal Code and that only those private documents that were meant to certify a particular fact of legal consequence (such as a school diploma), or that were provided under oath or under threat of a penalty for perjury could be considered as such.

He further held that, in any event, the applicant’s defence that he had believed that the disciplinary measure had been removed from his record was arguable, and that no criminal intent could therefore be inferred from the circumstances of the case.

The dissenting judge considered that criminal courts were not competent to make a final determination that the applicant’s dismissal in 1997 disqualified him from holding the position of SAC judge. Moreover, even assuming that the 1997 dismissal had disqualified the applicant, his appointment as an SAC judge had only been possible because of the failure of the Ombudsperson and Parliament to verify whether he fulfilled the relevant criteria, rather than being solely attributable to the application that the applicant had lodged with the Ombudsperson.

He also referred in that respect to Italian jurisprudence on “falso inutile” (useless falsity) in private documents, which was to be distinguished from criminal falsification in official documents.

20.  On 17 January 2022 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint.

21.  On 26 September 2022 the Constitutional Court remitted the case to the Supreme Court because one of the judges of the Supreme Court panel that had heard the case had also participated in deciding a request for a security measure lodged by the prosecution at an earlier stage in the proceedings.

22.  On 21 March 2023 the Supreme Court again dismissed the applicant’s appeal, finding that there were no grounds to reverse its previous judgment. It added that:

“... falsification [of a private document] will be considered committed when the author of the document has obtained unfair benefits or caused harm to third parties by way of the falsification; hence, not merely by the evidence of false content without consequences, but by requiring in this way the entailing of a consequence,  which in this case means that a private document is identified as obtaining an illegal benefit accruing to the falsifier of the document, or as causing harm to third parties.”

The Supreme Court relied on its judgment of 12 July 2017 (see paragraph 40 below).

23.  On 19 June 2023 the applicant lodged a fresh constitutional complaint. He complained, inter alia, that his right not to be punished without law had been violated.

24.  On 21 September 2023 the Constitutional Court, by five votes to four, dismissed the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The reasoned judgment was served on the applicant on 20 October 2023.

The majority endorsed the Supreme Court’s interpretation of Article 186 of the Criminal Code, finding that it was not unreasonable or arbitrary.

Regarding the applicant’s claim that the Supreme Court had created a new criminal norm and acted as the legislator in its determination of the relevant criminal actions and omissions, the Constitutional Court held that the criminal offence of falsifying documents was provided for in Albanian criminal law and that the concepts of “material falsification (falsifikim material)” and “intellectual falsification (falsifikim ideologjik ose intelektual)” were not new and did not constitute an extended interpretation of the (criminal) provision. In fact, the Supreme Court had relied on its previous case-law concerning the interpretation of the concept of “intellectual falsification”. The Constitutional Court observed that the interpretation of concepts of criminal law and of the Criminal Code was a task for the Supreme Court and that that court had given adequate reasons for its interpretation of Article 186 of the Criminal Code in the applicant’s case.

25.  The four dissenting judges argued that the Supreme Court appeared to have adopted a novel and expansive interpretation of the notions of “document” and “falsification” as regards the criminal offence at issue, without relying on an established line of case-law. As such, it had failed to properly engage with the applicant’s Article 7 claims.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
Domestic law
The Criminal Code

26.  The relevant part of the Criminal Code reads as follows:

Article 186

Falsification of documents

“Falsifying a document or using a falsified document is punishable by imprisonment for a period of up to three years.

...

When the falsification is done by a person who is responsible for issuing the document concerned, it is punishable by imprisonment for a period of between one and seven years.”

Article 187

Falsifying school documents

“Falsifying school documents or using falsified school documents is punishable by a fine or up to three years’ imprisonment.

When an individual authorised to issue the document carries out the falsification, such an act is punishable by a fine or by up to five years’ imprisonment.”

Article 188

Falsifying health-related documents

“Falsifying health-related documents or using falsified health-related documents is punishable by a fine or up to three years’ imprisonment.

When an individual authorised to issue the document carries out the falsification, such an act is punishable by a fine or by up to five years’ imprisonment.”

Article 189

Falsifying identity cards or visas

“Falsifying identity cards, passports or visas or using falsified identity cards, passports or visas is punishable by a fine or by up to five years’ imprisonment.

When an individual authorised to issue identity cards or passports carries out the falsification, such an act is punishable by three to seven years’ imprisonment.”

Article 190

Falsifying seals, labels or forms

“Falsifying seals, labels [stampave] or forms [formularëve], or using falsified seals, labels or forms, or providing false information on forms submitted to State bodies, is punishable by a fine or by up to five years of imprisonment.

When the falsification is carried out by an individual authorised to prepare them, such an act is punishable by three to seven years of imprisonment.”

Article 191

Falsifying civil records

“Falsifying civil records or using falsified civil records is punishable by a fine or by up to three years of imprisonment.

When an individual authorised to issue such a record commits the falsification, it is punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment.”

Article 306

Perjury

“Perjury before the court constitutes a criminal offence [that] shall be punishable by a fine or imprisonment for a term of up to two years.

Where false testimony is given for the purpose of obtaining a benefit or any other advantage that has been offered, promised or provided, the offence shall be punishable by a fine or by imprisonment for a term of up to three years.

The same offence, where committed in connection with the criminal offences provided for in Articles 234/a, 234/b, 284/a, 333 and 333/a of this Code, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of between two and six years.”

The Code of Criminal Procedure

27.  The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure read as follows:

Article 191

The acquiring of documents

“The acquisition of documents concerning facts, persons or objects shall be permitted through photographing, filming, audio recording or any other means.

When the original document has been damaged, lost or disappeared, a copy may be acquired.

Documents constituting material evidence shall be acquired irrespective of the person who created or holds them.”

Article 450

Grounds for revision [Rastet e rishikimit]

“An application for revision [of a final judgment] may be made:

(...)

(e)  when grounds for revision of a final judgment stem from a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights which makes revision indispensable....”

The Transitional Re-evaluation of Judges and Prosecutors Act (Law no. 84/2016, the “Vetting Act”)

28.  Section 6 of the Vetting Act, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:

Section 6 – Conditions for the appointment of members of the [vetting bodies]

“1. An Albanian citizen may be appointed as a member of the [Independent Qualification] Commission or [Special] Appeal Chamber if he or she fulfils the following conditions:

...

c) [he or she] has received positive evaluations of his or her professional skills, ethics and moral integrity, in the event that he or she has been subject to previous evaluations;

...

dh) has no disciplinary measure of dismissal from office [previously imposed on] him or her or any other disciplinary measure that is still in force, pursuant to the legislation at the time of his or her applying [for a position on the vetting bodies].”

29.  Sections 7 to 12 regulate the procedure for applications and for the preselection, interviewing and selection of candidates. The members of the vetting bodies are to be selected by a vote of Parliament.

The relevant part of section 7 reads as follows:

“4. The candidate refers in his/her application to the vacancy for which he or she is interested to apply. If the candidate indicates no preference, the application is considered [as made] for all vacancies. The candidate shall attach to the application two copies of the following documents:

a) Curriculum vitae including contact details, official email and postal address;

b) A notarised copy of the [university] diploma or equivalent copy issued by the respective institutions;

c) Notarised or equivalent copies of the documents issued by the respective institutions, which attest [that the] requirements under section 6 of this Law [are met];

...”

The 2008 Judiciary Act (Law no. 9877/2008 of 18 February 2008 on the organisation and functioning of the judiciary, as amended) – repealed on 22 November 2016

30.  The relevant sections of the 2008 Judiciary Act read as follows:

Section 32 - Disciplinary violations

“1. Disciplinary violations by judges are divided into the following categories:

a) very serious;

b) serious;

c) minor.

...”

Section 33 - Disciplinary measures

“1. Disciplinary measures shall be proportional vis-à-vis the violation committed.

2. The disciplinary measures that may be imposed are:

a) a reprimand;

b) a reprimand with a warning;

c) temporary demotion to a lower-level court for a period of one to two years;

ç) a transfer for one to two years to a court of the same level outside the judicial district to which the judge [in question] was appointed;

d) dismissal from office.

3. For very serious violations ... the disciplinary measure [of dismissal from office] provided in point “d” of subsection 2 of this section shall be imposed.

4. For serious violations ..., the disciplinary measures provided in points “c” or “ç” of subsection 2 of this section shall be imposed.

5. For minor violations ..., the disciplinary measures provided in points “a” or “b” of subsection 2 of this section shall be imposed.

6. For the purposes of disciplinary proceedings, serious disciplinary measures are removed [from the record of the person concerned] within three years of the date on which they were imposed if no other disciplinary measure has been imposed, while minor disciplinary measures are removed within two years from the date on which they were imposed if no other disciplinary measure has been imposed.”

Law on Civil Servants (Law no. 152/13 – amended by Law no. 178/2014 of 18 December 2014, Official Gazette No. 211)

31.  Section 61 of the Law on Civil Servants provides that any disciplinary sanction imposed on civil servants relating to their employment expires seven years after the civil servant concerned was notified of the sanction.

Law on the Status of Judges and Prosecutors (Law no. 96/2016)

32.  Section 150(3) of the Law on the Status of Judges and Prosecutors reads as follows:

“The disciplinary measure of dismissal shall not be erased and shall not be removed from [an individual’s] record.”

The Administrative Procedure Act (Law no. 44/2015)

33.  The relevant provision of the Administrative Procedure Act provides as follows:

Section 58

Form and content of a request

“1. Except in cases when the law requests a specific form, any request, by which parties address a public body in an administrative procedure, may be:

a) in writing;

b) declared verbally in front of the public body and registered by the latter;

c) in any other appropriate form.

2. The request should be sufficiently clear in defining the applicant and the purpose [of the application], unless the law has provided for a specific content.

...”

The Decriminalisation Act

34.  Under sections 2 to 5 of the Decriminalisation Act (Law no. 138/2015 on ensuring the integrity of persons exercising, elected or appointed to public functions”), as amended by Law no. 38/2016, persons seeking appointment to certain public offices must complete and sign a self-declaration form declaring the absence of grounds preventing their appointment, such as, inter alia, the absence of a final criminal conviction resulting in a sentence of imprisonment for a number of offences listed in the Law. It is expressly provided that a false declaration is punishable under Article 190 of the Criminal Code.

Practice of DOMESTIC COURTS
Case-law submitted by the applicant
Case of A.F.

35.  On 2 July 2020 H.M. lodged a criminal complaint with the Special Prosecution Office against A.F., a member of the IQC. H.M. alleged that A.F. had omitted information concerning her prior dismissal from office as a judge in 1996 when applying for a position on the vetting bodies, and that she had therefore committed the criminal offence of falsification of documents.

36.  On 11 February 2021, after the investigation was concluded, the Special Court of First Instance granted the prosecutor’s request to discontinue the proceedings. It reasoned that the offence of falsification of documents could only be committed in one of two ways: either by interfering directly with an existing document by making changes or by creating a new document. In A.F.’s case the alleged act amounted only to ‘intellectual forgery’. A.F. had included in her application her employment booklet, which contained information on her dismissal from office. Furthermore, she had not declared any “untrue facts” before the selection committee. She had informed them that she had served as a judge previously without mentioning the reason for her departure, and the members of the committee had not asked her for it. Furthermore, A.F., unlike the other candidates, had not submitted any written statement certifying or documenting that there was no disciplinary measure of dismissal in force against her.

37.  On 6 May 2021 the Special Court of Appeal upheld the decision of the Special Court of First Instance. It endorsed the prosecution’s arguments, finding further that under the Criminal Code and the Code of Civil Procedure, the term “document” referred to “written materials created and intended to prove a legally relevant fact”. It also interpreted falsification as “the intentional act of erasing, destroying, damaging, adding to or altering a document in such a manner as to change or distort it by presenting false information or circumstances, or the drafting of an entirely new document claiming to be original but containing false information”.

It further held that the legal significance of the application form and declaration before Parliament or the vetting bodies, “lay solely in the expression of the candidate’s intention to apply for a position” within the vetting bodies. Any other written statement contained in the application could not produce legal consequences and, therefore, the falsification thereof could not entail criminal liability.

38.  In its judgment no. 00-2025-676 of 24 April 2025, the Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal lodged by H.M. It noted that H.M.’s arguments had already been raised during the investigation and before the special courts, which had provided sufficient and appropriate reasons for discontinuing the criminal proceedings against A.F.

The Supreme Court’s judgment no. 00-2023-1529 (257) of 26 September 2023 (case of E.Ç.)

39.   E.Ç., an IQC member, was accused of the criminal offence of falsification of documents. It was alleged that she had been a party to fictitious contracts containing false information and signed before a public notary. The Supreme Court, in so far as relevant, held as follows:

“188. ... it is concluded that the submission of such a document in 2017 to the High Inspectorate of the Declaration and Control of Assets and Conflicts of Interest (HIDAAC) by the judge does not constitute the committing of the criminal offence of falsification of documents under paragraph 1 of Article 186 of the Criminal Code. A fictitious contract (signed when E.Ç. was not subject to declaration duties) is not considered a falsified document. Therefore, even the use of this contract does not constitute the objective element of the criminal offence of falsification of documents.

189. In these circumstances, for the above reasons, it does not result that the criminal offence of falsification of documents has been committed by E.Ç., since drafting a simulated contract and subsequently using it does not constitute a criminal offence in itself and [such contracts] therefore cannot be seen as falsified documents. They can constitute another criminal offence, if all the elements [of that offence] are met, which the court has not found in the case at issue.”

Case-law submitted by the Government
Judgment of the Supreme Court no. 00-2017-581 (111) of 12 July 2017

40.  In this case, the alleged criminal offence concerned the use by the accused of an entirely falsified public document used to obtain ownership of a plot of land. The falsified document was an official document that had supposedly been issued by the Commission on Property Restitution and Compensation. The Supreme Court quashed the lower courts’ judgment acquitting the accused and remitted the case for fresh assessment. In so far as relevant, the Supreme Court held as follows:

“3. The criminal offence of document falsification under Article 186 of the Criminal Code is to be understood as the presentation in a document of false circumstances or the drafting of a falsified document, as well as the use of falsified documents.

...

5. The criminal offense of document falsification ... can be committed in two ways: either by intervening directly in the document, by making illegal additions or alterations, or by any other material change to a previously existing document. In that case, we will be faced with ‘material’ falsification; whereas falsifying the content of the document, without affecting its form, by changing the concept and content of the document, is ‘intellectual’ falsification that violates the descriptive-declarative part of the document.”

41.  In paragraph 7 of the judgment the Supreme Court noted in passing that the objective element of the criminal offence of falsification of documents could also be committed by private persons.

Judgment of the Supreme Court no. 00-2017-659 (116) of 19 July 2017

42.  In this judgment, the alleged criminal offence concerned the falsification of a document used to obtain ownership of a plot of land. The allegedly falsified document was an official document issued by the relevant authorities, namely a renovation permit that had been issued in 1989 by the urban planning office of a local government authority.

43.  In paragraphs 8 and 9 of the judgment the Supreme Court held that the criminal offence of document falsification could be committed in two ways: either by falsifying a document or by using a document that had already been falsified, whether by the same person who had falsified it or by someone else who had an interest in its use. In the first case, establishing who had falsified the document was essential, whereas in the second case what mattered was identifying the person who had used the falsified document.

Judgment of the Supreme Court no. 00-2024-1833 (277) of 7 November 2024

44.  This judgment concerned the criminal offences of fraud in public procurement and falsification of documents. The defendants were accused of falsifying documents (inspection and completion certificates confirming that the building had been completed) to ensure that private companies could benefit from public procurement.

45.  In paragraphs 19-23 of that judgment the Supreme Court reiterated its previous position as regards the interpretation of Article 186 of the Criminal Code. It held that that criminal offence was classified as a formal offence, as it was considered committed by the act of falsifying the document itself, irrespective of whether that act actually brought about any harmful consequence. It also stated that the offence covered both public and private documents.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Albania of Article 7 (No punishment without law) concerning Nullum crimen sine lege in this case

FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF CHERKASOV AND KUZIN v. UKRAINE

(Applications nos. 72982/17 and 74407/17)



JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

8 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Cherkasov and Kuzin v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Kateřina Šimáčková, President,
Gilberto Felici,
Andreas Zünd,
Diana Sârcu,
Mykola Gnatovskyy,
Vahe Grigoryan,
Sébastien Biancheri, judges,
and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the applications (nos. 72982/17 and 74407/17) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Oleksandr Volodymyrovych Cherkasov (“the first applicant”) and Mr Sergiy Volodymyrovych Kuzin (“the second applicant”), on 25 September and 11 October 2017, respectively;

the decision to give notice to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and to declare the Article 6 § 1 complaint (lack of access to a higher court) raised in application no. 74407/17 inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 2 December 2025 and 8 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on the latter date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The present case mainly concerns the applicants’ complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14 of the Convention, that the suspension of their pension payments on the grounds that social benefits for internally displaced persons (“IDPs”) could only be paid into accounts opened with a designated State bank was discriminatory and violated their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions.

THE FACTS

2.  The first applicant was born in 1958 and lives in Stari Bohorodchany, Ivano-Frankivsk Region. He was represented by Mr O. Fomichov, a lawyer practising in Ivano-Frankivsk.

3.  The second applicant was born in 1952 and lives in Kyiv. He was represented by Mr A. Yakovlev, Mr R. Martynovskyy, Ms V. Petruk, Mr M. Tymochko, lawyers practising in Kyiv. At the time of his application, the second applicant was also represented by Mr M. Kikkas.

4.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Sokorenko, from the Ministry of Justice.

5.  The circumstances of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

Background information

6.  After Russia occupied and claimed jurisdiction over the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol, and owing to armed hostilities in certain parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions of Ukraine, in 2014 and later many residents of those regions had to leave their homes and move to government-controlled territories. The majority of those who moved registered themselves as IDPs, being entitled to the same social benefits as other Ukrainian citizens. However, from 1 July 2016 onwards, to continue receiving those benefits, IDPs were required to have an account with the Derzhavnyy Oshchadnyy Bank of Ukraine (the State Savings Bank – “Oshchadbank”) and to undergo periodic physical identification there (see Shylina v. Ukraine, no. 2412/19, § 5, 15 February 2024, with further references).

Circumstances of the case

7.  The applicants used to live in Donetsk. Owing to hostilities in the area, they relocated to government-controlled territories and obtained IDP status. They were entitled to a retirement pension.

Application no. 72982/17

8.  The first applicant was registered as a pensioner with the Bohorodchany Department of the Pension Fund in the Ivano-Frankivsk Region (“the Bohorodchany Pension Fund”). He had been receiving his pension through the post office at his new place of residence.

9.  In June 2016 the Bohorodchany Pension Fund informed the first applicant that from 1 July 2016 onwards social payments to IDPs would be made through Oshchadbank. His pension payments were suspended the following month because he did not provide details of an account opened with Oshchadbank.

10.  In August 2016 the first applicant requested the Bohorodchany Pension Fund to resume his pension payments and transfer them into his new account opened with a private bank, P. He was informed that this would not be possible, as Resolution no. 637 of the Cabinet of Ministers of 5 November 2014 as amended in June 2016 (see paragraph 25 below) explicitly provided that payment of social benefits to IDPs could only be made to accounts opened with Oshchadbank.

11.  In September 2016 the first applicant instituted proceedings against the Bohorodchany Pension Fund, seeking payment of his pension into his account with bank P. He relied, in particular, on section 47 of the Law on Compulsory State Pension Insurance (no. 1058-IV of 9 July 2003 – “the 2003 Law”), which provided that pension payments could be made to a bank account specified by the pensioner (see paragraph 24 below). He argued that, as the 2003 Law had higher legal force, the Cabinet of Ministers could not limit the rights of pensioners.

12.  On 18 October 2016 the Bohorodchany Local Court of the Ivano-Frankivsk Region found for the first applicant. It held that, under section 47 of the 2003 Law, the choice of bank account for the receipt of pension payments lay with the pensioner and could not be restricted by subordinate legislation. The court further observed that the suspension of the applicant’s pension from 1 July 2016, on the sole ground that he had not opened an account with Oshchadbank as required by the Cabinet of Ministers’ Resolution No. 637 (as amended), lacked a proper legal basis in primary legislation and thus contravened the principle that public authorities must act within the limits of the law. It considered that the impugned by-law effectively narrowed the scope of the applicant’s statutory right to receive his pension in a bank of his choice, which was incompatible with the governing legislative framework and constitutional guarantees of social protection. Accordingly, the court ordered the immediate resumption of pension payments to the applicant’s account with bank P., including payment of the outstanding amount for July 2016, which he received in October 2016.

13.  According to the first applicant, he was in quite a dire situation: he had to drastically reduce spending on food and medication and borrow money from a friend. As he needed money for everyday expenses, in December 2016 he opened an account with Oshchadbank, following which his pension payments were resumed. He also received payment of his pension arrears for August to December 2016.

14.  On 24 January 2017 the Lviv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of 18 October 2016, endorsing the first-instance court’s reasoning that section 47 of the 2003 Law gave the pensioner the right to determine the bank account to which his pension should be transferred. The appellate court rejected the Pension Fund’s reliance on Cabinet of Ministers Resolution no. 637, as amended by Resolution no. 167, which required internally displaced persons to receive pensions exclusively through Oshchadbank. It held that the termination of the applicant’s pension from 1 July 2016 had no basis in primary legislation. In particular, it emphasised that section 49 of the 2003 Law contained an exhaustive list of grounds for terminating pension payments, none of which applied to the applicant’s situation (see paragraph 24 below). The court therefore concluded that the Pension Fund had acted unlawfully and had violated the applicant’s constitutional rights, including the protection against narrowing existing rights and freedoms.

15.  On 21 March 2017, following an appeal on points of law, the Higher Administrative Court overruled the lower courts’ decisions and dismissed the first applicant’s claim. It held that, although section 47 of the 2003 Law provides that a pension may be paid to a bank account designated by the pensioner, that provision must be interpreted in conjunction with the special legal framework governing IDPs. In particular, Resolution no. 637 established a specific procedure for the payment of pensions to that category, requiring that such payments be made exclusively through accounts with Oshchadbank, which constituted a permissible regulation of the technical modalities of payment rather than a restriction of the right to a pension itself. As regards section 49 of the same Law, the court found that the list of grounds for the termination of pension payments was not exhaustive, as it expressly referred to “other cases provided for by law”, thereby allowing additional regulation through normative acts adopted within the competence of the Cabinet of Ministers. In those circumstances, and given that the applicant had been duly informed of the applicable requirements but failed to comply with them, the court concluded that the suspension of his pension payments had been carried out in accordance with the applicable legal framework.

Application no. 74407/17

16.  The second applicant was registered as a pensioner with the Livoberezhnyi Department of the Pension Fund in Kyiv (“the Livoberezhnyi Pension Fund”). He had been receiving his pension payments into his account with bank P.

17.  In July 2016 the Livoberezhnyi Pension Fund suspended the second applicant’s pension payments because he did not provide details of an account opened with Oshchadbank. He filed complaints and requests to have his pension payments paid into his account with bank P. but was told that that would not be possible, as Resolution no. 637 explicitly provided that social benefits to IDPs could only be paid into accounts opened with Oshchadbank. In view of that response, in July 2016 the second applicant complied with the above requirement and had his pension payments resumed.

18.  In August 2016 the second applicant instituted proceedings against the Livoberezhnyi Pension Fund. The applicant challenged the suspension of his pension payments following his refusal to receive them through Oshchadbank, seeking recognition of the unlawfulness of the authorities’ decisions, restoration of pension payments and payment of arrears to his account with another bank, compensation for non-pecuniary damage, and an order preventing the authorities from imposing the Oshchadbank-only requirement in the future. He argued that the requirement for IDPs to receive their pension payments exclusively through Oshchadbank accounts was discriminatory, as other categories of pensioners were free to choose their bank. He further argued that the suspension of his pension payments had deprived him, an unemployed individual and a person with disabilities, of the financial resources necessary to survive, even though he was entitled, under section 47 of the 2003 Law (see paragraph 24 below) to receive his pension through a bank account of his choice. According to the second applicant, this was also inconsistent with section 49 of the 2003 Law (see paragraph 24 below), since the absence of an account with Oshchadbank was not among the grounds for the termination of pension payments.

19.  On 18 October 2016 the Pecherskyi District Court of Kyiv dismissed the second applicant’s claim. It found that the Livoberezhnyi Pension Fund had acted in accordance with the applicable legislation, including Resolution no. 637, and that its actions could not therefore be declared unlawful. The case was examined in abridged proceedings.

20.  In December 2016 the Livoberezhnyi Pension Fund paid the second applicant’s pension arrears for July to November 2016 into his account with Oshchadbank.

21.  In February 2017 the second applicant appealed against the judgment of 18 October 2016, reiterating his arguments that the contested measure was unlawful and that the requirement to have an account with Oshchadbank was discriminatory.

22.  On 13 March 2017 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of the first-instance court, fully endorsing its findings. The court held that the refusal to continue paying the pension to the claimant through his chosen bank account was lawful because the authorities had acted within their statutory powers and in accordance with the applicable regulatory framework governing payments to IDPs. It found that, although the general rule under section 47 of the 2003 Law allowed pensioners to receive payments via a bank of their choice, subsequent resolutions of the Cabinet of Ministers – adopted in the context of internal displacement and based on its constitutional competence to implement social policy – introduced a specific procedure requiring such payments to be made exclusively through Oshchadbank. The court relied on the Constitutional Court’s position (Decision No. 20-рп/2011) that adjustments to the mechanisms of social payments are permissible so long as they do not undermine the essence of the right to social protection. It concluded that the claimant had not been deprived of his pension as such, but only required to comply with a different payment procedure, and that the suspension of payments resulted from his failure to meet that requirement. The appellate court pointed out that its decision could be challenged by way of an appeal on points of law.

23.  In April 2017 the second applicant lodged such an appeal, but on 11 April 2017 the Higher Administrative Court refused to entertain it, stating that the decision of 13 March 2017, having been adopted in abridged proceedings, was not amenable to appeal on points of law.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK
Law on Compulsory State Pension Insurance

24.  The relevant provisions of the 2003 Law, as worded at the time of the applicants’ claims to the domestic courts, read as follows:

Section 47 – Payment of pensions

“1.  Pensions shall be paid monthly by organisations responsible for paying and delivering pensions ... at the pensioner’s actual place of residence in Ukraine or transferred to a bank account specified by the pensioner, in accordance with the procedure established by law.

...”

Section 49 – Termination of pension payments and renewal

“1.  Pension payments shall be terminated by decision of the local pension fund authorities or a court:

(1) if the pension was granted on the basis of documents containing inaccurate information;

(2) for the entire period of the pensioner’s residence abroad, unless otherwise provided for by an international treaty of Ukraine, the binding nature of which has been acknowledged by the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine[1];

(3) in case of the pensioner’s death;

(4) in case of non-receipt of the pension for six consecutive months;

(5) in other cases provided for by law.

...”

In September 2016 the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine introduced to the Parliament a draft law on a package of labour, pension, and social-finance changes, which also included amendments to section 47. Those were adopted by Law no. 1774-VIII of 6 December 2016 (entered into force on 1 January 2017) in the following wording:

Section 47 – Payment of pensions

“1.  Pensions shall be paid monthly ... at the pensioner’s actual place of residence in Ukraine, by organisations carrying out the payment and delivery of pensions or through banking institutions in accordance with the procedure established by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine.

...”

Other relevant domestic law

25.  Other relevant domestic law, as summarised in Shylina v. Ukraine (cited above, §§ 17-21), includes the following: (i) the Law on the Prevention of and Fight Against Discrimination in Ukraine (no. 5207-VI of 6 September 2012); (ii) the Law on Internally Displaced Persons’ Rights and Freedoms (no. 1706-VII of 20 October 2014); and (iii) Resolution no. 637 of the Cabinet of Ministers of 5 November 2014 on welfare payments to internally displaced persons, as amended by Resolution no. 167 of 14 March 2016, Resolution no. 365 of 8 June 2016 and Resolution no. 689 of 13 September 2017.

More specifically, as amended on 8 June 2016, Resolution no. 637 provided that from 1 July 2016 onwards the payment of all social benefits, including pensions, to the IDPs should be made solely through the accounts and the network of offices and devices of Oshchadbank. In order to identify those recipients of social benefits who are IDPs and to ensure the payment of these benefits to them, payment cards were to be issued. IDPs had to undergo physical identification in an Oshchadbank office every six months on the first two occasions, and every twelve months subsequently. If an IDP failed to undergo the identification, the bank was required to suspend outgoing transactions from the person’s current account and to inform the social security department which had issued the IDP registration certificate and the Ministry of Finance.
