full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF ATRESMEDIA CORPORACION DE MEDIOS DE COMUNICACION S.A. v. SPAIN

(Application no. 29807/23)



JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

8 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of ATRESMEDIA CORPORACION DE MEDIOS DE COMUNICACION S.A. v. Spain,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Kateřina Šimáčková, President,
María Elósegui,
Gilberto Felici,
Andreas Zünd,
Diana Sârcu,
Sébastien Biancheri,
Nicholas Emiliou, judges,
and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 29807/23) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Spanish company, Atresmedia Corporación de Medios de Comunicación S.A. (“the applicant company”), on 26 July 2023;

the decision to give notice to the Spanish Government (“the Government”) of the complaint under Article 10 of the Convention;

the observations submitted by the respondent Government and the observations in reply submitted by the applicant company;

the comments submitted by Media Defence, which was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section;

Having deliberated in private on 8 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The application concerns a complaint under Article 10 by the applicant company – a private media broadcasting group – about a decision of the Central Electoral Commission not to accept the format of a political debate proposed by the applicant company during the election campaign for the national parliamentary elections in 2019.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant company is a private media broadcasting group which was established in 1988 and has its registered seat in San Sebastian de Los Reyes (Madrid). The applicant company was represented by Mr I. Salama Salama, a lawyer practising in Madrid.

3.  The Government were represented by their co-Agents, Ms H. E. Nicolás Martínez and Mr J.A. Jurado Ripoll.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

I.        Background to the case and political debate proposed by the applicant company

5.  The applicant company is a broadcasting and media business group which includes various private television channels, including Antena 3, which broadcasts news and entertainment programmes.

6.  Ahead of the national parliamentary elections on 28 April 2019, the applicant company decided to organise an election debate between five candidates for the office of Prime Minister, which was to be held on 23 April 2019 and televised on Antena 3. Those five candidates represented Partido Popular (PP), Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE), Unidas Podemos (UP), Ciudadanos and Vox. The applicant company based its selection of participants on their affiliation with the five political parties that had a national presence and were expected to obtain more than 10% of the votes, according to a pre-election survey published in March 2019 by the Spanish Centre for Sociological Research (Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas – “the CIS” – an independent public body responsible for official social statistics). The participants were therefore likely candidates to become Prime Minister.

7.  Prior to the 2019 elections, four out of the five above-mentioned political parties – that is, all except Vox – had secured parliamentary representation in the previous general elections held in June 2016. They had the biggest representation in Congress at the time. Vox had received 0.2% of the votes in the 2016 elections and had not secured parliamentary representation.

8.  During elections to the Parliament of Andalusia held in December 2018, Vox had obtained 10.96% of the votes.

9.  According to its March 2019 pre-election survey, on the basis of opinion poll data from approximately 16,000 interviews, the CIS estimated that Vox’s vote share was 11.9% (29 to 37 seats).

II.      Proceedings before the Central Electoral commission

10.  In the period preceding the elections, three regional political parties participating in the general election campaign (Coalición Canaria, Electoral Coalition Junts and Euzko Alderdi Jeltzalea-Basque Nationalist Party (EAJ-PNV)) lodged complaints with the Central Electoral Commission (“the CEC”), contesting the criteria which the applicant company had applied in selecting the participants in the debate. They asserted that the forthcoming televised debate did not adhere to the principles of pluralism, proportionality, equality and neutrality as set out in section 66(2) of Institutional Law no 5/1985 of 19 June 1985 on the General Electoral System (“the LOREG”) (see paragraph 44 below). They submitted that, unlike Vox, they had secured parliamentary representation in the previous equivalent elections. They further maintained that Vox did not qualify as a significant political group (grupo político significativo) within the meaning of Instruction no. 4/2011 of the CEC of 24 March (see paragraph 47 below). The political parties which had lodged the complaints therefore considered that the inclusion of Vox’s candidate for Prime Minister in the debate, to the exclusion of their own, was contrary to the above principles. They accordingly requested that the applicant company be ordered to either refrain from holding the debate without their participation or give them equivalent compensatory airtime.

11.  In reply, the applicant company stated that the planned five-way debate was clearly informative, given that VOX had secured 10.96% of the votes in the recent elections to the Parliament of Andalusia; was one of the main contenders in the forthcoming general election; had electoral lists throughout the country; and was the fifth-largest political force according to the polls. The company also stated that all the above information was objective and verifiable. It noted that EAJ-PNV was expected to receive fewer votes than Vox, according to the CIS survey, and that, unlike Vox, it had candidates only in certain provinces, while the debate was to be broadcast throughout the entire country. Vox could therefore be considered a relevant and significant political group for the purposes of the LOREG. The company also stated that it was willing to offer airtime to the regional political parties which had complained. In particular, it pointed out that a debate was scheduled to take place on 20 April 2019 as part of the programme “La Sexta Noche”, in which representatives of the parties that had secured political representation in the previous general elections, including the complainants, had been invited to participate. The company also listed other programmes in which the representatives of the parties that had complained would be given an opportunity to appear. The applicant company therefore argued that those parties would receive sufficient airtime. Lastly, it emphasised its unwavering respect for the principles of pluralism, equality, proportionality and neutrality, by which it had always abided, in full compliance with the LOREG and the Instructions of the CEC.

12.  By a single decision of 16 April 2019 the CEC allowed the three complaints. Having reiterated the content of section 66(2) of the LOREG, it noted that under Article 8 of Instruction no. 4/2021, adopted to implement it, where a private television broadcaster organised or broadcast electoral interviews or debates, it should have particular regard to the results obtained by each political formation in the previous equivalent elections. According to the CEC, the criterion of proportionality “[did] not prevent the provision of information concerning [parties] which had not participated in or secured representation in the previous elections; however, it [did] determine that [those who had not secured representation] could not receive more airtime than political formations which had secured representation in the previous elections”. It stressed that it was bound by the relevant criteria, which could not be substituted by other criteria, such as the news in question supposedly being topical, or opinion poll data.

13.  Turning to the proposed debate, the CEC found that there could be “no objection to the participation” of representatives from PP, PSOE, UP and Ciudadanos, as they had secured the most parliamentary representation and the highest number of votes in the most recent elections to the Congress of Deputies held in 2016. However, that did not apply to Vox, as it had not secured parliamentary representation and had received 0.1% of the votes in those elections. Conversely, the political parties which had complained had secured parliamentary representation and a higher percentage of valid votes – factors which were relevant to “the legally established criteria for applying the principle of proportionality to election debates and interviews”.

14.  The CEC further found that Vox did not meet the criteria of “a significant political group” for the purposes of section 4 (2.3) of Instruction no. 2/2011 (see paragraph 47 below) either, as it had not received 5% or more of the valid votes cast. The CEC acknowledged that Vox had received 10.96% of the valid votes cast in the recent elections to the Parliament of Andalusia, which would entitle it to such status in Andalusia. However, the disputed debate was to be held at national level, and Vox had not received 5% of the valid votes cast and could therefore not be regarded as a significant political group at that level.

15.  Lastly, the CEC was unable to accept the applicant company’s argument that it had proposed to organise a debate on 20 April 2019 in which Vox would not take part because “the proportionality principle [had] been given priority”. The CEC noted that section 66(2) of the LOREG did not provide for the voluntary application of the principle of proportionality, but imposed it unconditionally. There was no scope for privately owned broadcasters to exercise discretion in applying the principle of proportionality to debates of their choice; it was to be applied to all debates organised during the electoral process.

16.  The CEC concluded as follows:

5.  It follows from the foregoing that the [complaints by the three political parties] must be upheld and that the five-candidate debate proposed by [the applicant company] runs counter to the principle of proportionality, which must be respected by private television broadcasters during election periods, as set out in section 66(2) of the LOREG. Consequently, that debate cannot be held under the terms indicated; instead, if the broadcaster so decides, it must be modified to comply with the requirements of that principle.”

III.      Proceedings before the Supreme Court

17.  On 12 June 2019 the applicant company lodged an administrative appeal with the Supreme Court against the CEC’s decision of 16 April 2019, and formalised the claim by means of written submissions dated 11 September 2019. In those written submissions, the company requested that the decision issued by the CEC be annulled as unlawful, and that section 8(2) of Instruction no. 4/2011 be declared null and void.

18.  In support of its above claims, the applicant company argued, firstly, that any restriction on the freedoms set out in Article 20 § 1 (d) of the Constitution had to meet strict requirements. The CEC’s decision, based on Instruction no. 4/2011, breached Articles 53 and 81 of the Constitution (see paragraphs 39 and 40 below). Section 8 of the Instruction, which was relevant to the present case, established substantive rules for debates organised by private media during the election period. While section 66(2) of the LOREG provided for only limited regulation, Instruction no. 4/2011 introduced a comprehensive framework, exceeding its remit by supplementing the principles of proportionality and neutrality in media coverage, and effectively imposing a single debate format based on previous election results. The applicant company noted that such limits had been expressly adopted by the legislature in other contexts, but not in relation to debates. The reference in section 66(2) to the CEC’s power to issue instructions did not authorise it to regulate such a matter independently, but only within constitutional limits and in respect of secondary aspects. However, Instruction no. 4/2011 imposed a significant restriction on freedom of information, thereby encroaching on a domain reserved for the legislature.

19.  The applicant company further argued that the CEC’s decision infringed Article 20 § 1 (a) and (d), Article 23 and Article 38 of the Constitution by restricting the essence of fundamental rights, preventing voters from receiving complete information and forcing partial reporting, which was particularly unjustified in a developing multi-party system. It submitted that the restriction lacked a legitimate aim and was disproportionate, and criticised the CEC for favouring established parties and creating barriers for new ones, contrary to equality. The applicant company maintained that organising a debate for candidates with strong national electoral prospects was reasonable, and argued that less restrictive measures were available, such as allowing the debate to take place and arranging for compensatory airtime. Lastly, it argued that the restriction was disproportionate, as it harmed the public interest by depriving citizens of relevant election information for no clear benefit.

20.  Vox stated that it intended to participate in the proceedings, but subsequently withdrew its complaint.

21.  On 25 February 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed the administrative appeal; it found that neither the decision of the CEC of 16 April 2019 nor Instruction no. 4/2011 (referred to in that decision) infringed the Constitution or the domestic laws.

22.  The Supreme Court held that the applicant could refer to the alleged unlawfulness of section 8(2) of the Instruction as grounds for seeking the annulment of the impugned decision of the CEC, and that the Supreme Court had jurisdiction to review and, where appropriate, annul a regulatory provision.

23.  The Supreme Court further reiterated that freedom of expression and the freedom to impart accurate information enjoyed overriding protection, including in the context of elections, even though such primacy was not unlimited. Rights set out in Article 23 of the Constitution (the right to participate in public affairs through freely elected representatives, see paragraph 38 below) placed restrictions on freedom of expression and the freedom to impart information. Those restrictions applied equally to both publicly and privately owned media. The principles applicable to private television broadcasters in particular, in respect of debates, interviews and reporting related to the election campaign, stemmed directly from section 66(2) of the LOREG and not Instruction no. 4/2011. Indeed, the impugned provision of the LOREG did not set out identical rules for public and private media. The difference lay in the fact that, in respect of public media, it assigned primary responsibility for ensuring compliance with the substantive limits to the relevant administrative bodies, whose decisions were subject to review by the CEC. As regards private media, it entrusted the CEC with issuing instructions in accordance with which those limits were to be respected.

24.  As regards the alleged prioritising of statutes over the constitutional provisions (Article 53 § 1 and Article 81 of the Constitution), the Supreme Court held that, as the CEC’s jurisdiction to review the decisions of private television broadcasters under section 66(2) of the LOREG was not in dispute, and as the relevant restrictions derived from that LOREG itself, any alleged breach of the constitutional provisions in question could arguably have resulted from only section 8(2) of Instruction no. 4/2011. However, no such violation could be discerned, as section 8(2) did not impose substantive restrictions on the exercise of the freedom to impart information. Rather, it affirmed the freedom of private broadcasters to decide whether to organise election debates and interviews, only requiring that, should they choose to do so, they take into account the results of the most recent equivalent elections. Instruction no. 4/2011 set down a criterion that was neither arbitrary nor novel, but instead derived from the LOREG itself, which employed it in several contexts. There was no explicit legislative provision in that regard, as private broadcasters were not obliged to organise debates or interviews, unlike other election-related obligations expressly regulated by law, such as making venues and airtime available to candidates and providing advance payments of subsidies to those entitled to them. In such cases, the LOREG used the criterion relating to the most recent equivalent elections. Moreover, “the variety of circumstances in which it [was] invoked suggest[ed] that this [was] the rule to be followed”. Accordingly, Instruction no. 4/2011 merely reflected a general rule already underlying the legislative framework and did not encroach upon matters reserved to statute.

25.  The Supreme Court further noted that, where a private broadcaster organised a debate limited to the two leading candidates from previous elections, it was required to provide compensatory airtime or alternative debates for “other political groups represented in those previous elections”. The same obligation applied, in the court’s view, in the present case: the obligation to provide such compensation stemmed from the right enshrined in the LOREG in favour of those parties that had secured representation in the previous equivalent elections. It followed that other parties had to be offered debates or airtime in order to compensate for their absence from the initial debate – a point which the applicant company did not dispute. Moreover, “nothing prevent[ed] the representatives of [parties] which [had] failed to secure seats in the previous elections from being added to those debates, provided that the opportunity [was] afforded to those which [had] secured [such seats]”. The Supreme Court emphasised that no single format was imposed, and that there was “sufficient flexibility” for private broadcasters.

26.  The Supreme Court found that the disputed provisions of Instruction no. 4/2011 were based on “the rule laid down by the Institutional Law [the LOREG]”. Reiterating that Instruction no. 4/2011 did not encroach upon matters reserved to the legislature, it further considered that it did not infringe Article 10 § 2 of the Convention, since it had a sufficient legal basis; pursued the aim of ensuring “accurate, pluralistic, complete and neutral information”, so that voters might decide freely; was appropriate and necessary for that purpose; and was not disproportionate, because it did not affect the content of the information but the manner in which it was communicated.

27.  As regards the applicant company’s proposed debate format, the Supreme Court held as follows:

“In contrast, [the applicant company’s proposal] does not ensure that people will be made aware of all the options; it disregards those who have already secured representation and gives preference to those who do not have it, on the basis of a prediction which may or may not materialise. It thus rests upon an unverified hypothesis as opposed to an effective reality. It therefore fails to have regard to the principles of safeguarding political pluralism and equality between the [candidates], [is] partial [and] is neither neutral nor proportionate. In short, it is not in accordance with the law for those reasons, not because there are no better solutions – there are. [The applicant company’s proposal] was insufficient in the light of section 66(2) of the [LOREG].”

28.  With regard to the governing principles applicable to private television broadcasters in the context of elections, the Supreme Court stated that “it [did] not appear objectionable to require private television channels to respect political pluralism [and] the principle[s] of equality, neutrality in media coverage and proportionality”. It clarified that proportionality served as a yardstick for assessing whether the other principles – in particular neutrality in media coverage – had been respected. The court further observed that section 66 of the LOREG was “of crystalline clarity”: public media and private television broadcasters alike were required to operate within the scope resulting from those principles.

29.  The Supreme Court considered that the applicant company had not challenged the restrictions flowing from those principles, and had constructed its entire argument without taking them into account. It concluded that Instruction no. 4/2011, which concerned only the manner in which debates were to be organised, did not curtail the material scope of the freedom to impart accurate information, since it merely articulated the way in which the above-mentioned principles – as chosen by the legislature itself – were to be made effective in election debates, while allowing sufficient flexibility for private broadcasters to organise such debates in accordance with their own interests. In the court’s assessment, none of this affected the essential content of the freedoms guaranteed by Article 20 of the Constitution; on the contrary, it was fundamental to ensuring that voters had at their disposal all the elements necessary to form their judgment.

30.  As regards the alleged discriminatory treatment of private television in comparison with the written press, radio and digital media, the Supreme Court held that section 66 of the LOREG clearly made private television broadcasters subject to the principles of political pluralism, equality, proportionality and neutrality in media coverage. In accordance with the same section, however, private radio stations were only subject to the principles of political pluralism and equality. That distinction was justified by the exceptional reach and influence inherent in the medium of television, and the powerful effect that images and sound had on public opinion. As regards the lack of equivalent regulation for digital media, the Supreme Court explained that by referring to the legislative context prevailing at the time of the enactment of the LOREG and the subsequent amendments to it. The Supreme Court noted, in this regard, that since television had not yet lost its primacy or communicative force, the regime established by section 66(2) of the LOREG continued to apply to private television broadcasters, without prejudice to any future regulation of new forms and channels of communication.

31.  Lastly, the Supreme Court noted that the changes in the political landscape resulting from the party system being transformed from a broadly bipolar configuration to a multi-party one did not call into question the legislature’s approach, as clarified by Instruction no. 4/2011. The increase in the number of participants in the election only reinforced the need to ensure that the coverage provided by the relevant television channels, including private broadcasters, extended to all of them. In particular, such coverage had to include those parties that had previously gained sufficient public support to secure representation without excluding new actors, regardless of whether they already qualified as significant political groups. The court concluded that neither the CEC’s decision nor Instruction no. 4/2011, on which the decision was based, was in breach of the LOREG or the Constitution.

IV.     Proceedings before the Constitutional Court

32.  On 5 April 2021 the applicant company lodged an amparo appeal based on Article 20 § 1 of the Constitution (the right to freedom of expression) in conjunction with Article 23 (the right to participate in public affairs through freely elected representatives), as well as Article 53 § 1 (judicial protection of fundamental rights) and Article 81 § 1 (the definition of institutional laws and the requirement of an absolute majority for their adoption).

33.  On 27 March 2023 the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible on the grounds that there had clearly been no violation of a fundamental right protectable in amparo proceedings.

V.     Other developments

34.  On 22 April 2019 the public television channel TVE held debates in which the candidates from PP, PSOE, UP and Ciudadanos participated.

35.  Following the CEC’s decision, the applicant company held the planned debate on 23 April 2019 but withdrew Vox’s invitation to participate. The debate was held with the participation of the PP, PSOE, UP and Ciudadanos candidates and broadcast on two television channels belonging to the applicant company (Antena 3 and La Sexta) and on its radio network called Onda Cero; the debate was also available on its Atresplayer digital platform.

36.  Vox obtained 10.26% of the votes in the general elections of 28 April 2019 and secured parliamentary representation. As the political parties were unable to form a government following the elections, Parliament was dissolved and new elections were called, to take place on 10 November 2019. During the election campaign prior to those elections, the applicant company organised and broadcast through its private channel, La Sexta, a debate involving the participation of candidates for the office of Prime Minister (the President of the Government) who represented the eight parties with the largest representation in Congress, including Vox.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Relevant domestic Law

A.   The Constitution of Spain

37.  Under Article 20 § 1 (a) and (d) of the Constitution, the right to freely express and disseminate thoughts, ideas and opinions through words, in writing or by any other means of communication, and the right to freely communicate or receive accurate information by any means of dissemination are recognised and protected.

38.  Under Article 23 § 1 of the Constitution, citizens have the right to participate in public affairs directly or through representatives freely elected in periodic elections by universal suffrage.

39.  Under Article 53 of the Constitution, rights and liberties recognised in the Constitution are binding on all public authorities. The exercise of such rights and liberties may be regulated only by law, which shall, in any case, respect their essential content.

40.  Under Article 81 of the Constitution, institutional laws are those relating to the development of fundamental rights and public liberties, those which establish Statutes of Autonomy and the general electoral system, and other laws provided for in the Constitution.

B.   Institutional Law no. 5/1985 of 19 June 1985 on the General Electoral System (“the LOREG”)

41.  According to the Preamble of the LOREG, in a democratic State, an electoral system must guarantee the free expression of popular sovereignty as its core element. This generic freedom is accompanied by a range of other freedoms, including freedom of expression, information, assembly and association.

42.  Under section 9 of the LOREG, the CEC is a permanent body composed of eight judges of the Supreme Court appointed by the General Council of the Judiciary and five active professors of law, political science or sociology appointed at the joint proposal of the parties, federations, coalitions or groups of electors represented in the Congress of Deputies (section 9(1)). Appointments are made within 90 days of the inaugural sitting of the Congress of Deputies. Where no proposal is made within that time-limit, the Bureau of the Congress of Deputies, having consulted the political groups present in the Chamber, will proceed to make an appointment, taking into account the existing representation therein (section 9(2)). CEC members are appointed by Royal Decree and remain in office until the new CEC takes up its duties at the start of the next parliamentary term (section 9(3)).

43.  The CEC is competent to decide on complaints, claims and challenges addressed to it in accordance with the LOREG or other domestic provisions giving it such jurisdiction (section 19(h)); to unify the interpretative criteria of the Electoral Commissions, the Provincial Commissions and, where appropriate, the Electoral Commissions of the Autonomous Communities, in the implementation of electoral regulations (section 19(f)); and to address infringements of the electoral process, provided they do not constitute a criminal offence, and impose fines up to the maximum amount provided for in the LOREG (section 19(k)).

44.  Section 66 of the Law reads as follows:

“1. Respect for political and social pluralism, as well as equality, proportionality and neutrality in media coverage in the programming of publicly‑owned media during the election period, shall be guaranteed by the organisation of [such] media and by their oversight as provided for in the law. The decisions of the administrative bodies of the above-mentioned media during the indicated election period may be challenged before the competent electoral commission in accordance with the provisions of the previous section, and in accordance with the procedure established by the Central Electoral Commission.

2.  During the election period, privately‑owned broadcasters must respect the principles of pluralism and equality. Likewise, during that period, private television stations must also respect the principles of proportionality and neutrality in media coverage in election debates and interviews, as well as in information relating to the election campaign, in accordance with the instructions issued for this purpose by the competent electoral commission.”

45.  Under section 153 of the LOREG, any infringement of the mandatory rules set out by that Law which does not constitute a criminal offence is punishable by the competent electoral commission. Fines range from 300 to 3,000 euros (EUR) for authorities or civil servants, and from EUR 100 to 1,000 for private individuals (por particulares).

C.   Instruction no. 4/2011 of 24 March 2011 of the CEC

46.  According to the Preamble to Instruction no. 4/2011 of 24 March 2011, issued by the CEC, on the interpretation of section 66 of Institutional Law no. 5/1985 on the General Electoral System with regard to the guarantees of the media’s respect for the principles of pluralism, equality, proportionality and neutrality in media coverage during the election period, that instrument replaced the previous Instruction of 1999 in the light of changing circumstances. Such circumstances included, in particular, the 2010 reform of the audiovisual sector, which resulted in the expansion of digital television and privately owned channels, and the amendment of section 66 of the LOREG. Under the amended provision, during the election period, private broadcasters were required to respect the principles of pluralism, equality, proportionality and neutrality in media coverage. The CEC was entrusted with issuing instructions defining the scope of those obligations. As regards the duty incumbent on privately owned media to comply with the principles of proportionality and neutrality in media coverage, the CEC emphasised that its “unequivocal legal mandate” in that regard had to be reconciled with fundamental rights, namely the right to freedom of expression and to disseminate ideas and opinions, and the right to freely communicate and receive accurate information (Article 20 of the Constitution), and freedom of enterprise within the framework of a market economy (Article 38 of the Constitution). Accordingly, the CEC differentiated between public and private media and adapted the Instruction of 1999 (which originally applied to publicly owned broadcasters) to privately owned television channels.

47.  The relevant parts of Instruction no. 4/2011 read as follows:

[Section 4]. Plans for media coverage of the election campaign

“...

2.2  Plans for media coverage must include the [candidates] of those political forces which did not stand in the previous equivalent elections or did not secure representation in them, and which possess the status of a significant political group. Such coverage may not be equal to or greater than that afforded to the [candidates] who secured representation.

2.3  The status of significant political group shall be granted to those political formations standing in the elections in question which, despite not having stood in the previous equivalent elections or not having secured representation in them, have subsequently, in recent electoral processes and within the territorial scope of the media outlet, obtained a number of votes equal to or greater than 5% of the valid votes cast.

In the case of electoral coalitions, these may only be regarded as a significant political group if any of the political parties comprising them meets, on its own, the requirement laid down in the preceding subsection.

2.4  Media coverage of [candidates] from political formations which did not stand in the previous equivalent elections or which did not obtain representation in [those elections] may not be equal to or greater than that given to those which are recognised as a significant political group.

...”

[Section 7]. Principles to be upheld by privately owned radio and television broadcasters

“1.  During election periods, the management bodies of privately owned radio and television broadcasters shall guarantee respect for the principles of pluralism and equality, as provided for in section 66(2) of the LOREG.

2.  In particular, during the election period, private television channels shall also respect the principles of proportionality and neutrality in media coverage in election debates and interviews, as well as in the information relating to the election campaign which they decide to broadcast, as established in the above-mentioned section 66(2) of the LOREG.”

[Section 8]. The principle of proportionality that must be guaranteed by private television channels

“1.  The information specifically devoted to the election campaign that private television channels decide to broadcast shall comply not only with the principles of pluralism, equality and neutrality in media coverage, but also with the principle of proportionality, understood in the sense that such [coverage] shall give preferential consideration to the results obtained by each political formation in the most recent equivalent elections, without this criterion preventing the provision of other information regarding those [candidates] who did not stand or did not secure representation in the most recent elections. In any case, th[is] latter [group of candidates] may not receive greater media coverage than the political formations that secured representation in the most recent elections.

2.  It is for the management bodies of private television channels to decide freely whether to organise or broadcast election interviews or debates; however, if they do so, they must take particular account of the results obtained by each political formation in the most recent equivalent elections.

In the event that a media outlet decides to broadcast a debate between the two candidates who received the highest number of votes in the most recent equivalent elections, it shall broadcast other bilateral or multilateral debates, or provide sufficient compensatory airtime for the other candidates who also secured representation in the most recent equivalent elections.”

[Section 9]. Challenges to broadcasts and programmes aired by privately owned radio and television broadcasters

“During election periods, broadcasts and programmes aired by privately owned broadcasters which have an impact on the election may be challenged before the competent electoral commissions, in accordance with the provisions of section six of this Instruction, subject to the following specific provisions:

(a) challenges to broadcasts and programmes aired by privately owned radio broadcasters may only be based on a breach of the principles of pluralism and equality;

(b) challenges to broadcasts and programmes aired by privately owned television broadcasters may only be based on a breach of the principles of pluralism and equality, unless they concern election interviews and debates, or specific information regarding the election campaign, in which case they may also be based on a breach of the principles of neutrality in media coverage and proportionality.”

II.      the Council of Europe

A.   The Committee of Ministers

48.  In Recommendation No. R(99)15 of the Committee of Ministers to member States on measures concerning media coverage of election campaigns, adopted on 9 September 1999, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe stressed that the fundamental principle of editorial independence of the media assumed special importance in election periods. It highlighted its awareness of the need to take account of the significant differences which existed between print and broadcast media, and emphasised that the coverage of elections by broadcast media should be fair, balanced and impartial. It further acknowledged that any regulatory framework on the coverage of elections should respect the fundamental principle of freedom of expression protected under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, as interpreted by the Court. According to the Appendix to the Recommendation, during election campaigns, regulatory frameworks should encourage and facilitate the pluralistic expression of opinions via broadcast media. With due respect for the editorial independence of broadcasters, regulatory frameworks should also provide for the obligation to cover election campaigns in a fair, balanced and impartial manner in the overall programme services of broadcasters. Such an obligation should apply to both public service broadcasters and private broadcasters in their relevant transmission areas (section II.1 of the Appendix). Where self-regulation did not provide for this, member States should adopt measures whereby public and private broadcasters, during the election period, should in particular be fair, balanced and impartial in their news and current affairs programmes, including discussion programmes such as interviews or debates (section II.2 of the Appendix).

49.  According to Recommendation CM/Rec(2007)15 of the Committee of Ministers to member States on measures concerning media coverage of election campaigns (adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 7 November 2007 at the 1010th meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies), regulatory frameworks on media coverage of elections should respect the editorial independence of the media. Member States should ensure that there is an effective and manifest separation between the exercise of control of media and decision-making as regards media content and the exercise of political authority or influence (Principles, § I.3).

B.   The European Commission for Democracy through Law

50.  At its 51st and 52nd sessions on 5-6 July and 18-19 October 2002, the European Commission for Democracy through Law (Venice Commission) adopted its guidelines on elections and an explanatory report (CDL-AD(2002)023). Together, these two documents make up the Code of Good Practice in Electoral Matters, which was approved in 2003 by the Parliamentary Assembly and the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe. The relevant parts of the guidelines read as follows:

2.3. Equality of opportunity

“a. Equality of opportunity must be guaranteed for parties and candidates alike. This entails a neutral attitude by state authorities, in particular with regard to:

i. the election campaign;

ii. coverage by the media, in particular by the publicly owned media;

iii. public funding of parties and campaigns.

b. Depending on the subject matter, equality may be strict or proportional. If it is strict, political parties are treated on an equal footing irrespective of their current parliamentary strength or support among the electorate. If it is proportional, political parties must be treated according to the results achieved in the elections. Equality of opportunity applies in particular to radio and television airtime, public funds and other forms of backing.

c. In conformity with freedom of expression, legal provision should be made to ensure that there is a minimum access to privately owned audiovisual media, with regard to the election campaign and to advertising, for all participants in elections.

d. Political party, candidates and election campaign funding must be transparent.

e. The principle of equality of opportunity can, in certain cases, lead to a limitation of political party spending, especially on advertising.”

51.  The explanatory report, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:

“Equality of opportunity should be ensured between parties and candidates and should prompt the state to be impartial towards them and to apply the same law uniformly to all. In particular, the neutrality requirement applies to the electoral campaign and coverage by the media, especially the publicly owned media, as well as to public funding of parties and campaigns. This means that there are two possible interpretations of equality: either ‘strict’ equality or ‘proportional’ equality. ‘Strict’ equality means that the political parties are treated without regard to their present strength in parliament or among the electorate. It must apply to the use of public facilities for electioneering purposes (for example bill posting, postal services and similar, public demonstrations, public meeting rooms). ‘Proportional’ equality implies that the treatment of political parties is in proportion to the number of votes. Equality of opportunity (strict and/or proportional) applies in particular to radio and television airtime, public funds and other forms of backing. Certain forms of backing may on the one hand be submitted to strict equality and on the other hand to proportional equality.

The basic idea is that the main political forces should be able to voice their opinions in the main organs of the country’s media and that all the political forces should be allowed to hold meetings, including on public thoroughfares, distribute literature and exercise their right to post bills. All of these rights must be clearly regulated, with due respect for freedom of expression, and any failure to observe them, either by the authorities or by the campaign participants, should be subject to appropriate sanctions.

...

The most important thing is to draw up a list of the media organisations in each country and to make sure that the candidates or parties are accorded sufficiently balanced amounts of airtime or advertising space, including on state radio and television stations. In conformity with freedom of expression, legal provision should be made to ensure that there is a minimum access to privately owned audiovisual media, with regard to the election campaign and to advertising, for all participants in elections.”

C.   The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe

52.  According to Resolution 2254 (2019) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, entitled “Media freedom as a condition for democratic elections”, free elections are a pillar of every democratic society, and the electorate cannot be said to have genuine freedom of choice if that choice is not a well-informed one. Consequently, the right to freedom of information and media freedom are essential preconditions of the right to free elections, in accordance with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The media must be free to inform the public, without being subject to any political, economic or other pressure, and with due regard for professional ethics. The professional media are subject to various obligations designed to ensure balanced and impartial coverage of elections and the fair participation of all candidates and political parties in the election process.

case_name: CASE OF OCAK AND OTHERS v. TÜRKİYE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF OCAK AND OTHERS v. TÜRKİYE

(Applications nos. 54358/19 and 25 others –

see appended list)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

13 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Ocak and Others v. Türkiye,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Péter Paczolay, President,
Gediminas Sagatys,
Stéphane Pisani, judges,
and Dorothee von Arnim, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the applications against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by the Turkish nationals listed in the appended table (“the applicants”), on the various dates indicated therein;

the decision to give notice of the complaints under Article 5 of the Convention concerning the alleged lack of reasonable suspicion regarding the commission of an offence, the alleged lack of relevant and sufficient reasons when ordering and extending the applicants’ pre‑trial detention, the length of the pre‑trial detention and the alleged ineffectiveness of the judicial review of the lawfulness of detention to the Turkish Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent at the time, Mr Hacı Ali Açıkgül, former Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye, and to declare the remainder of the applications inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the examination of the applications by a Committee;

Having deliberated in private on 22 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The present applications mainly concern the arrest and pre-trial detention of the applicants in the aftermath of the attempted coup d’état of 15 July 2016 on suspicion of their membership of an organisation described by the Turkish authorities as the “Fetullahist Terror Organisation/Parallel State Structure” (Fetullahçı Terör Örgütü/Paralel Devlet Yapılanması; hereinafter “FETÖ/PDY”), which was considered by the authorities to be behind the attempted coup d’état of 15 July 2016 (further information regarding the events that unfolded after the coup attempt, including the details of the state of emergency declared by the Turkish government between 21 July 2016 and 18 July 2018, and the ensuing notice of derogation given to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe, may be found in Baş v. Turkey, no. 66448/17, §§ 6‑14 and 109‑10, 3 March 2020).

2.  On various dates the applicants were arrested and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY, an offence punishable under Article 314 of the Criminal Code (see Baş, cited above, § 58). Challenges brought by them against their detention were dismissed, including by the Constitutional Court.

3.  On various dates in the course of the ensuing criminal investigations and trials the competent judicial authorities ordered the applicants’ continued detention. The applicants were held in custody for periods of up to 11 months and 10 days.

4.  It is apparent from the information and documents in the case files that, when ordering and extending the applicants’ pre-trial detention, the competent judicial authorities relied on various evidential grounds, including but not limited to: (a) witness statements alleging that the applicants had taken an active part in the hierarchical structure of the FETÖ/PDY; (b) possession of pro-FETÖ/PDY publications; (c) working in, or being a member of, institutions with ties to the organisation in question or an organisation shut down by the state‑of‑emergency legislative decrees; (d) provision of financial support to FETÖ/PDY or to institutions with ties to FETÖ/PDY; (e) attending or holding meetings (sohbet); (f) communication with senior members of the organisation; (g) ensuring communication among FETÖ/PDY members; (h) using the ByLock encrypted messaging application; (i) staying in FETÖ/PDY houses; and (j) carrying out various other activities on the orders of the organisation.

5.  It is further apparent from material in the case files that, in accordance with Articles 100 and 101 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (for the text of those provisions, see Kavala v. Turkey, no. 28749/18, §§ 71-72, 10 December 2019), the competent judicial authorities mainly justified their decisions to deprive the applicants of their liberty not only on the basis of the existence of reasonable suspicion, but also on grounds of the nature and severity of the alleged offence of membership of an illegal armed organisation and the fact that that offence was among the “catalogue” offences listed in Article 100 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Without making an individualised assessment, they also relied on the state of the evidence and the risk of the applicants’ absconding and tampering with evidence, and considered that detention would be a proportionate measure in the circumstances. Moreover, in the later stages of the proceedings, the competent judges took into account the time spent by the applicants in pre‑trial detention when deciding to extend their detention, without explaining the relevance of that factor to their decision.

6.  The applicants’ detention was periodically reviewed by the competent courts, either on requests for their release or during regular monthly reviews under Article 108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In their subsequent decisions extending the applicants’ detention, the domestic courts largely reiterated the reasoning contained in the initial detention order. They considered that alternative measures would not be sufficient to ensure the proper conduct of the proceedings.

7.  In the meantime, the applicants lodged one or more individual applications with the Constitutional Court in respect of the detention orders, complaining of, inter alia, an alleged lack of reasonable suspicion that they had committed an offence and an alleged lack of reasons to justify the decisions ordering and extending their pre-trial detention, which were declared inadmissible by the Constitutional Court in summary fashion.

8.  According to the latest information provided by the parties, most of the applicants were convicted of membership of an illegal armed organisation by the courts of first instance on the basis of evidence that was present at the time of their detention or that appeared at a later stage in the proceedings. It is further apparent that some of the criminal proceedings are still pending before the appellate courts or the Constitutional Court.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Türkiye of Article 5 (Right to liberty and security) concerning Reasonableness of pre-trial detention in this case

case_name: CASE OF DEVEKOM DOO  NIŠ v. SERBIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF DEVEKOM DOO NIŠ v. SERBIA

(Application no. 16947/22)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

13 October 2026









This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of Devekom DOO Niš v. Serbia,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Ioannis Ktistakis, President,
Peeter Roosma,
Lətif Hüseynov,
Diana Kovatcheva,
Úna Ní Raifeartaigh,
Mateja Đurović,
Canòlic Mingorance Cairat, judges,
and Milan Blaško, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 16947/22) against the Republic of Serbia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Devekom DOO Niš (“the applicant company”), a company registered in Serbia, on 31 March 2022;

the decision to give notice to the Serbian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint concerning the applicant company’s right to peaceful enjoyment of its possessions and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 22 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The present case concerns the applicant company’s right to peaceful enjoyment of its possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant company complains, in particular, that it had to bear an excessive burden because the customs authorities refunded customs duties paid by it only after a considerable period of time and without interest.

THE FACTS
THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

2.  The applicant company is registered in Niš, Serbia. It was represented by Mr N. Stanković, a lawyer practising in Niš.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Z. Jadrijević Mladar.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

5.  In 2006, the applicant company imported goods from Bosnia and Herzegovina and from Croatia under a preferential customs regime, without payment of customs duties (uvozne dažbine), in accordance with the relevant domestic legislation and international agreements duly ratified and in force at the material time. The Niš Customs Office (hereinafter “the first-instance customs authority”) issued following declarations (deklaracije) in that regard: JCI UV4 1071 of 2 March 2006, JCI UV4 2469 of 3 May 2006, JCI UV4 2751 of 15 May 2006, JCI UV4 3185 of 31 May 2006, JCI UV4 3393 of 30 June 2006, JCI UV4 4170 of 7 July 2006, JCI UV4 4591 of 27 July 2006, JCI UV4 5500 of 30 August 2006, JCI UV4 6282 of 28 September 2006, JCI UV4 6600 of 11 October 2006 and JCI UV4 7035 of 26 October 2006.

6.  In 2009 the first-instance customs authority began, on its own initiative, a post-clearance check (naknadna kontrola deklaracija) of the above-mentioned declarations and found that the preferential treatment should not have been applied, concluding that the imports in question had not met the conditions required for the granting of preferential origin. They therefore ordered the applicant company, in twelve sets of proceedings, to pay customs duties on the imported goods. In particular, the first-instance customs authority issued the following decisions: nos. 02/6 UP/I-1595/2009 of 30 October 2009; 02/4 UP/I-1596/2009 of 30 October 2009; 02/1 UP/I-1597/2009 of 30 October 2009; 02/6 UP/I-1598/2009 of 30 October 2009; 02/6 UP/I-1603/2009 of 5 November 2009; 02/1 UP/I-1604/2009 of 5 November 2009; 02/1 UP/I-1605/2009 of 5 November 2009; 02/1 UP/I-1606/2009 of 5 November 2009; 02/6 UP/I-1599/2009 of 10 November 2009; 02/6 UP/I-1600/2009 of 11 November 2009; 02/6 UP/I-1601/2009 of 11 November 2009 and 02/6 UP/I-1602/2009 of 11 November 2009.

7.  The applicant company appealed against those decisions, but since the appeal did not have suspensive effect it had to pay the amounts due immediately. The sum of 7,381,148 Serbian dinars (RSD – approximately 78,360 euros (EUR) at the time) was therefore collected.

8.  After several remittals of the case, the customs authorities decided that the goods imported by the applicant company were not subject to customs duties, ordered that the amount paid in that respect be refunded to the applicant company and dismissed its claim for interest on that amount. That conclusion was contained in the following decisions, given on 13 November 2018, of the first-instance customs authority: nos. 04/7 UP/I-8666/2018; 04/7 UP/I-8667/2018; 04/7 UP/I-8668/2018; 04/7 UP/I-8669/2018; 04/7 UP/I-8670/2018; 04/7 UP/I-8671/2018; 04/7 UP/I-9021/2018; 04/7 UP/I-9022/2018; 04/7 UP/I-9049/2018; 04/7 UP/I-9050/2018; 04/7 UP/I-9051/2018 and 04/7 UP/I-9052/2018.

9.   The applicant company appealed against the fact that it had not been awarded interest, but between 6 June and 16 July 2019 all the decisions were upheld by the relevant department of the Ministry of Finance, specifically the Department for Second-Instance Customs Procedure within the Sector for Second-Instance Tax and Customs Procedure (hereinafter “the second‑instance customs authority”). In particular, the second‑instance customs authority issued following decisions: nos. 483-00-51/2019-39 of 6 June 2019; 483-00-52/2019-39 from 6 June 2019; 483-00-54/2019-39 of 6 June 2019; 483-00-55/2019-39 of 6 June 2019; 483-00-59/2019-39 of 6 June 2019; 483-00-60/2019-39 of 6 June 2019; 483-00-61/2019-39 of 6 June 2019; 483-00-56/2019-39 of 10 June 2019; 483-00-58/2019-39 of 10 June 2019; 483-00-53/2019-39 of 12 June 2019; 483-00-62/2019-39 of 12 June 2019 and 483-00-57/2019-39 of 16 July 2019.

10.  In the period from 29 July to 29 August 2019 the exact amount paid by the applicant company in respect of customs duties was refunded to it. The refunds thus totalled RSD 7,381,148 (approximately EUR 62,671 at the time).

11.  The applicant company brought actions with the Administrative Court (Upravni sud) against the above-mentioned decisions of the customs authorities. The court dismissed the applicant company’s claims and upheld the disputed decisions. In particular, the Administrative Court – Niš Division issued the following judgments: nos. 11-3 U. 12252/19 of 20 May 2021; 11-1 U. 12253/19 of 3 June 2021; 11-2 U. 13134/19 of 16 September 2021; II-3 U. 12186/19 of 8 April 2021; 11-5 U. 12192/19 of 27 May 2021; 11-5 U. 12195/19 of 27 May 2021; 11-5 U. 12251/19 of 27 May 2021; 11-9 U. 12254/19 of 25 October 2021; II-3 U. 12198/19 of 20 May 2021; 11-8 U.12197/19 of 4 June 2021; II-4 U. 12182/19 of 27 May 2021; and II-7 U.12181/19 of 4 June 2021.

12.  Dissatisfied with the excessive duration and outcome of the customs proceedings and the proceedings before the Administrative Court, the applicant company lodged constitutional appeals (ustavna žalba) in that connection with the Constitutional Court (Ustavni sud). By decisions of 14 October 2021 and 24 February 2022, the Constitutional Court found that the length of the customs proceedings had been excessive and awarded EUR 3,600 in total to the applicant company for non-pecuniary damage in that respect. The Constitutional Court dismissed the company’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, which concerned the non‑payment of interest, stating that it had failed to invoke any constitutionally-related grounds under Article 58 of the Constitution and, therefore, the criteria for the opening of the proceedings had not been met. The Constitutional Court further held that the contested judgments contained sufficient reasoning explaining why the applicant company’s claims were dismissed as unfounded, and that a proper conclusion regarding the factual circumstances had been drawn from the established facts.

OTHER RELEVANT FACTS
Reasoning of the second-instance customs authority

13.  All of second-instance decisions contain almost identical reasoning because of the adoption of the same legal position in all of the proceedings. The reasoning provided in decision no. 483-00-58/2019-39 of 10 June 2019 can be taken as representative. That decision stated, inter alia, the following:

“Pursuant to Article 278 § 1 of the Customs Act (Official Gazette of the RS, nos. 18/10, 111/12, 29/15, 108/16), where the customs authority refunds a customs debt [paid by a taxpayer], including any interest or default interest charged at the time of payment of that debt, the customs authority shall not pay interest. However, paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that, by way of exception to [the rule in] paragraph 1, the customs authority shall, in accordance with Article 269 § 1 of the Act, pay interest where the decision approving the request for a refund has not been implemented within three months from the date of its adoption. Having regard to the aforementioned provisions, as well as to the fact that the issue of interest following the approved refund of paid customs debt does not constitute a customs procedure within the meaning of Article 5 § 1 item 14 of the Customs Act (Official Gazette of the RS, nos. 18/10, 111/12, 29/15, 108/16), and bearing in mind that Article 308 of the said Act prescribes that customs procedures initiated prior to the entry into force of that Act shall be completed in accordance with the regulations applicable until the date of its entry into force, it cannot be considered that a customs procedure has been initiated. For this reason, the issue of interest cannot be addressed within the meaning of Article 237 of the former Customs Act (Official Gazette of the RS, nos. 73/03, 61/05, 85/05, 62/06 and 9/10). This position has also been adopted by the Administrative Court, Niš Department, in its decision II-I U. 16603/12 of 22 August 2013. Therefore, the appellant may submit a request for the payment of interest only in cases where the decision approving the request for a refund has not been implemented within three months from the date of its adoption. Such a request would be subject to a separate administrative matter to be decided upon in accordance with Article 178 of the Customs Act (Official Gazette of the RS, nos. 18/10, 111/12, 29/15, 108/16). For these reasons, the issue of payment of interest under Article 278 of the aforementioned Act could not have been addressed by the contested decision.”

The inflation rate in Serbia during the relevant period (2009-2019)

14.  Based on the report of the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia of 12 May 2025, in the period from 2009 to 2019 inflation amounted to 69.6%.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
The Constitution of the Republic of Serbia (Ustav Republike Srbije; published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia (“OG RS”) no. 98⁄06)

15.  Article 58 of the Constitution guarantees the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and other property rights acquired by law. The “right to property” (pravo na imovinu) may be revoked or restricted only in the public interest (as established by the law) and in return for compensation, which cannot amount to less than the market value. The law may restrict the manner in which property is used. Seizure or restriction of property to collect taxes or other levies or fines shall be permitted only in accordance with law.

THE CUSTOMS ACT (CARINSKI ZAKON; published in OG RS nos. 73/03, 61/05, 85/05, 62/06 and 9/10) in force from 1 January 2004 to 2 may 2010

16.  Article 24 of the Customs Act, in force from 1 January 2004 to 2 May 2010, provided that an appeal (žalba) could be lodged with the Appeals Committee of the Customs Administration against a first‑instance decision taken by a customs authority in administrative proceedings. Such an appeal did not suspend the enforcement of the decision.

17.  Article 25 provided that a second‑instance decision given in administrative proceedings could, in accordance with the provisions of the Administrative Disputes Act, be challenged in an administrative dispute (upravni spor) before the competent court.

18.  Article 105 §§ 1 to 7 regulated the customs declarations post and clearance check procedure. It provided that the customs authority could conduct a post‑clearance check of the declaration after the goods had been released, including verification of the accuracy of the information and examination of commercial documents. If it was established that the declaration was based on incorrect or incomplete data, the authority had to take corrective measures to ensure proper application of customs regulations. All such audits and measures could be carried out within a five‑year period from the date the declaration had been accepted.

19.  Article 231 § 2 prescribed that compound interest (kamata) had to be calculated and paid starting from the due date, at a rate equal to the annual discount rate of the central bank of issue, increased by 15 percentage points.

20.  Article 237 prescribed that if the customs authority repaid an amount of import duties, including credit interest and interest on arrears collected on payment of that debt, it had to calculate and pay interest on the repaid amount from the date of collection of the duties to the date of repayment.

THE CUSTOMS ACT (CARINSKI ZAKON; published in OG RS nos. 18/10, 101/12, 29/15, 108/16 and 113/17) in force from 3 May 2010 to 17 june 2019

21.  Article 254 of the Customs Act in force from 3 May 2010 to 17 June 2019 defined repayment as the total or partial refund of a customs debt which had been paid.

22.  Article 269 prescribed that, where the amount of the customs debt has not been paid within the prescribed period, the customs authority had to apply simple interest on the amount of the debt from the due date, at a rate equal to the annual discount rate of National Bank of Serbia, increased by 10 percentage points.

23.  Article 273 § 1 prescribed that, should it be established that a paid customs debt had not been legally owed, the amount unlawfully collected had to be repaid. Article 273 §§ 4 and 5 prescribed that the customs authority could grant such repayment upon receipt of an application submitted by the person or legal person concerned, or on its own initiative.

24.  Article 278 § 1 provided that repayment by the customs authority of customs debts paid to it, including credit interest and interest on arrears collected on payment of such debt, should not give rise to the payment of interest by the customs authority. Article 278 § 2 provided that, notwithstanding paragraph 1 of that provision, interest had to be paid in accordance with provisions of Article 269 § 1 of the Act where a decision to grant a request for repayment was not implemented within three months from the date the decision was issued.

25.  Article 308 provided that customs procedures initiated before the date of entry into force of the new Act had to be completed in accordance with the regulations that were in force until the date of its entry into force.

ADMINISTRATIVE DISPUTES ACT (ZAKON O UPRAVNIM SPOROVIMA; PUBLISHED IN OG RS No. 111/09)

26.  Article 4 of the Administrative Disputes Act provides that an administrative act is an individual legal act by which the competent public authority, by direct application of the regulations, decides on a certain right or obligation of a natural or legal person, that is, another party to the administrative matter.

27.  Article 11 § 1 provides that a natural, legal or other person can bring an administrative dispute before a court of law if it is believed that that person’s rights or interests, based on the law, have been violated by an administrative act.

OBLIGATIONS ACT (ZAKON O PARNIČNOM POSTUPKU; published in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia nos. 29/78, 39/85, 45/89, and 57/89, the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia no. 31/93, and OG RS no. 18/20)

28.  Article 154 of the Obligations Act defines different grounds for claiming civil compensation.

29.  Article 172 § 1 provides that a legal entity is liable for any damage caused by one of “its own bodies”.

30.  Article 210 establishes liability for unjust enrichment.

31.  Article 214 defines the consequences of unjust enrichment.

DOMESTIC CASE-LAW REFERRED TO BY THE GOVERNMENT

32.  The Government provided the Court with one decision given by the Commercial Court in Belgrade (Privredni sud u Beogradu) and one decision given by the Commercial Court in Niš (Privredni sud u Nišu) in civil proceedings for compensation in which the claimants had been successful in their claims for interest on overpaid amounts of customs duties.

33.  In judgment P. 101/19 of 12 March 2019, the Commercial Court in Belgrade examined a situation in which the claimant company had been ordered by the first-instance customs authority, on 8 November 2011, to pay import duties and other duties, which have been collected through enforcement proceedings. Following an appeal, the second-instance customs authority established that the previously charged amounts had been unlawfully collected and ordered a reimbursement of the nominal sum, but without interest. In the ensuing civil proceedings, the claimant sought statutory default interest for the period from the date of payment to the date of reimbursement of the overpaid amount, the return of the portion of the payment that had not been reimbursed, as well as lost profits, relying on the provisions of the Law on Obligations governing compensation of damage and unjust enrichment. The court held that, under the applicable legal framework, a party who had been required to pay undue customs was entitled to interest for the period from the date of payment to the date of reimbursement of the overpaid amount. This judgement was upheld by the Supreme Court of Cassation on 3 February 2022.

34.  In judgment P. 187/20 of 29 October 2020, the Commercial Court in Niš examined a situation in which the claimant company had been ordered by the first-instance customs authority, on 28 September 2017, to pay excise duty and value added tax, which have been collected through enforcement proceedings. Following an appeal, the second-instance customs authority annulled the abovementioned decision on the ground that the company had not been given the opportunity to comment on the expert opinion relied upon in the customs procedure. In the ensuing civil proceedings, the claimant sought the return of the previously collected amounts relying on the provisions of the Law on Obligations governing unjust enrichment, as well as statutory default interest from the date the claim was filed. The court held that the claimant was entitled to reimbursement of the unlawfully collected sums together with statutory default interest from the date the claim was filed. That judgement was upheld by the Commercial Court of Appeal on 26 April 2023.
target_provision: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property)
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Serbia of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property) concerning Peaceful enjoyment of possessions in this case

case_name: CASE OF HOXHA AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF HOXHA AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA

(Application no. 5805/23)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

13 October 2026





This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Hoxha and Others v. Albania,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Diana Kovatcheva, President,
Darian Pavli,
Vasilka Sancin, judges,
and Olga Chernishova, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 5805/23) against the Republic of Albania lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 31 January 2023 by ten Albanian nationals (“the applicants”), whose relevant details are listed in the appended table, and who were represented by Mr E. Syziu, a lawyer practising in Tirana;

the decision to give notice of the complaint concerning access to a court to the Albanian Government (“the Government”), represented by Mr O. Moçka, General State Advocate;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 22 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

1.  The case concerns an alleged violation of the applicants’ right of access to the Supreme Court.

2.  On 2 September 1995 the Commission for the Restitution and Compensation of Property (“the Commission”) recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights on a plot measuring 5,878 sq. m situated in Tirana. It decided to restore part of that plot measuring 2,999.6 sq. m and to award compensation for 2,501.4 sq. m in one of the ways provided for by law. It further awarded the applicants the right to first refusal of a plot of 615 sq.m. In 1996 the title to the restored property was entered in the land register. The reasoning of the 1995 Commission decision expressly stated that the property had an actual surface area of 7,600 sq. m.

3.  On 12 September 2007 the Immovable Property Registration Office of Tirana (“the IPRO”) informed the applicants that because of an inconsistency between the plot restored under the decision and the accompanying map, it was unable to take any further action in respect of their property. On 12 March 2008 the applicants requested the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property (“the Agency” - the successor of the Commission) to correct that inconsistency.

4.  On 18 March 2008 the Agency informed the applicants that they should submit a request for the correction of the Commission’s decision to the Agency’s Regional Office for the Restitution and Compensation of Property (“the regional office”) in accordance with Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure.

5.  On 4 April 2008 the applicants submitted a request to the regional office for the rectification of the 1995 decision. On 14 November 2008 the regional office dismissed that request for lack of jurisdiction. It also indicated that under section 18 of the Property Act, the power to amend the Commission’s decision of 1995 rested with the Agency.

6.  On 25 November 2008 the applicants addressed the Agency’s central office (“the central office”), seeking the correction of the 1995 Commission’s decision. The proceedings before it lasted for more than three years because they were suspended pending the Constitutional Court’s decisions of 2010 and 2011 (see paragraph 15 below).

7.  On 7 November 2011 the Agency held that the Commission’s decisions were no longer subject to administrative review because the Agency lacked jurisdiction, as those decisions were considered quasi-judicial. It further noted that the 2008 decision of the regional office had been lawful, since at the time the request was lodged, the Agency’s central office had had the power to review decisions of former commissions. However, that jurisdiction had been removed following a ruling of the Constitutional Court in 2010.

8.  Following that response, the applicants brought a civil action in the Tirana District Court (“the District Court”), seeking the quashing of the Agency’s decision and the rectification of the 1995 Commission’s decision. On 3 December 2012 that court partly allowed the applicants’ claim. Relying on an expert report, it found that the documents establishing the applicants’ ancestor’s property rights referred to an outdated unit of measurement. It therefore ordered the rectification of the Commission’s decision of 1995 by adding the word “old” to the unit of measurement used in the operative part of that decision.

9.  The Agency and the State Advocate’s office appealed against that decision, arguing, inter alia, that the claim should be dismissed as time‑barred.

10.  On 26 June 2014 the Tirana Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. The correction was entered in the land register.

11.  On 6 April 2022 the Supreme Court reversed in camera the lower courts’ judgment and dismissed the applicants’ claim as time-barred. It held that the applicants should have brought proceedings within 30 days of becoming aware of the discrepancy between the 1995 decision and the accompanying map. The Supreme Court held that even assuming that the applicants had not been aware of the inconsistency in 1995, the 30-day time‑limit to address the courts had started to run from the moment the IPRO had informed them of its existence. It further found that rather than lodging an administrative complaint, the applicants should have brought the matter directly before the domestic courts.

12.  On 12 October 2022 the Constitutional Court dismissed a constitutional complaint lodged by the applicants, on the grounds that it was of a fourth-instance nature.

RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

13.  Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure provides that if an administrative act is valid but is found to contain inaccuracies or obvious errors, the competent authority may, either of its own motion or at the request of a party to the proceedings, correct any clerical errors or manifest inaccuracies in the act without altering its substance. Such corrections are not subject to any statutory time-limit.

14.  Section 18 of the 2004 Property Act, as amended by law no. 9684/2007, provided at the material time that, in respect of appeals against decisions given by the former local commissions recognising property rights or ordering the restitution of or compensation for property, both the expropriated party and the State Advocate’s office were entitled to lodge an appeal with the central office of the Agency. The expropriated party could subsequently appeal against that decision to the Tirana District Court within 30 days of its notification.

15.  An overview of the relevant domestic constitutional case-law is presented in Gaba v. Albania (no. 33369/17, §§ 51-56, 17 December 2024).
