case_name: CASE OF ISANYANS v. ARMENIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF ISANYANS v. ARMENIA

(Application no. 40610/17)













JUDGMENT



STRASBOURG

22 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Isanyans v. Armenia,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Andreas Zünd, President,
Mykola Gnatovskyy,
Sébastien Biancheri, judges,

and Viktoriya Maradudina, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 1 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1.  The case originated in an application against Armenia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 20 April 2017.

2.  The applicant was represented by Mr T. Yegoryan, a lawyer practising in Yerevan.

3.  The Armenian Government (“the Government”) were given notice of the application.

THE FACTS

4.  The applicant’s details and information relevant to the application are set out in the appended table.

5.  The applicant complained under Article 5 of the Convention of the unlawful deprivation of liberty. He also raised additional complaints under Article 6 of the Convention.

FACTUAL DETAILS FROM THE APPENDED TABLE
Application no. Date of introduction: 40610/17 20/04/2017
Applicant’s name Year of birth: Dvin ISANYANS 1989
Date of arrest: 13/05/2014
Other relevant information: On 13/05/2014 the applicant took part in a protest held in the Mashtots park in Yerevan, where the Armenian and French Presidents were to meet there. According to the findings of the domestic courts, which were based on police reports and a video recording of the incident, the applicant had repeatedly attempted to pass through a police cordon to access the area where the Presidents were supposed to meet and had refused to comply with orders to cease those attempts. As a result, he was subjected to a three-hour-long administrative arrest and escorted to a police station for the purpose of drawing up an administrative-offence report. The police subsequently instituted administrative proceedings against the applicant, seeking to have a fine imposed on him. The applicant filed a counterclaim challenging the lawfulness of the police’s actions. The Administrative Court examined both claims jointly, deciding to impose a fine of 50,000 Armenian drams on the applicant for his failure to comply with a lawful order of the police. It dismissed the applicant’s counterclaim. Those findings were upheld by the Administrative Court of Appeal. As regards the necessity of the applicant’s arrest under Article 259 of the Code of Administrative Offences – which allowed an administrative arrest, inter alia , in order to prepare an administrative-offence report if it could not be done on the spot – the Court of Appeal found that the police had not breached the law by not preparing an offence report at the site of the protest. Given the nature of the applicant’s socially disruptive conduct, the police had been authorised to take preventive measures. The final court decision was served on the applicant on 20/10/2016. Article 259 of the Code permitted an individual to be deprived of his or her liberty in order to: (i) halt the commission of an administrative offence where other preventive measures had proven ineffective; (ii) establish a person’s identity; (iii) draw up an administrative offence report if it is mandatory that such a report be drawn up but cannot be done on the spot; or (iv) ensure the timely and orderly examination of cases of administrative offences and the execution of decisions in respect thereof.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Armenia of Article 5 (Right to liberty and security) concerning Lawful arrest or detention in this case

case_name: CASE OF HANDZLÍK AND ŠUSTER v. SLOVAKIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIRST SECTION

CASE OF HANDZLÍK AND ŠUSTER v. SLOVAKIA

(Applications nos. 23301/23 and 35966/23)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

22 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Handzlík and Šuster v. Slovakia,

The European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Frédéric Krenc, President,
Davor Derenčinović,
Alain Chablais, judges,

and Viktoriya Maradudina, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 1 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1.  The case originated in applications against Slovakia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on the various dates indicated in the appended table.

2.  The Slovak Government (“the Government”) were given notice of the applications.

THE FACTS

3.  The list of applicants and the relevant details of the applications are set out in the appended table.

4.  The applicants complained of the excessive length of criminal proceedings.

FACTUAL DETAILS FROM THE APPENDED TABLE
Application no. Date of introduction: 23301/23 25/05/2023
Applicant’s name Year of birth: Rudolf HANDZLÍK 1958
Representative’s name and location: Rudolf Priečinský Bratislava

End of proceedings: 15/01/2015 pending

Domestic court File number Domestic award (in euros): Constitutional Court no. II. US 259/2022 0

Representative’s name and location: Silvia Benhatchi Kosice
Start of proceedings: 17/01/2008

22 October 2026

In the case of Gondal v. Greece,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Úna Ní Raifeartaigh, President,

and Viktoriya Maradudina, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 1 October 2026,

case_name: CASE OF G.G. v. GREECE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF G.G. v. GREECE

(Application no. 84038/17)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

20 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of G.G. v. Greece,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Peeter Roosma, President,
Ioannis Ktistakis,
Lətif Hüseynov, judges,
and Olga Chernishova, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 84038/17) against the Hellenic Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 28 November 2017 by a Greek national, G.G. (“the applicant”), who was born in 1965, lives in Athens and was represented by Mr V. Sotiropoulos, a lawyer practising in Athens;

the decision to give notice of the complaints under Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14, as well as the complaint under Article 6 of the Convention, to the Greek Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Ms N. Marioli, and their Agent’s delegate, Ms O. Patsopoulou, Legal Advisor at the State Legal Council, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the decision not to have the applicant’s name disclosed;

the observations submitted by the respondent Government and the observations in reply submitted by the applicant;

the comments submitted by the Greek Helsinki Monitor (GHM), which was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section;

Having deliberated in private on 29 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The application concerns the exclusion of the applicant from a memorial service of his late same‑sex partner, by family members of the latter. The applicant complained under Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14 that the authorities had failed to protect him from discrimination based on his sexual orientation. He also complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention of excessive length of proceedings.

2.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

3.  The applicant had lived for 17 years with his same-sex partner, V.K., in a steady relationship. V.K. had bought a house in 2008 and ever since the couple lived there. On 7 November 2003 they founded a company in which the applicant was the silent partner.

4.  On 17 March 2009 V.K. died unexpectedly. Following his death, the relationship between the applicant and his late partner’s heirs, namely his parents and his sister, became troubled. Judicial proceedings were initiated concerning financial issues arising from the company that the applicant and his late partner had founded together.

5.  On 3 May 2009 a 40-day memorial service for V.K. was organised. The applicant arrived and his late partner’s sister, F.K., asked him to leave. The applicant stated that she had used humiliating expressions, such as “What do you want here, you fag?”(“Τι θες μωρή πουστάρα εδώ;”) and “Get lost, you fag, from here” (“Εξαφανίσου μωρή πουστάρα από δω”), with the intention of attacking him personally and insulting him on the basis of his sexual orientation. The applicant then left the memorial service.

6.  On 11 June 2009 the applicant lodged a civil claim with the Athens One-Member Court of First Instance against F.K. concerning the above‑mentioned incident, claiming 20,000 euros (EUR) in respect of non‑pecuniary damage and requesting that F.K. refrain from such insults in the future. The hearing was scheduled for 10 March 2011. On that date it was adjourned until 5 April 2012 so that it could be heard along with two other claims which had been lodged by V.K.’s parents and his sister. In particular, on 15 March 2010 F.K. had lodged a claim in respect of non-pecuniary damage, claiming that the applicant had personally insulted her in his allegations submitted in his above-mentioned legal action. On the same date, V.K.’s parents lodged a civil claim in respect of non-pecuniary damage, claiming that the applicant had personally insulted them and the memory of their son during an incident that had taken place on 11 April 2009. They argued that on that date, the applicant had come to their house and had insulted the memory of their son (his late partner) and then pushed V.K.’s father, who had ended up in the hospital for several days.

7.  The three claims were heard on 5 April 2012. On 19 June 2013 the Athens One-Member Court of First Instance delivered judgment no. 3420/2013, by which it partly granted the applicant’s and V.K.’s parents’ claims and rejected F.K.’s claims. Following appeals lodged by all parties, on 21 September 2015 the Athens Court of Appeal delivered judgment no. 4107/2015. Having reviewed several witness written testimonies that had been given in the context of the first-instance proceedings or in the context of other judicial proceedings, the applicant’s deposition and photographs adduced by the parties, it found that F.K. could not have used humiliating expressions related to the applicant’s sexual orientation, as that would have also insulted her brother’s memory, but had merely asked him to leave the memorial service. It considered the applicant’s witnesses unreliable and consequently rejected the applicant’s claim. It partly granted F.K.’s and V.K.’s parents’ claims against the applicant.

8.  On 17 July 2017 the Court of Cassation published decision no. 1293/2017 rejecting an appeal on points of law lodged by the applicant. It considered that the applicant’s exclusion from the memorial service had been at the discretion of V.K.’s heirs, namely his parents and his sister, as they had organised it. Although the memorial service had been held in a public church, the decision as to whom should have been invited had lain with the organisers of the service and thus the exclusion of a person had not constituted a personal insult. It therefore rejected the relevant grounds for the appeal on points of law in which the applicant had submitted that his exclusion from the service had violated his right to respect for his family life because it had denied him the status of same-sex partner.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

9.  The relevant domestic legislation can be found in Margari v. Greece (no. 36705/16, § 15, 20 June 2023) and Balaskas v. Greece (no. 73087/17, § 16, 5 November 2020).
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Greece of Article 6 (Right to a fair trial) concerning Civil proceedings; Article 6-1 - Reasonable time in this case

case_name: CASE OF ZOUVELOS AND OTHERS v. GREECE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF ZOUVELOS AND OTHERS v. GREECE

(Application no. 42800/18)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

20 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Zouvelos and Others v. Greece,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Peeter Roosma, President,
Ioannis Ktistakis,
Lətif Hüseynov, judges,
and Olga Chernishova, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 42800/18) against the Hellenic Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 31 August 2018 by five Greek nationals (“the applicants”), whose relevant details are listed in the appended table, who were represented by Ms K. Gouvitsa, a lawyer practising in Amaliada;

the decision to give notice of the complaints concerning Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention to the Greek Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Ms N. Marioli, President of the State Legal Council, and their Agent’s delegate, Ms S. Papaioannou, Senior Advisor at the State Legal Council, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 29 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The application concerns the amount of compensation payable to the applicants following the expropriation of their properties.

2.  By a joint ministerial decision issued on 11 February 2008 and published in the Official Government Gazette on 25 February 2008, the expropriation of the applicants’ properties, located in Amaliada, was ordered for the construction of a highway.

3.  On 24 February 2009 the Greek State lodged an application for the determination of the provisional compensation payable to the applicants.

4.  Hearings took place on 15, 29 and 30 October 2009.

5.  By judgment no. 53/2010 of 26 April 2010, the Amaliada Court of First Instance determined the provisional unitary amounts of compensation payable to the applicants as follows: 10.08 euros (EUR) per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 5.42 per sq. m for plot no. 206 belonging to the first applicant; EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plot no. 300 and EUR 4.50 per sq. m for plot no. 305 belonging to the second applicant; EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no.078 belonging to the third applicant; EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no. 079 belonging to the fourth applicant; and EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plots nos. 316 and 318 and EUR 4.28 per sq. m for plot no. 321 belonging to the fifth applicant. The calculation was based on the values of the properties on the dates of the hearings before the first-instance court.

6.  The Amaliada Court of First Instance further held that the non-expropriated part of the properties would derive a special benefit from the execution of the works, as they would have access to the highway.

7.  On 20 October 2010 the Greek State lodged an application for the determination of the final compensation payable to the applicants.

8.  After two adjournments, on 12 May 2011 and 21 March 2013, the hearing took place on 15 January 2015.

9.  The applicants responded by taking the following legal actions. On 19 January 2011 the first applicant lodged a counterclaim seeking the determination of the final compensation and challenging the presumption that his remaining, non-expropriated properties would benefit from the execution of the works and submitted a written request to intervene in the proceedings. In addition, the first, second and fifth applicants challenged the presumption of benefit by orally requesting leave to intervene in the proceedings at the hearing held on 15 January 2015. The third and fourth applicants challenged the presumption of benefit by way of written submissions filed in the hearing of 15 January 2015. Lastly, on 14 October 2010 the fifth applicant lodged a separate application seeking the determination of the final compensation and challenging the presumption of benefit.

10.  By judgment no. 78/2016 of 31 May 2016, the Patras Court of Appeal dismissed as inadmissible the applicants’ claims as regards the presumption of benefit. In particular, it held that the first applicant had failed to comply with the provisions of Article 33 § 7 of Law no. 2971/2001, which set out that the presumption of benefit could be challenged within a time-limit of six months from the date of determination of provisional compensation (which, in the case at hand, had occurred on 26 April 2010; see paragraph 5 above). It further held that the oral requests by the first, second and fifth applicants to intervene in the proceedings and the written submissions of the third and fourth applicants had been aimed at extending the scope of the application for the determination of the final compensation, contrary to national procedural rules. Lastly, it held that the fifth applicant’s claims lacked factual details as to the parts of his properties to which the presumption of benefit had been applied.

11.  Furthermore, the Patras Court of Appeal determined the final unitary amounts of compensation payable to the applicants as follows: EUR 8 per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 2.60 per sq. m for plot no. 206 belonging to the first applicant; EUR 2 per sq. m for plots nos. 300 and 305 belonging to the second applicant; EUR 6.50 per sq. m for plot no. 078 belonging to the third applicant; EUR 6.50 per sq. m for plot no. 079 belonging to the fourth applicant; and EUR 2.50 per sq. m for plots nos. 316, 318 and 350 and EUR 2 per sq. m for plot no. 321 belonging to the fifth applicant. It based its judgment on Article 17 § 2 (c) of the Greek Constitution and Article 13 § 1 (b) of Law no. 2882/2001, which set out that the final compensation should be calculated on the basis of the values of the expropriated properties on the date of the hearing before the appellate court (15 January 2015 in the case at hand), where more than one year has passed from the date of the hearing concerning the provisional compensation. It further based its judgment on the depreciation of property values from 2009 onward. As regards plots nos. 078 and 079, they had been recorded as lying within the settlement boundaries, an error that had subsequently been rectified, thus aligning their unit prices with the remainder of the plots in question.

12.  The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, complaining that the appellate court had taken the date of the hearing before it, rather than the date of the hearing on the determination of the provisional compensation, as the critical date for determining the final compensation, resulting in lower amounts awarded to them. They further argued that the appellate court had erred in dismissing as inadmissible their claims regarding the presumption of benefit.

13.  The Court of Cassation examined the applicants’ arguments on the merits and dismissed them by way of judgment no. 2062/2017, which became final on 1 March 2018. With respect to the critical date for determining the final compensation, the Court of Cassation ruled that Article 17 § 2 (c) of the Greek Constitution and Article 13 § 1 (b) of Law no. 2882/2001 applied regardless of any increase or decrease in property values occurring between the hearing in respect of the provisional compensation and that in respect of the final compensation. With respect to the applicants’ claims challenging the presumption of benefit, the Court of Cassation upheld the findings of the appellate court and further held that, in any event, all of the applicants’ claims lacked sufficient factual details concerning the parts of their properties which, allegedly, would not benefit from the execution of the works.

14.  The applicants complained of a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, reiterating the arguments they had made before the domestic courts.
target_provision: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property)
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Greece of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property) concerning Peaceful enjoyment of possessions in this case

case_name: CASE OF TCHIGLADZE v. GEORGIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FOURTH SECTION

CASE OF TCHIGLADZE v. GEORGIA

(Application no. 8684/20)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

20 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Tchigladze v. Georgia,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Sebastian Răduleţu, President,
András Jakab,
Corinna Wissels, judges,
and Simeon Petrovski, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 8684/20) against Georgia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 5 February 2020 by a Georgian national, Mr Gela Tchigladze (“the applicant”), who was born in 1964 and lives in Tbilisi, and was represented initially by Mr B. Botchorishvili and subsequently by Mr G. Lemonjava, lawyers practising in Tbilisi;

the decision to give notice of the application to the Georgian Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Mr B. Dzamashvili, of the Ministry of Justice;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 29 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The present case primarily concerns the applicant’s complaints under Article 3 of the Convention regarding injuries observed on him upon his arrest, and the alleged ineffectiveness of the related criminal investigation.

2.  The applicant was arrested on 21 June 2019, during a dispersal of a demonstration (for broader background, see Tsaava and Others v. Georgia [GC], nos. 13186/20 and 4 others, §§ 14-43, 11 December 2025).

3.  The arrest took place over six hours after the police had started to disperse the demonstration, when the majority of the demonstrators had left the area, and only a small number of individuals remained at the site. Various individuals engaged in acts of vandalism and threw various objects at police officers (ibid., § 42).

4.  According to the applicant’s administrative arrest report, signed by him, he was arrested for verbally insulting police officers and throwing stones at them. The report also noted a scratch on the right side of his waist, a bruise on his left side and scabs on both shins. The administrative-offence report, also signed by the applicant, referred to Article 166 (disorderly conduct) and Article 173 (disobeying lawful orders of the police or insulting law‑enforcement personnel) of the Code of Administrative Offences.

5.  Before the first-instance court, the applicant stated that he had been merely talking on the phone in the courtyard of a residential building when some demonstrators ran in, trying to escape the police, and he had followed them. He also stated that he “partly agreed” with the charges and that he had been “unable to control himself” due to the developments of that day. In response to the judge’s request to clarify what he had meant, he explained that he had joined in the chanting of some phrases, but claimed that “a man of his age would not” have sworn at the police or thrown stones at them. The arresting officers submitted, by contrast, that he had been aggressive, throwing items and swearing at them, and that they had chased him, together with two of his co-accused, to the roof of a building, where he was arrested.

6.  On 21 June 2019 the trial court found the applicant, along with his co‑accused, guilty of the relevant administrative offences (see the preceding paragraph). He was given a fine of 1,500 Georgian laris (GEL – approximately 480 euros (EUR)). It reasoned that the applicant had partly admitted to the charges, and the parties’ submissions and the evidence available in the case file indicated that he had committed the offences in question.

7.  Subsequently, the applicant obtained two medical reports indicating the presence of bruises on his chest and a haematoma on his right thigh, and post‑traumatic stress disorder.

8.  On 1 July 2019 the applicant appealed against his conviction, stating that Article 6 of the Convention had been breached on account of the trial court’s failure to distinguish the factual circumstances specifically relating to him from those relating to his co-accused. He stated that he had arrived at the demonstration around midnight, in order to look for his son, and had then stayed to help injured demonstrators. He also maintained that he had been arrested in the courtyard of a residential building and had been beaten with truncheons, after which he had been escorted out and put in a police car.

9.  On 6 August 2019 the appellate court held an oral hearing. The applicant maintained his arguments (see paragraph 8 above). The appellate court found that, in light of the material before it, the lower court’s reasoning had not been deficient. It emphasised that, given the time and location of the offence, the statements given by the arresting officers during the appellate proceedings were consistent with other evidence in the case file. It thus upheld the lower court’s judgment, but reduced the sanction to GEL 1,000 (approximately EUR 320). It also informed the prosecuting authorities of the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment.

10.  On 21 August 2019 the applicant was questioned by a prosecutor, as part of a broader investigation into the events related to the dispersal of the demonstration (see Tsaava and Others, cited above, § 107). The applicant reiterated that he had been ill-treated during his arrest but noted that he had been arrested on the roof of a residential building. When reminded of his earlier statements (see paragraphs 5 and 8 above), he explained that he had not paid attention to the facts at that time.

11.  On 22 August 2019 the prosecutor collected the applicant’s medical documents and ordered a forensic medical examination. The resulting report (dated 11 March 2021) noted that the injuries were minor and had not caused any deterioration of the applicant’s health. The applicant was then granted the procedural status of victim.

12.  On 27 September 2019 the authorities implemented an investigative experiment with the applicant’s participation to determine the course of the events. They also attempted to obtain recordings made by the surveillance cameras of three private entities located there. None could be retrieved on account of technical issues and/or the videos having been deleted. The relevant reports noted that the investigating authorities had previously retrieved the recordings, in June and July 2019, as part of the investigative activities related to the dispersal of the demonstration.

13.  The applicant’s co-accused were questioned in April and June 2021 and noted that they had not been arrested together with the applicant and that the applicant had neither shown signs of ill-treatment nor made any complaints in that connection when they had met him. The applicant’s arresting officers were questioned in June 2021. One of the officers stated that he had observed injuries on the applicant, which, according to the applicant’s explanation at the time, had occurred before his arrest.

14.  In 2025, criminal proceedings were instituted in absentia against the Minister of Internal Affairs at the time of the disputed events. He was charged with organising the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm against more than two persons, a criminal offence under Article 117 § 3 of the Criminal Code, on account of allegations that he had instructed the special forces, in breach of the applicable regulations, to use kinetic impact projectiles, tear gas and water cannon simultaneously, without prior warning allowing peaceful demonstrators to leave the area. The proceedings against him are pending before a first-instance court. The broader criminal investigation concerning the events of 20-21 June 2019 is also ongoing.

15.  Relying on Article 3 of the Convention the applicant complained that he had been ill-treated during his arrest, and that the ongoing criminal investigation in that connection had been ineffective. The applicant also complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to provide sufficient reasons for his conviction.
target_issue: Degrading treatment; Inhuman treatment; substantive aspect
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Georgia of Article 3 (Prohibition of torture) concerning Degrading treatment; Inhuman treatment; substantive aspect in this case

case_name: CASE OF SHEVCHENKO AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF SHEVCHENKO AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 48646/13)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

22 October 2026







This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of Shevchenko and Others v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

María Elósegui, President,
Andreas Zünd,
Mykola Gnatovskyy, judges,
and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 48646/13) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 15 July 2013 by five Ukrainian nationals, whose relevant details are listed in the appended table (“the applicants”), and who were represented by Ms Y. Zakrevska and Ms Y. Naumenko, lawyers practising in Kyiv;

the decision to give notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Ms M. Sokorenko, of the Ministry of Justice;

the decision not to have the name of the third applicant (Y.K.) disclosed;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 1 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The case concerns the dispersal of a demonstration organised by the applicants and various issues arising from it.

Demonstration organised by the applicants and their subsequent detention

2.  On 2 October 2012 the Ukrainian Parliament approved legislation prohibiting “propaganda of homosexuality” at the first reading.

3.  The applicants informed the Kyiv State Administration that they planned to hold a demonstration on Maidan Nezalezhnosti, the main square in Kyiv, on 8 December 2012, to mark the upcoming International Human Rights Day and to express their disagreement with the new legislation.

4.  On 7 December 2012 the Kyiv District Administrative Court prohibited the applicants from holding the demonstration on Maidan Nezalezhnosti. On 28 March 2013 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal rejected an appeal lodged by the applicants. On 7 November 2013 the Higher Administrative Court rejected the appeal in cassation lodged by the first applicant.

5.  On 7 December 2012 the first applicant informed the Kyiv State Administration that the applicants would hold the demonstration, but in a different location on 8 December 2012 from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m.

6.  At 1 p.m. on 8 December 2012 the applicants arrived at the intended location and saw that the police were already there. The applicants started their demonstration. The police formed a circle around the applicants, which, according to the applicants, prevented the general public from seeing or joining them.

7.  At around 2.10 p.m. two people forced their way through the police circle and started spraying tear gas and attacking the demonstrators. In particular, one of them started moving in the direction of the third applicant, swinging her hands. The third applicant backed away from the attacker, trying to shield himself with his hands. The attacker grabbed the third applicant’s hand and pulled it. At that moment the police apprehended the second, third, fourth, and fifth applicants and took them to a police station under Article 260 of the Code on Administrative Offences which envisaged that law enforcement bodies could detain a person committing an administrative offence in order to draw a report on the offence.

8.  At the police station the police checked the applicants’ identity papers and discovered that the third applicant, who looked and identified as male, was female according to his identity papers. According to the applicants, the police “mocked and insulted” the third applicant after this discovery and also mocked the other applicants by asking them about their sexual orientation. According to the applicants, they were released in about three hours.

Administrative offence proceedings Brought against the applicants

9.  By two separate decisions of 10 December 2012, the Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv found the second and fifth applicants guilty of administrative offences under Article 173 (petty hooliganism)[1] of the Code of Administrative Offences (“the CAO”) for having “pushed other citizens in a crowd”. On 17 and 21 January 2013 respectively, the Kyiv Court of Appeal quashed both decisions of 10 December 2012, having found no corpus delicti in the actions of the second and fifth applicants. The decisions of the Kyiv Court of Appeal became final.

10.  By another decision of 10 December 2012, the Shevchenkivskyy District Court also found the fifth applicant guilty of disobeying a lawful order of a law-enforcement officer under Article 185 of the CAO and ordered him to pay a fine of 136 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH)[2]. On 16 January 2013 the Kyiv Court of Appeal quashed that decision, having found no corpus delicti in the fifth applicant’s actions.

11.  Nevertheless, on 13 December 2012 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court found the first applicant guilty of infringing the procedure for organising or conducting public events (Article 185-1 § 2 of the CAO) and ordered her to pay a fine of UAH 850[3]. On 18 January 2013 that decision was upheld on appeal and became final.

12.  On 17 December 2012 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court closed the administrative proceedings against the fourth applicant under Article 173 of the CAO. That decision was not appealed against and became final. The court found that, during the demonstration, a certain G. had tried to attack the third applicant, and the fourth applicant had placed himself between G. and the third applicant. The whole incident had lasted for about fifteen seconds.

13.  On 18 December 2012 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court found the third applicant guilty under Article 173 of the CAO of breaching public order on 8 December 2012. According to the court, Y.K. had “pushed other citizens in a public place” and had thus disrupted public order. The court found that the actions of the third applicant constituted an administrative offence under Article 173. However, as the violation had been of a minor nature, the court exempted the third applicant from administrative liability. On 1 February 2013 that decision was upheld on appeal and became final.

Proceedings instituted by the applicants

14.  On 13 June 2013 the second, fourth and fifth applicants instituted judicial proceedings under the Code of Administrative Justice challenging their detention at the police station on 8 December 2012 and the disruption of their demonstration by the police. They asked the court to establish that their detention had been unlawful and claimed compensation for non-pecuniary damage under Article 1176 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They submitted that they had felt frustrated and had suffered psychological distress on account of the unfairness of the situation. They had felt helpless and had lost their trust in law-enforcement officials. They stated that, following their detention, it had been difficult for them to attend other public events for fear that they might be unlawfully detained again. They further stated that during their detention they and the other applicants had been mocked and insulted by the police because they had participated in an event held in support of the LGBTI community. In particular, the police officers had mockingly asked them about their sexual orientation.

15.  On 18 September 2013 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court decided not to examine the fifth applicant’s complaint in view of his repeated failure to appear in court. That decision became final.

16.  On 25 November 2013 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal ruled that the second applicant’s detention had been unlawful, but refused to award him compensation for non-pecuniary damage, there being no evidence that he had sustained any such damage. That decision was upheld by the Higher Administrative Court on 15 January 2014.

17.  On 30 July 2014 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court found that the fourth applicant’s arrest and detention had been unlawful but refused to award him any compensation in respect of non-pecuniary damage reasoning that he had not provided any evidence that he had actually sustained any non‑pecuniary damage. By a final decision of the Higher Administrative Court of 9 April 2015, an appeal lodged by the fourth applicant was dismissed.

18.  On 16 March 2018 the third applicant’s legal gender was changed on his birth certificate. His legal name and surname were also changed to reflect his male gender.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Ukraine of Article 11 (Freedom of assembly and association) concerning Freedom of peaceful assembly in this case

case_name: CASE OF ZHYTNIKOV v. UKRAINE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF ZHYTNIKOV v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 39259/18)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

22 October 2026







This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of Zhytnikov v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

María Elósegui, President,
Andreas Zünd,
Mykola Gnatovskyy, judges,
and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 39259/18) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 9 July 2018 by a Ukrainian national, Mr Anatoliy Viktorovych Zhytnikov (“the applicant”), who was born in 1979 and lives in Mykolayiv, and was represented by Mr V.G. Byelik, a lawyer practising in Mykolayiv;

the decision to give notice of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the sanction imposed on the applicant in connection with an alleged breach of customs regulations – by the final decision of the Mykolayiv Regional Court of Appeal on 28 February 2018 – to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Ms M. Sokorenko, of the Ministry of Justice, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 1 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that the sanction imposed on him following proceedings in respect of a customs-related offence was unlawful and disproportionate.

2.  The applicant was a logistics manager at a private company, R. (“the R. company”). His duties included submitting documents to the customs authorities in connection with the importation of goods by that company. On 15 June 2017 he submitted an electronic customs declaration concerning goods imported by the R. company, including 45 kg of garlic oil valued at 43,065.73 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) (equivalent to 1,460 euros (EUR) at the time). The declaration was accompanied by an electronic copy of a consignment note pertaining to the Convention on the Contract for the International Carriage of Goods by Road (“CMR”), which bore stamps indicating that sanitary and epidemiological controls had been carried out on the goods. On the basis of those documents, the goods were cleared through customs and released into free circulation.

3.  Following information received from the Security Service of Ukraine in the context of criminal proceedings concerning alleged offences connected with the activities of the R. company, the customs authorities obtained letters from the relevant sanitary and laboratory authorities. Those authorities stated that no sanitary or epidemiological controls had been carried out in respect of the goods covered by the applicant’s declaration and that no relevant request had been made by the R. company. Criminal proceedings concerning the alleged use of forged documents during customs clearance were subsequently joined to those proceedings; they were later discontinued without the applicant being notified of any suspicion.

4.  On 1 November 2017 the Mykolayiv customs office drew up a report on a violation of customs rules under Article 483 § 1 of the Customs Code. It alleged that the applicant had submitted a forged CMR document bearing forged stamps confirming that sanitary and epidemiological controls had been carried out and had used that as the basis for moving the goods across the customs border.

5.  On 16 November 2017 the Central District Court of Mykolayiv (“the District Court”) found the applicant guilty of a customs offence under Article 483 § 1 of the Customs Code. It held that the applicant, as the authorised customs declarant of the R. company, had submitted a CMR consignment note bearing stamps allegedly confirming that sanitary and epidemiological controls had been carried out, although the competent authorities had stated that no such controls had been carried out in respect of the goods. The court imposed a fine of UAH 43,065.73, an amount equivalent to the value of the goods, and ordered confiscation of the goods. Since the goods had already been released into free circulation and were no longer available for confiscation, the court relied on Article 541 § 2 of the Customs Code, which provided that, where confiscation of goods from persons who had violated customs rules was impossible, their value could be recovered through a court decision. It accordingly ordered the recovery from the applicant of the value of the goods, also in the amount of UAH 43,065.73.

6.  On 28 February 2018 the Mykolayiv Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) upheld the first-instance decision. It rejected the applicant’s arguments that the alleged forgery of the CMR consignment note and the stamps had not been established by an expert examination and that he could not be held liable for alleged omissions or wrongdoing of other persons or institutions. Relying on information from the relevant sanitary and laboratory authorities, the Court of Appeal held that the CMR consignment note submitted by the applicant bore forged stamps certifying that sanitary and epidemiological controls had been carried out. It further held that the applicant, as the person authorised to deal with customs matters for the R. company, could be treated as an official of that company for the purposes of customs liability. As regards the sanction, the Court of Appeal held that it had been imposed within the limits of Article 483 § 1 of the Customs Code. The decision was final.

7.  On 4 April 2018 two sets of enforcement proceedings were opened: one concerning recovery of the value of the goods and the other concerning recovery of the fine. On 8 April 2025 the State Bailiffs Service received payment in full in respect of both amounts, namely the value of the goods (UAH 43,065.73, equivalent to EUR 950 at the time) and the fine (UAH 43,065.73), together with enforcement fees and costs. On 14 May 2025 both sets of enforcement proceedings were terminated on the ground that the decision had been fully enforced.
target_provision: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property)
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Ukraine of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property) concerning Peaceful enjoyment of possessions in this case

case_name: CASE OF GENDERDOC-M v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF GENDERDOC-M v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA

(Application no. 23907/15)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

29 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Genderdoc-M v. the Republic of Moldova,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

María Elósegui, President,
Diana Sârcu,
Sébastien Biancheri, judges,
and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 23907/15) against the Republic of Moldova lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 5 May 2015 by Public Association Centre for Information Genderdoc‑M (Asociaţia Obştească Centrul de Informaţii Genderdoc-M; “the applicant association”), registered in Chișinău and represented by Ms D. Străisteanu, a lawyer practising in Chișinău;

the decision to give notice of the application to the Moldovan Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent at the time, Mr D. Obadă;

the parties’ observations;



Having deliberated in private on 8 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The case concerns the failure to carry out an effective investigation and punishment of persons involved in the interruption of a gay pride march.

2.  On 17 May 2014 a march called “A year without discrimination” was organised in Chișinău by the applicant association to mark the international day against homophobia. The march was under heavy protection by the police and special units, which separated the participants from the several dozens of rather aggressive persons wishing to disrupt it. Some of those persons chanted homophobic slogans and insults and explicitly threatened participants of the march with violence, even stating that they would hang such persons. C., an orthodox priest who had repeatedly protested against events organised by the LGBT community, managed to approach the participants of the march and to wrestle away from the hands of one of the organisers (D., who worked for the applicant association) a rainbow flag, tearing it apart. According to D.’s statement to the police, she had been holding the flag firmly and C. had hit her hands several times in order to obtain it. Witnesses E. and M., who also worked for the applicant association, told the police that they had seen C. aggressively wrestle away the flag. In doing so, he had hit E. on the shoulder and had also hit other participants of the march, who had been frightened. The applicant association and a number of witnesses noted that the media had followed the march closely, recording all the events. One of the videos apparently shows a priest being stopped by the police from reaching the demonstrators and subsequently resisting them, and managing to break free from their hold using energetic movements.

3.  Another protestor (G.) grabbed a banner from the organisers leading the march and refused to return it or to move, thus blocking their passage. Eventually, the participants of the march had to abandon the banner and continue their march, while the police arrested G.

4.  On 26 June 2014 the applicant association lodged two criminal complaints about the actions of C. and G., notably under Article 184 of the Criminal Code (violation of the right to freedom of assembly by unlawfully impeding a public event, while, inter alia, applying violence not threatening the life or health) and Article 187 (robbery). It referred to the attempts to block the march and to the fact that the two suspects had openly and forcibly taken from the applicant association’s staff two objects which were never returned to it.

5.  On 9 July 2014 a criminal investigation was initiated into the allegations made by the applicant association. On 27 October 2014 the prosecutor responsible for the case discontinued the investigation, finding that the actions of the two suspects did not amount to a criminal offence, but rather an administrative one. He found in particular that it had not been established that the two suspects had acted together. Moreover, in the absence of any forensic report there was no medical evidence of bodily harm to any participant of the march. Lastly, he found that the three-month prescription applicable to administrative offences prevented pursuing the accused for the administrative offence committed. That decision was upheld by a higher prosecutor.

6.  On 27 January 2015 the investigating judge of the Chișinău District Court (Râșcani District) annulled the prosecutors’ decisions, finding that not all actions had been taken, notably to verify whether the two suspects had planned and acted together.

7.  On 8 April 2015 the applicant association asked the prosecutor to inform it of the progress of the investigation and whether any decision had been taken. They subsequently found out that the investigation had been reopened and more witnesses heard on 11 February and 9 March 2015, following which the investigation had once more been discontinued on 20 March 2015. The applicant association did not challenge that decision.

target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by the Republic of Moldova of Article 14 (Prohibition of discrimination) concerning Discrimination; Freedom of assembly and association; Positive obligations; Article 11-1 - Freedom of peaceful assembly in this case

case_name: CASE OF FIŠIĆ v. CROATIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIRST SECTION

CASE OF FIŠIĆ v. CROATIA

(Application no. 18788/22)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

29 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Fišić v. Croatia,

The European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Erik Wennerström, President,
Raffaele Sabato,
Frédéric Krenc,
Davor Derenčinović,
Alain Chablais,
Artūrs Kučs,
Anna Adamska-Gallant, judges,
and Liv Tigerstedt, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 18788/22) against the Republic of Croatia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Croatian national, Mr Oliver Fišić (“the applicant”), on 6 April 2022;

the decision to give notice to the Croatian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint concerning access to a court and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that he had been denied access to a tribunal to defend his rights in relation to a mayoral decision adopted in a public tender procedure in which he had participated as a bidder.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1968 and lives in Brašina. He was represented by Mr B. Radan, a lawyer practising in Zagreb.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Š. Stažnik.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

CALL FOR TENDERS FOR THE LEASE OF PUBLIC AREAS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF ŽUPA DUBROVAČKA

5.  On 15 March 2017 the mayor of Župa dubrovačka ordered a municipal committee to organise a call for tenders for the lease of certain of the municipality’s public areas, to be used, inter alia, for vending stands.

6.  The tender, which was published on 20 March 2017, set out the eligibility criteria, the lease duration, minimum bid amounts and the deadline for submissions.

It also stated that the best bidder would be selected in accordance with the municipality of Župa dubrovačka’s decision on the lease of public areas (“the municipality’s Decision”, see paragraph 24 below).

7.  The applicant submitted a bid of 16 Croatian kunas (HRK) per square metre per day for a vending stand in Brašina. Another bidder, N.P., submitted a bid of HRK 11 per square metre per day for the same location.

8.  On 5 April 2017 the committee found that both bids had been submitted on time and complied with the specifications. As the bids differed, it decided under section 13 of the municipality’s Decision (see paragraph 24 below) that N.P., as the previous lessee, would be offered the lease at the higher price submitted by the applicant. On 21 April 2017 N.P. agreed to pay the higher price.

9.  On 26 April 2017 the mayor accepted N.P.’s bid and concluded a lease agreement with her.

10.  The applicant lodged an objection, arguing that the mayoral decision had been unlawful. On 27 July 2017 the Municipal Council dismissed the objection, emphasising that section 13 of the municipality’s Decision granted priority to the previous lessee in order to ensure legal certainty for entrepreneurs.

11.  On 28 July 2017 the municipality, represented by the mayor, concluded a lease agreement with N.P.

PROCEEDINGS IN THE ADMINISTRATIVE COURTS

12.  The applicant brought an administrative action in the Split Administrative Court (Upravni sud u Splitu), challenging the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017. He argued that the misapplication of section 13 of the municipality’s Decision had placed him at a disadvantage vis-à-vis the other tenderer, whose bid was lower than his. He submitted that priority ought to be given to the previous lessee only if two identical bids were submitted, which had not been the case. Moreover, section 13 did not provide for the possibility for the previous lessee to have disclosed or match the highest bid.

13.  On 9 April 2019 the Split Administrative Court set aside the Municipal Council’s decision of 27 July 2017 (see paragraph 10 above) but upheld the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017 (see paragraph 9 above).

It noted that, pursuant to a practice direction adopted by the Administrative Court of the Republic of Croatia on 28 April 2008 (see paragraph 25 below), acts granting the lease of public areas constituted administrative acts – that is, individual acts by which the public authority decided on the rights, obligations or legal interests of an individual in an administrative matter (see paragraph 21 below). Such decisions were therefore subject to a review of their lawfulness in administrative disputes where the administrative courts applied the Constitution and the relevant statutory law.

The Split Administrative Court further noted that the legislation did not allow for the lodging of an appeal against individual mayoral acts deciding on the rights, obligations and legal interests of an individual. Such decisions could instead be challenged in an administrative court. For that reason, the Split Administrative Court concluded that the Municipal Council had lacked competence to review the mayoral decision and, accordingly, set aside its decision of 27 July 2017.

It reviewed the lawfulness of the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017 and concluded that the facts had been properly established and that the relevant law had been properly applied.

14.  The applicant appealed against that judgment, reiterating the arguments set out in paragraph 12 above and adding that, had section 13 of the municipality’s Decision provided for the possibility of the previous lessee to have disclosed or match the highest bid, he would never have bothered to submit a bid in the first place.

15.  On 24 September 2020 the High Administrative Court quashed the Split Administrative Court’s judgment and declared the applicant’s administrative action inadmissible. It held that, pursuant to its decision of 26 January 2015 delivered in the context of a specific tender procedure (see paragraph 26 below), decisions on the lease of public areas did not constitute administrative acts but acts of property management and thus fell outside the scope of administrative judicial review.

CONSTITUTIONAL COURT PROCEEDINGS

16.  On 1 April 2021 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging violations of his constitutional rights to a fair trial, equality before the law, and entrepreneurial and market freedom. He relied on the State’s obligation to ensure that all entrepreneurs had equal status on the market (see paragraph 19 below).

17.  On 22 December 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It found that the restriction on the right of access to a court had been constitutionally acceptable, having regard to the sufficient and relevant reasons provided by the High Administrative Court.

18.  That decision was served on the applicant on 10 January 2022.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

19.  The relevant provisions of the Constitution (Ustav Republike Hrvatske, Official Gazette no. 56/1990, with subsequent amendments) read as follows:

Article 29 § 1

“Everyone shall be entitled to have his or her rights and obligations, or suspicion or accusation of a criminal offence, decided upon fairly and within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial court established by law.”

Article 49

“Entrepreneurial and market freedom are the foundations of the economic system of the Republic of Croatia.

The State shall ensure that all entrepreneurs have equal legal status on the market. The abuse of monopolies, as determined by law, is prohibited.

...”

20.  The relevant provision of the Trade Act (Zakon o trgovini, Official Gazette no. 87/2008, with subsequent amendments) reads as follows:

Section 4(2)

“A trader shall carry out trading activities freely and under equal conditions on the market, in such a way that competition is neither prevented, restricted nor distorted.”



21.  The relevant provisions of the Administrative Disputes Act 2010 (Zakon o upravnim sporovima, Official Gazette no. 20/2010, with subsequent amendments), as in force during the proceedings instituted by the applicant in the administrative courts, read as follows:

Section 3

“(1)  The subject matter of an administrative dispute is:

1.  review of the lawfulness of an individual decision by which a public authority has decided on the right, obligation or legal interests of an individual in an administrative matter (an administrative act) against which no ordinary legal remedy is permitted;

2.  review of the lawfulness of the conduct of a public authority in the field of administrative law by which a right, obligation or the legal interests of an individual has been infringed, and against which no ordinary legal remedy is permitted;

3.  review of the lawfulness of a failure on the part of a public authority in the field of administrative law to decide, within the time-limit prescribed by law, on a right, obligation, legal interests or ordinary legal remedy of an individual, or to act in accordance with a regulation;

4.  review of the lawfulness of the conclusion, termination or fulfilment of an administrative contract.

...”

Section 4

“(1)  An administrative dispute may not be brought in matters for which judicial protection is provided outside of an administrative dispute.

(2)  An administrative dispute may not be brought concerning the correctness of an individual decision made at the discretion of a public authority, but it may be conducted concerning the lawfulness of such a decision, the limits of authority, and the purpose for which the authority was granted.

...”

Section 5

“In an administrative dispute, the court shall issue a decision on the basis of the Constitution and relevant statutory law.”

22.  The relevant provisions of the Ownership and Other Rights In Rem Act (Zakon o vlasništvu i drugim stvarnim pravima, Official Gazette no. 91/1996, with subsequent amendments – “the Property Act”) read as follows:

Section 35

“(1)  The Republic of Croatia and other legal persons governed by public law which hold ownership rights shall, as owners, have the same status in legal relations as private owners, unless otherwise provided by law.

(2)  Property owned by the Republic of Croatia shall be disposed of, administered and used by the Republic of Croatia’s government or by a body authorised by it, unless otherwise provided by a special law. Powers of disposal, administration and use in respect of property owned by local and regional self-government units shall be exercised by the bodies of those units as designated by the legislation governing the organisation of local and regional self-government units, unless otherwise provided by a special law.

...

(8)  The rules governing ownership by the Republic of Croatia shall apply, mutatis mutandis, to the ownership rights of local and regional self-government units, unless otherwise provided for by law or where required otherwise by the nature of those entities. ...”

Section 391

“(1)  Immovable property owned by local and regional self-government units may be alienated or otherwise disposed of by the competent authorities only on the basis of a public tender procedure and for compensation determined at market value, unless otherwise provided by law.

(2)  The provisions of paragraph 1 of this section shall not apply where the ownership of immovable property owned by local or regional self-government units is acquired by the Republic of Croatia, local or regional self-government units, or legal persons owned wholly or predominantly by the Republic of Croatia, or by legal persons owned wholly or predominantly by local or regional self-government units, where this serves the interest and objective of the general economic and social development of their citizens.

(3)   Land owned by local or regional self-government units may be sold by the competent authorities at a price determined by the market without organising a public tender procedure:

–  to a person to whom part of that land is necessary for the development of a vacant plot of land in accordance with a zoning permit or detailed land-use plan, provided that such land does not exceed 20% of the total area; and

...

(5)  Legal transactions concluded contrary to the provisions of this section shall be null and void.”

23.  The relevant provisions of the Local and Regional Self‑Government Act (Zakon o lokalnoj i područnoj (regionalnoj) samoupravi, Official Gazette, no. 33/2001, with subsequent amendments) read as follows:

Section 48

“(1)  The municipal mayor, city mayor, or county prefect:

...

manages immovable and movable property owned by the local or regional self‑government unit, together with related revenue and expenditure, in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations;

...”

Section 67

“(1)  The assets of a local or regional self-government unit shall include all movable and immovable property, and property rights.

(2)  A local or regional self-government unit must manage, use, and dispose of its assets with the diligence of a prudent manager.”

24.  The Decision on the lease of public areas in the municipality of Župa dubrovačka (Odluka o zakupu javnih površina Župe dubrovačke, Official Gazette of the municipality of Župa Dubrovačka nos. 1/2010 and 15/2013) set out the conditions and procedure for the lease of public areas within the municipality. It provided that “public areas” included land designated for general use in accordance with spatial planning documents (such as streets, squares, and public green areas), the management of which was entrusted to the mayor.

Section 9 of the Decision provided that the municipal mayor was to organise a public call for tenders specifying the key details of the lease, including the public area concerned, its intended use, the starting rent per square metre, the deposit, the deadline and procedure for submitting bids, the lease duration, and any other relevant conditions.

Section 12 of the Decision provided that the selection of the most favourable bidder in the public tender shall be made by the municipal mayor on the proposal of the municipal committee.

Section 13 of the Decision provided that, when selecting the most favourable bidder, the municipal mayor would give priority based on the following order: (1) lessees from the previous year who had duly fulfilled their contractual obligations; (2) Croatian disabled war veterans; (3) family members of Croatian war veterans who were killed in the war; (4) individuals employing such veterans or their family members on a permanent basis on the premises concerned; (5) individuals who had voluntarily joined the Croatian armed forces between 1991 and 1992; (6) members of the Croatian armed forces or police involved in the war for at least six consecutive months between 1991 and 1992; and (7) on an equal basis, persons with permanent residence in the municipality. Following a final decision on the selection of the most favourable bidder, a lease agreement was to be concluded.

DOMESTIC COURT PRACTICE

25.  On 28 April 2008 the Administrative Court of the Republic of Croatia (Upravni sud Republike Hrvatske)[1] adopted practice direction no. 7 Su‑618/08-3 which stipulated that “acts awarding the use of public areas” constituted administrative acts. Such acts were therefore subject to administrative judicial review.

26.  This approach changed in 2015. Specifically, in decision no. Usoz‑38/14-5 of 26 January 2015, delivered in the context of a tender procedure in which the mayor of Zagreb had granted a lease of immovable property to the Croatian Football Federation, the High Administrative Court held – without providing detailed reasoning – that the mayoral decision had not constituted an administrative act but rather an act of property management (raspolaganje imovinom). By decision no. U-III-1276/2015 of 14 November 2019 the Constitutional Court found that the High Administrative Court had given relevant and sufficient reasons for its conclusion and held that the complainant’s right of access to a court had not been violated.

27.  Following this shift, the administrative courts treated mayoral decisions granting the lease of property in tender procedures as acts of property management that were not subject to review, and declared related administrative actions inadmissible. That approach was applied in a line of cases between 2016 and 2020 concerning both decisions granting leases and decisions annulling tender procedures, and was regularly upheld on appeal.

28.  Accordingly, in the decisions of 25 March 2016 (Split Administrative Court, no. Usl-120/14-6, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 28 September 2016, no. Usž-2432/16-2), 11 June 2018 (Rijeka Administrative Court, no. Usl-607/18-2, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 30 August 2018, no. Usž-3293/18-2), and 4 November 2020 (High Administrative Court, no. Usž-1426/20-2), administrative actions against mayoral decisions awarding leases of business premises were declared inadmissible on the grounds that such decisions did not constitute administrative acts but rather acts of property management.

29.  The same reasoning was applied in various decisions annulling tender procedures. In the decisions of 24 April 2017 (Rijeka Administrative Court, no. UsI-499/17-3, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 1 March 2018, no. Usž-1964/17-2) and 30 November 2017 (Rijeka Administrative Court, no. UsI-1536/17-2, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 18 July 2018, no. Usž-157/2018-2), the courts held that such decisions constituted acts of property management and were not subject to review.

30.  In the latter line of cases, the Constitutional Court held, in its decision of 23 September 2020 (no. U-III-4030/2018), that judicial protection had to be ensured in respect of all individual acts by public authorities, regardless of their nature. It pointed out that all courts were under an obligation to safeguard the constitutional and Convention right to judicial protection, particularly when reviewing decisions of public authorities. It added that the courts had to ensure that all the parties had access to a court by interpreting the law purposively – that is, at a minimum, by directing them to another available form of effective legal protection or, if none existed, by explaining why judicial protection was not required.

31.  In a number of cases from 2018 onwards, the administrative courts reverted to their earlier position, again classifying decisions granting the use of public areas as administrative acts subject to administrative judicial review, in accordance with the 2008 practice direction (see paragraph 25 above). In those cases, the courts examined the merits and, where appropriate, set aside mayoral decisions for lack of reasoning or unlawfulness.

32.  For example, by judgment no. Usl-871/17-22 of 23 March 2018, the Rijeka Administrative Court held that, pursuant to the 2008 practice direction, a mayoral decision in a public tender granting the lease of a public area constituted an administrative decision and was as such amenable to judicial review. It set aside the decision, finding that it had lacked the required statutory elements, including the reasons for selecting the winning bid. By judgment no. Usž-3246/18-2 of 19 November 2020, the High Administrative Court upheld that judgment, emphasising that, if the reasons for selecting a bid were not provided, it was impossible to assess either the correctness of the established facts, or the lawfulness of the contested decision.

33.  By decision no. Usž-3307/17-2 of 13 December 2018, the High Administrative Court quashed a decision by the Split Administrative Court declaring inadmissible an administrative action to challenge a mayoral decision granting the lease of a public area in a public tender. Referring to the 2008 practice direction, it held that such decisions constituted administrative acts and ordered the lower court to examine the case on the merits.

34.  By decision no. Usž-4094/22-2 of 15 February 2023, the High Administrative Court quashed a decision by the Rijeka Administrative Court declaring inadmissible an administrative action against a mayoral decision, likewise relying on the 2008 practice direction.

35.  In the remitted proceedings, by judgment no. Usl-356/2023-7 of 5 September 2023 the Rijeka Administrative Court examined the case on the merits and set aside the mayoral decision. In the tender procedure at issue, the complainant had submitted the highest bid; however, another bidder had been given priority on the basis of local residency, invited to match the offer, and ultimately selected.

The Rijeka Administrative Court found that such preferential treatment on the basis of residence had directly conflicted with the principles of free‑market competition and the equal legal status of entrepreneurs guaranteed by Article 49 of the Croatian Constitution and set out in Article 4(2) of the Trade Act (cited at paragraphs 19 and 20 above). Those provisions stipulated that economic activity should be conducted freely and under equal market conditions, without any restrictions on or distortions to competition. By favouring “local” bidders, the contested decision had violated those principles.

It further clarified that although local authorities could grant preferential access to public services (such as childcare or social programmes) to their residents, this did not extend to economic activities. The lease of public areas for commercial purposes was not a public service but rather a means of facilitating private business. Municipalities therefore lacked authority to grant advantages to local entrepreneurs in this context.

The court further observed that the contested mechanism had created only an illusion of equality and although the highest bid appeared to be the decisive criterion, local bidders had been allowed to match competing offers after their disclosure, a privilege not afforded to others. This had conferred an unjust advantage, undermined genuine competition and had violated the requirement that all bidders were to compete on equal terms.

Lastly, the court held that the measure had been incompatible with EU law, in particular Directive 2006/123/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 on services in the internal market (“the Bolkenstein Directive”), which prohibited discrimination on the basis of the location of the registered office and did not recognise residence as a valid overriding public-interest justification for restricting the freedom to provide services.

36.  By judgment no. Usž-2721/2023-2 of 10 July 2024, the High Administrative Court upheld that judgment.

case_name: CASE OF HÁTTÉR TÁRSASÁG AND AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL MAGYARORSZÁG v. HUNGARY
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF HÁTTÉR TÁRSASÁG AND AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL MAGYARORSZÁG v. HUNGARY

(Application no. 43901/22)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

3 November 2026





This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of Háttér Társaság and Amnesty International Magyarország v. Hungary,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Arnfinn Bårdsen, President,
Jovan Ilievski,
Péter Paczolay,
Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir,
Stéphane Pisani,
Juha Lavapuro,
Hugh Mercer, judges,
and Andrea Tamietti, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 43901/22) against Hungary lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Hungarian organisations, Háttér Társaság (“the first applicant organisation”) and Amnesty International Hungary (“the second applicant organisation) (collectively “the applicant organisations”), on 22 August 2022;

the decision to give notice to the Hungarian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the observations submitted by the respondent Government and the observations in reply submitted by the applicant organisations;

the comments submitted by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, which was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The applicant organisations complain of a violation of their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention and a violation of their right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention arising from a decision of the National Election Commission (hereinafter, “the NEC”) imposing fines on them for calling on voters to cast invalid ballots in a national referendum.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant organisations are based in Budapest. They were represented by Mr Tordai, a lawyer practising in Budapest.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. Tallódi, of the Ministry of Justice.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

BACKGROUND OF THE CASE

5.  In July 2021 the Hungarian Government organised a referendum, the stated aim of which was the protection of children’s best interests. They submitted the following questions to the NEC with a view to their being put to the people in the referendum: 1) “Do you agree with the idea of workshops presenting different sexual orientations being held for underage children in public education institutions, without the consent of their parents?” 2) “Do you agree with the promotion of gender reassignment surgeries to underage children?” 3) “Do you agree with the unrestricted exposure of underage children to sexually explicit media content that may influence their development?” 4) “Do you agree with the broadcasting of media content showing gender reassignment?” 5) “Do you agree with gender reassignment surgery being made accessible to underage children?”

6.  Following legal challenges, the President of the Republic announced that the referendum would be held on 3 April 2022 (“the 2022 Referendum”) and that it would include only the first four of the above-mentioned five questions.

7.   The applicant organisations, together with twelve other civil-society organisations, initiated a campaign encouraging voters to cast invalid ballots because they considered that the questions included in the referendum were misleading and promoted homophobic and transphobic policies.

8.  The referendum was held on 3 April 2022, on the same day as a general election. Approximately 1,700,000 voters casted an invalid ballot. The invalid votes constituted about 30% of the ballots cast. The results of the referendum were therefore invalid with respect to all four questions as the majority of all registered voters did not cast a valid vote.

PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT ORGANISATIONS
Decisions of the NEC

9.  Following a complaint by a third party, the NEC found that the first applicant organisation, by publishing on its Facebook page posts calling on voters to cast an invalid ballot, had infringed the “principle of exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose” (rendeltetésszerű joggyakorlás) laid down in section 2(1)(e) of Act no. XXXVI of 2013 on Electoral Procedure (hereinafter, “the EPA”, see paragraph 24 below). In a decision of 8 April 2022 (no. 324/2022) the NEC ordered the first applicant organisation to pay a fine of 3,000,000 Hungarian forints (HUF – approximately 7,400 euros (EUR)). The NEC explained that voters had the right to cast invalid ballots, but that a campaign encouraging voters to do so was not compatible with the purposes of the referendum. It continued that the first applicant organisation’s campaign activity had not been aimed at encouraging people to express their will but rather at obstructing the purpose of the referendum, which was to allow the people to express their will as legislators.

10.  On the same day, also following a complaint by a third party, the NEC issued decision no. 328/2022 finding that the applicant organisations had operated the website ervenytelenul.hu (meaning “invalid”), which had contained a call on voters to “Cast an invalid vote in response to an invalid question”. The website had advised voters how to mark their ballots at the referendum such that they were invalid. For the same reasons as in decision no. 324/2022, the NEC found that the applicant organisations’ campaign activity had infringed section 2(1)(e) of the EPA and the “principle of the exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose”. The NEC did not find it necessary to impose a fine on the applicant organisations, as the campaign period had terminated.

Decisions of the Kúria

11.  The first applicant organisation sought judicial review of decision no. 342/2022 (see paragraph 9 above) before the Kúria.
