It pointed out that a referendum was a direct manifestation of popular sovereignty; consequently, the referendum campaigning period that preceded referendums served as a crucial forum for the discussion of public affairs. Encouraging voters to adopt a certain conduct in respect of a referendum fell within the most highly protected aspect of the right to freedom of expression, as recognised in Article IX § 1 of the Fundamental Law. The purpose of referendum campaigning was to influence voters regarding whether to participate in a referendum and how to vote. In the view of the first applicant organisation, encouraging voters to cast an invalid vote, which was their lawful choice, was not contrary to the purpose of the referendum campaigning period. Thus, its own conduct of encouraging the casting of invalid votes had not violated the purpose of the referendum campaigning period but remained strictly within its scope. The first applicant organisation argued that the contested NEC decision imposing a fine for the infringement of the principle of exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose was not in accordance with section 2(1)(e) of the EPA.

12.  In its decision no. Kvk.IV.39.419/2022/4 of 13 April 2022 the Kúria rejected the first applicant organisation’s claim for judicial review without an examination of the merits. It held that although the first applicant organisation had formally cited a fundamental principle set out in the EPA, it had failed to demonstrate the specific grounds for its contention that the NEC decision did not conform to that provision. It had not explained why section 2(1)(e) of the EPA could not be interpreted in the way the NEC had done. Furthermore, although the first applicant organisation had stated that the NEC decision had disregarded the fundamental rights aspect of the case, it had failed to lay out the precise interests, rights or constitutional values which it claimed the NEC had failed to balance, or to explain what it thought the outcome of such a balancing exercise should have been.

13.  The applicant organisations also sought judicial review of the NEC’s decision no. 328/2022 (see paragraph 10 above), including essentially the same reasoning as had been presented in the claim for judicial review lodged by the first applicant organisation (see paragraph 11 above). In addition, the applicant organisations submitted that the restriction of their campaign activity could only have been justified if there had been a specific statutory basis for doing so and if the restriction had been necessary and proportionate. However, no specific statutory provision prohibited encouraging the casting of an invalid vote, nor was such a prohibition strictly necessary to ensure the exercise of another fundamental right or to protect a constitutional value; consequently, section 2(1)(e) of the EPA could be interpreted in a manner consistent with the Fundamental Law that would not render campaign activity encouraging the casting of an invalid vote unlawful.

14.  In decision no. Kvk.IV.39.420/2022/4 of 13 April 2022 the Kúria dismissed the claim for judicial review, on the same grounds as in decision no. Kvk.IV.39.419/2022/4 (see paragraph 12 above).

Decisions of the Constitutional Court

15.   The applicant organisations each lodged constitutional complaints, arguing that the Kúria’s decisions had infringed their right to freedom of expression, as protected by Article IX of the Fundamental Law, and their right to a fair trial, as protected by Article XXVIII of the Fundamental Law. They submitted that the Kúria had failed to adjudicate the merits of their claims and had not addressed their arguments concerning their campaign promoting the casting of invalid ballots, thereby disregarding the fundamental-rights element of their claim. They reiterated that the NEC’s decision restricting their right to freedom of expression had no legal basis and had been disproportionate.

16.  The Constitutional Court rejected the complaints on 22 April 2022 (decisions nos. 3216/2022 (V.11)AB and 3217/2022 (V.11)AB) on the same grounds. As regards the complaint concerning the alleged infringement of the right to a fair trial, the Constitutional Court held that the complaints did not raise a constitutional issue but challenged the legality of the Kúria’s decision. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant organisations’ argument that the Kúria had reached different conclusions in cases similar to theirs, reasoning that the Kúria was bound by the content of the claim for judicial review and finding that no information had been submitted to substantiate the contention that the Kúria had ruled differently on claims that were identical in terms of form and substance. As regards the alleged violation of the right to freedom of expression, the Constitutional Court reasoned in essence that the legality of the NEC’s decision had not been examined by the Kúria for procedural reasons, and that an examination by the Kúria was a precondition for a constitutional review.

OTHER CASES BEFORE THE DOMESTIC AUTHORITIES

17.  On 8 April 2022 the NEC issued three other decisions.

18.  In decision no. 325/2022 the NEC fined the second applicant organisation HUF 3,000,000 (approximately EUR 7,400) for publishing Facebook posts calling on voters to cast invalid ballots, in breach of section 2(1)(e) of the EPA.

19.  Following a claim for judicial review lodged by the second applicant organisation, the Kúria overturned the NEC’s decision (decision no. Kvk.V.39.421/2022/5) on 15 April 2022, holding that campaign activities formed part of the freedom to express opinions on public affairs. They could only be restricted to in order to give effect to another fundamental right or to protect a constitutional value, and even then only to the extent strictly necessary, in proportion to the intended objective and while respecting the essential content of the fundamental right (see paragraph 25 below).

20.  In decision no. 327/2022 the NEC fined the applicant organisations and fourteen other civil-society organisations HUF 176,400 (approximately EUR 430) each for publishing on the website of the second applicant organisation a political announcement which the NEC considered to be in breach of the principle of exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose.

21.  The civil-society organisations lodged a claim for judicial review of the decision with the Kúria. On 15 April 2022 by decision no. Kvk.V.39.422/2022/3 the Kúria overturned the NEC’s decision, reasoning that in the event of a conflict between the fundamental principle that rights had to be exercised in good faith and in accordance with their purpose – as set forth in section 2(1)(e) of the EPA – and the fundamental right of voters to freedom of expression, the latter could not be restricted without a constitutional basis and a statutory mandate. The Kúria held that the claimants had taken a position on a matter of public interest regarding the casting of invalid votes in the referendum and had exercised their fundamental right to freedom of expression; that right could not be lawfully restricted on the grounds cited by the NEC (see paragraph 26 below).

22.  In decision no. 329/2020 the NEC held that a civil-society organisation, the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union, had breached section 2(1)(e) of the EPA by publishing on its website a call to “cast an invalid ballot in the Government’s discriminatory referendum!”. The NEC did not find it necessary to impose a fine on the organisation, as the campaign period had ended.

23.  In decision no. Kvk.VI.39.423/2022/6 of 15 April 2022, the Kúria overturned the NEC’s decision. The Kúria held that the exercise of the right to freedom of expression – guaranteed by the Fundamental Law – by the Civil Liberties Union during its campaign activity could not be classified as a violation of the fundamental principle set forth in section 2(1)(e) of the EPA in the absence of an explicit statutory restriction established with detailed reasoning by the NEC (see paragraph 27 below).

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

24.  The relevant domestic law is set out in the case of Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt v. Hungary ([GC], no. 201/17, §§ 31-32, 20 January 2020). Additional relevant provisions of the EPA read as follow:

Judicial review

Section 222

“(1) A natural person, a legal entity or an organisation without legal personality affected by the case may submit a claim for judicial review against a second-instance decision of an election commission or a decision of the [NEC].

...”

Section 229

“(1)  The Kúria shall adjudicate such claims for judicial review.

(2)  The court shall decide on claims for judicial review in non-contentious proceedings, in a panel composed of five professional judges.

...”

Section 233

“(1) A constitutional complaint against a judicial decision – given pursuant to this Act in the context of a legal remedy concerning a decision of an election body – may be lodged with the Constitutional Court within three days of the handing down of the contested decision.

(2) The Constitutional Court shall decide on a constitutional complaint against a judicial decision – given pursuant to this Act in the context of a legal remedy concerning a decision of an election body – within five days of its receipt.

...”

25.  Decision no. Kvk.V.39.421/2022/5 of the Kúria (see paragraph 19 above) contains the following relevant passages:

“...

[53] In its decisions nos. 3313/2019 (XI. 21.) and 3279/2019 (XI. 5.), the Constitutional Court established that, pursuant to Article I § 3 of the Fundamental Law, the right to freedom of expression may only be restricted by an Act of Parliament; therefore, in the absence of an express statutory provision, the necessity of restricting a fundamental right cannot be established by judicial interpretation.

[54] Given that there is no statutory provision restricting or prohibiting the casting of an invalid vote or calling [on people] to do so – and considering that an invalid vote qualifies as a vote – the claimant’s campaign activity did not effectively infringe upon the essence of the referendum as defined by the Fundamental Law, nor did it affect the voting autonomy of citizens.

[55] Accordingly, in the view of the Kúria, the claimant’s freedom of speech – which enjoys a heightened level of protection during a campaign – cannot lawfully be restricted by invoking the purpose of the referendum.

[56] The Kúria has found that the [NEC] failed to recognise that the [case] involved a potential restriction of the claimant’s fundamental right to freedom of expression and thus failed to take into account that such a fundamental right may only be restricted in accordance with Article I § 3 of the Fundamental Law. Instead, it erroneously proceeded from the premise that the stage of the referendum process concerning the validation of questions requires examining whether an unequivocal answer can be given to the questions and whether the ballot paper excludes any third response option alongside “yes” and “no”. The objection concerned the referendum campaign rather than the validation stage; consequently, the criteria for its assessment necessarily differ. The decision of the [NEC] – challenged via a claim for [judicial] review – has resulted in the restriction of one of the claimant’s highly protected fundamental rights without constitutional grounds or a legal basis.

...

[58] The Kúria maintains its interpretation set forth in decision no. Kvk.IV.37.359/2014/2, according to which a violation of the requirement to exercise rights in accordance with their purpose does not follow from a mere finding of a legal infringement; there must be an obvious intent to exploit the substance of the legal institution in an unlawful manner under the guise of formal compliance with the law. According to the Kúria[‘s case-law], although a call to cast an invalid vote may run counter to the constitutional purpose of the referendum as a legal institution and to the spirit of the Initiating Referendums, European Citizens’ Initiative and Referendum Procedure Act and the [EPA], thereby potentially raising the issue of an exercise of rights contrary to their intended purpose, freedom of speech warrants special protection, even in the context of a referendum initiated by the Government, and its restriction would have been permissible only on constitutional and lawful grounds. Through their campaign activity, the claimant was exercising their fundamental right to freedom of expression, which cannot be lawfully restricted based on the grounds cited by the [NEC]. In the posts to which objection was raised, the claimant did not act abusively but rather – exercising its constitutional right – encouraged visitors to their social media page to cast invalid votes as an expression of their opinion on a matter of public interest; thus, they did not violate the fundamental principle of referendum procedure requiring the exercise of rights in good faith and in accordance with their intended purpose, as stipulated in section 2(1)(e) of the [EPA], as applicable pursuant to section 1(1) of the Initiating Referenda, European Citizens’ Initiative and Referendum Procedure Act.

...”

26.  Decision no. Kvk.V.39.422/2022/3 of the Kúria (see paragraph 21 above) contains the following relevant passages:

“...

[30] ... Under Article XXIII § 7 of the Fundamental Law, participation in a referendum is not an obligation for voters but a fundamental right; voters may exercise that right by abstaining from the referendum, or by participating and casting either a valid or an invalid vote. Casting an invalid vote does not constitute a violation of law; rather, it expresses the voter’s intent to refrain from making a substantive decision regarding the questions posed. The expression of opinion by the claimants participating in the referendum campaign – and their influencing of how voters exercise their right to participate in the referendum (in the manner described in the statement) – does not infringe upon essence of the referendum as a constitutional value under the Fundamental Law, nor does it impair the voting autonomy of the electorate, given that voters have a lawful means of exercising their referendum rights through abstention or by casting an invalid vote.

...

[32] ... The practice of the Constitutional Court is also consistent in finding that public communications (when the information shared is related to public life) are subject to enhanced fundamental-law protection. Decision 7/2014. (III. 7.) AB pointed out: ‘Freedom of speech requires special protection when it affects public affairs and the exercise of public power by persons performing public duties or taking part in public life. [Where] persons participating in the exercise of public power [are concerned], a restriction of freedom of expression would be justified in a much narrower range of cases under the constitutional requirements arising from the democratic rule of law.’ ...

...

[34] Regarding the requirement of exercising rights in accordance with their purpose, the [NEC] decision referred to the consistent judicial practice embodied in the Kúria’s decision no. Kvk.IV.37.359/2014/2. According to this practice, the requirement to exercise rights in accordance with their purpose – derived from civil law regulations prohibiting the abuse of rights – permeates the entire legal system. It implies that those entitled to exercise legal rights must do so in a manner consistent with the specific purpose and substance of those rights. Statutory protection and recognition are accorded only to the exercise of a right where its true substance is discernible beyond mere formal compliance with the rules governing that right. A violation of the requirement to exercise rights in accordance with their purpose goes beyond a mere finding of illegality; it must be an obvious intent to exploit the substance of the legal institution under the guise of formal compliance. In the present case, the Kúria has held that while a call to cast an invalid vote might conflict with the constitutional purpose of the referendum and the spirit of the relevant Acts (the Initiating Referenda, European Citizens’ Initiative and Referendum Procedure Act and the [EPA]), thereby potentially raising the issue of exercising a right contrary to its intended purpose, freedom of speech – specifically the expression of opinion on matters of public interest, including in the context of a referendum initiated by the Government – merits special protection; any restriction thereof is permissible only on the basis of the constitutional and legal grounds.

...

[37] ... Undoubtedly, the will of the people manifested through a referendum may be expressed not only by casting “yes” or “no” votes but also by a voter abstaining or – albeit with a different effect – casting an invalid vote. As the claimants rightly pointed out, the latter – as an expression of political opinion – constitutes a position that voters may adopt and articulate, regardless of the fact that its effect amounts to an exercise of rights contrary to their intended purpose. Indeed, there is no provision of law prohibiting a campaign message advocating the casting of an invalid vote. When assessing any restriction on political opinion, due regard must always be paid to the right to freedom of expression and the heightened constitutional protection afforded to political communication.

[38] The claimants correctly derived the primacy of freedom of expression from Article I § 3 of the Fundamental Law; freedom of expression holds a distinguished place among constitutional fundamental rights, and it cannot be curtailed simply by classifying a call to cast an invalid vote as an exercise of rights contrary to their intended purpose.

[39] Consequently, based on the arguments set forth in the claim for judicial review, no violation of section 2(1)(e) of the [EPA] could be established.

...”

27.  Decision no. Kvk.VI.39.423/2022/6 of the Kúria (see paragraph 23 above) contains the following relevant passages:

“...

[49] Constitutional Court decision no. 3313/2019 (XI. 21.) AB clearly stated that campaign activities not prohibited by the [EPA] are lawful, and that the fundamental principles of the [EPA] must also prevail during the campaign period. The aim of activities carried out during an election campaign is to influence, or attempt to influence, the will of the electorate. When assessing restrictions on campaign activities, due regard must always be given to the right to freedom of expression and the heightened constitutional protection afforded to political communication.

[50] The decision of the [NEC] does not state that the fundamental principle set out in section 2(1)(e) of the [EPA], or the provisions concerning election campaigns, restrict in any manner or to any extent the fundamental rights of participation in a national referendum and freedom of expression. In the absence of a statutory restriction – established and justified in detail by the NEC with reference to the provisions of the Fundamental Law – the expression of an opinion by the claimant during its campaign activity (a right guaranteed by the Fundamental Law) cannot be objected to.

[51] While the claimant’s campaign activity encouraged people to cast invalid votes, it did not affect the voters’ participation in the referendum or their voting autonomy. Voters remained free to decide, if they choose to exercise their right to participate, whether to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’, or to deliberately cast an invalid vote.

[52] The [NEC] was required to evaluate the claimant’s campaign activity, not the result that emerged as a consequence of that activity. It had to assess the campaign activity independently, rather than in the light of the result.

[53] In decisions nos. Kvk.III.37.107/2008/2, Kvk.IV.37.468/2006/2 and KvkIII.37.211/2006/3, the Supreme Court, in accordance with Act C of 1997 on Electoral Procedure, established that a violation of the fundamental principle of exercising rights in good faith and for their intended purpose occurs when election participants exercise their election-related rights in a manner intended to mislead voters, by concealing or distorting facts, thereby diminishing the electoral prospects of their political opponents.

[54] In decisions nos. Kvk.IV.37.359/2014/2 and Kvk.I.37.394/2014/2, the Kúria, addressing the principle of exercising rights in good faith and in accordance with their purpose, found that the requirement to exercise rights for their intended purpose is one that permeates the entire legal system, including the rules of the [EPA]; this requirement derives from civil law regulations prohibiting the abuse of rights, dictating that the subjects of legal institutions may utilise them only in a manner consistent with their specific purpose and substance. Legal protection and recognition are only afforded to the exercise of a right when it reflects the true substance [and purpose of that right], beyond the formal requirements of the entitlement. A violation of the principle of exercising rights in accordance with their purpose goes beyond the mere establishment of an infringement: it must clearly manifest an intent to exploit the substance of a legal institution while ostensibly complying with the law.

[55] The claimant’s campaign activity, as established by the [NEC], could not have infringed upon freedom of expression, given the absence of statutory restrictions on the relevant Fundamental Law provisions; nor did it involve any intentional violation aimed at curtailing the will of the electorate or misleading voters; consequently, no violation of the fundamental principles of good faith and the exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose could be established.

...”
target_issue: Freedom of expression; Freedom to impart information; Freedom to receive ideas
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Hungary of Article 10 (Freedom of expression) concerning Freedom of expression; Freedom to impart information; Freedom to receive ideas in this case

case_name: CASE OF TAŞ v. TÜRKİYE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF TAŞ v. TÜRKİYE

(Application no. 40838/23)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

3 November 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Taş v. Türkiye,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Jovan Ilievski, President,
Gediminas Sagatys,
Hugh Mercer, judges,
and Dorothee von Arnim, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 40838/23) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 9 November 2023 by a Turkish national, Mr Ersan Taş (“the applicant”), who was born in 1984, lives in Istanbul and was represented by Mr K. Altıparmak, a lawyer practising in Ankara;

the decision to give notice of complaint concerning Article 10 of the Convention to the Turkish Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Mr Abdullah Aydın, Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye, and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;

the parties’ observations;

the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the examination of the application by a Committee;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The application concerns a prison sentence combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, imposed on the applicant following his criminal conviction for the offences of insulting the President of the Republic and insulting a public official.

2.  At the time of the events in question the applicant was the holder of an account on the social media platform then called Twitter. The applicant’s account, named “@06melihchina”, was followed by more than 55,000 users of the platform. It was a parody account that portrayed jokes concerning the then mayor of Ankara, İ.M.G.

3.  On 24 September 2014 the official account of İ.M.G. on the same platform posted a photo and a mocking statement in respect of the then chairman of the main opposition party, K.K. On the same day, the applicant made a comment under that post. The applicant’s comment included a derisive image pertaining to the President and İ.M.G. accompanied by the following statement: “We continue to work and steal tirelessly with our President, God willing” (Cumhurbaşkanımızla birlikte hiç durmadan çalışmaya ve çalmaya devam ediyoruz Allah’ın izniyle).

4.  On 17 December 2014 İ.M.G filed a criminal complaint against the applicant on account of the content of his comment.

5.  On 26 September 2017 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance (hereinafter “the Criminal Court”) sentenced the applicant to eleven months and twenty days’ and ten months’ imprisonment for insulting the President of the Republic and insulting a public official on account of his functions, respectively. It decided, however, to suspend the pronouncement of the judgment under Article 231 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see, for the text of this provision at the material time, Durukan and Birol v. Türkiye, nos. 14879/20 and 13440/21, § 23, 3 October 2023) and to apply a five‑year supervision period.

6.  On 9 November 2017 the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the objection lodged by the applicant against that decision, finding that it had been made in accordance with both procedural and substantial law.

7.  On 20 December 2017 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, he complained, inter alia, about his conviction owing to the comment in question.

8.  On 29 March 2023 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression, in a judgment grouping similar applications, in accordance with its findings in its Atilla Yazar and Others judgment (see, for detailed information regarding that judgment, Durukan and Birol, cited above, §§ 28-31).

9.  To redress the violation, the Constitutional Court ordered a retrial and decided to send a copy of its judgment to the Criminal Court for the reopening of the criminal proceedings. Moreover, it ordered the reimbursement of the court fees paid by the applicant before the Criminal Court, as well as his legal representation costs. However, it rejected the applicant’s just satisfaction claims in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The decision was served on the applicant’s lawyer on 13 July 2023.

10.  On 9 November 2023 the applicant introduced his application before the Court.

11.  On the same day, the applicant lodged a petition with the Criminal Court seeking a retrial in order to secure the implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgment.

12.  On 12 December 2023 the Criminal Court rejected the applicant’s request with a final decision, stating that the Constitutional Court had not yet delivered its decision concerning the applicant’s individual application.

13.  On 15 November 2024 the Constitutional Court filed a petition with the Criminal Court requesting information on the retrial proceedings.

14.  On 21 November 2024 the Criminal Court informed the Constitutional Court that the retrial proceedings had not been commenced, without providing any reasons.

15.  In his application to the Court, relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complained that his right to freedom of expression had been breached on account of his conviction and prison sentence, combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, owing to a comment he had posted on social media.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Türkiye of Article 10 (Freedom of expression) concerning Freedom of expression in this case

case_name: CASE OF F.W. v. SPAIN
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF F.W. v. SPAIN

(Application no. 8122/24)







JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

5 November 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of F.W. v. Spain,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Kateřina Šimáčková, President,
María Elósegui,
Andreas Zünd,
Diana Sârcu,
Mykola Gnatovskyy,
Sébastien Biancheri,
Nicholas Emiliou, judges,
and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 8122/24) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Syrian national, Ms F.W. (“the applicant”), on 16 March 2024;

the decision to give notice to the Spanish Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the decision not to have the applicant’s name disclosed;

the observations submitted by the respondent Government and the observations in reply submitted by the applicant;

the comments submitted by Fundación Save the Children, Gentium, MEDUSA Human Rights, Plena Inclusión España and Women’s Link Worldwide, who were granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The case concerns the declaration of the applicant’s children as being in a situation of neglect and their subsequent placement in care. Three provisional administrative decisions taken in May 2018 were confirmed by an administrative decision in December 2020, which was subsequently upheld by the domestic courts. The applicant argued that the decisions had violated her right to family life under Article 8 of the Convention. She also alleged discrimination contrary to Article 14 of the Convention, taken in conjunction with Article 8, stating that the decisions had been influenced by her status as a woman with a disability and by her socio-economic circumstances.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1981 and lives in Madrid. The applicant was represented by Ms P. García de Viedma Alonso, a lawyer practising in Madrid.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Brezmes Martínez de Villarreal.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

family circumstances prior to the declaration that the children were in a situation of neglect

5.  The applicant is a Syrian woman. She has four children: a girl born in 2010 (child A), a boy born in 2011 (child B), a boy born in 2016 (child C) and a girl born in November 2018 (child D).

6.  According to a certificate issued in January 2019 the applicant has a 79% disability on account of functional limitations in both the upper and lower limbs. The decision was considered as definitive as there were no prospects of improvement. Other documents in the file mention a disability of 86% or 88% but they do not seem to be based on any official assessment.

7.  Her second child, B, has a disability resulting from cerebral palsy. According to a document issued in Türkiye in 2017 the degree of his disability was assessed at 76%. A certificate issued in Spain in 2023 indicated that he suffered from a neuro-muscular dysfunction caused by cerebral palsy and dyskinesia syndrome of perinatal origin. His disability was assessed at 80%.

8.  In July 2017 the applicant and her family arrived in Spain from Türkiye in the framework of a resettlement programme and were granted subsidiary protection. They were given accommodation in a refugee reception centre (hereinafter “the CAR”) in the Madrid region and were granted additional material assistance and access to healthcare.

9.  On 27 July 2017 the applicant and her husband at the time, I.A., had an argument in the CAR during which he slapped her in the face in front of their children. On 5 September 2017 I.A. was convicted of the offence of domestic violence (malos tratos en el ámbito familiar) and sentenced to nine months and one day of imprisonment. On 6 June 2018 the prison sentence was suspended for two years subject to conditions, including that I.A. refrain from approaching the applicant and/or communicating with her.

10.  Meanwhile on 14 September 2017 the applicant, I.A. and the children voluntarily left the reception centre and moved to Germany.

11.  In April 2018 the family returned to Spain and, having lost their place at the CAR, they were accommodated in a social emergency reception centre (SAMUR Social – hereinafter “the SAMUR”).

12.  A report issued by the CAR on 18 April 2018, subsequently submitted to the Directorate General on Family and Children of the Madrid Region (“the DGFC”), provided details on the interventions carried out in respect of the family. It noted that the family had been provided with medical care and material assistance (approximately 2,000 euros (EUR)) upon arrival and that, following coordination between several public and private institutions, they had been provided with wheelchairs for the applicant and B and other equipment. It further indicated that I.A. had beaten the applicant but she had not wanted to report him, and that there were suspicions of ill-treatment by I.A. against the applicant and the children. It further noted the existence of criminal proceedings against I.A., and the fact that the family had left the centre. It observed that the family had sometimes refused to attend medical appointments and that the applicant had refused the assistance of the centre’s staff, so A had been taking care of the applicant and the younger children. Lastly, it noted that the applicant and I.A. had had a negative attitude despite the assistance provided.

administrative proceedings declaring the applicant’s children to be in a situation of neglecT and the family’s circumstances during that period (may 2018 - december 2020)

13.  On 21 May 2018 the SAMUR sent a report to the Child Guardianship Authority (“the Guardianship Authority”) of the DGFC asking it to take protection measures in respect of the three children. It indicated that the applicant was not able to carry out basic day-to-day activities, that she had refused the assistance of caregivers during her stay at the CAR, and that A was taking care of both the applicant and B. It further stated that I.A. had been expelled from the reception centre for repeatedly violating the centre’s rules, acting in an aggressive manner towards his family and staff, and being accused of sexually abusing another resident. It added that following his expulsion, he had returned to the centre intoxicated and had demonstrated sexually inappropriate behaviour towards A.

14.  On 22 May 2018 the DGFC started the proceedings to assume guardianship (tutela) of the three children, observing that there was a possible situation of neglect (desamparo).

15.  The SAMUR subsequently sent a second report on the children’s situation. It stated that since I.A.’s expulsion from the centre the children had been under the staff’s care, as their mother was unable to take care of them. It stated that the parents had not been informed of the request for protection measures, as they feared the family would flee, noting in that regard that they had previously left the CAR, that they had financial means and that I.A. was in contact with other members of the family.

16.  On 24 May 2018 the Guardianship Authority issued three separate decisions declaring the children A, B and C as being in a situation of neglect. The decisions indicated that the children were lacking protection based on the following grounds:

“– Children of Syrian origin, provisionally hosted in the SAMUR.

– [I.A.] expelled from the centre for sexual aggression against another resident, with a restraining order from the centre. His current whereabouts are unknown. He has been accused of gender violence against [the applicant] – without conviction. Abuse of alcohol.

– [The applicant] has an 86% disability, is six months pregnant ... and is unable to perform basic day-to-day activities.

– [The applicant] is not aware of the situation and refuses medical assistance for her and the children, one of them with a 76% disability. Victim of gender [violence] by [I.A.]

– [The applicant] refuses to be assisted by professionals in caring for the children and does not have relatives who can assist them.

– [The applicant] lacks the necessary capacity to take care of and protect her children.

– The SAMUR is arranging a place in a centre for persons with disabilities for [the applicant].

In accordance with Article 172 of the Civil Code this is to be considered as a situation of neglect, owing to the inadequate exercise of the protection duties established by law on parents [regarding] their children and because the child is being deprived of the necessary moral and material assistance.

In accordance with section 10 of Decree no. 121/1988 of 23 November 1988, as amended by Decree no. 17/1992 of 12 November 19992 of the Madrid Community, in relation to section 53 of Law no. 6/1995 of 28 March 1995 on Safeguards of the rights of children and adolescents of the Madrid Community, and other related rules, [it is decided]:

– To declare that the child is in a situation of neglect.

– To assume guardianship of the child on a provisional basis through this public authority, pending completion of the proceedings.

– The [guardianship] will be provisionally exercised under the custody of the director of a protection centre of the Madrid Community.”

17.  The decisions indicated that the applicant and I.A. could request a review by the board of the Guardianship Authority and that the decisions could be challenged before a first-instance court. Furthermore, the applicant and I.A. could ask for the termination of the guardianship arrangement within the next two years if there was a change in circumstances. The applicant did not appeal against those decisions.

18.  On 25 May 2018 the three children were transferred to an initial protection centre (centro de primera acogida). According to the documents in the file, the applicant could visit the children, but they were not authorised to leave the centre with her on weekends or during holidays.

19.  On 4 June 2018 the children were examined by the centre’s doctor, who reported that they were in a good general condition. With regard to B, the doctor stated that his condition had to be further examined to confirm a diagnosis and that some of the tests that had been recommended had not been performed.

20.  On 20 June 2018 the DGFC refused a request by the applicant to allow the children to spend the weekends with her out of the centre, considering that such an arrangement was not appropriate at that time. The decision noted that the applicant had a stable emotional bond with the children, but required assistance to take care of them, and it was not possible for the staff of the centre where she was living to take care of the children on the weekends.

21.  On 4 July 2018 the children were transferred to a different child protection centre (“the CPC”).

22.  In July 2018 the SAMUR sent an updated report stating that the applicant was being provisionally accommodated at a centre for persons with disabilities until a more permanent place could be found. The report concluded that the applicant had a high level of dependency and required assistance from third parties which, together with a lack of support from I.A. and a lack of financial means, made family reunification unfeasible.

23.  On 19 July 2018 the applicant and I.A. had a meeting with an officer from the Guardianship Authority. According to the minutes of the meeting, they were informed about the protection measure and that if the situation changed, the children would be returned to their care. They were further informed of the importance of asking for assistance from social services and other institutions, in particular in relation to housing and employment.

24.  On 5 September 2018 the SAMUR submitted an updated report, in which it stated that the request for protection measures had resulted from I.A.’s expulsion from the centre. It explained that no stable place in a centre for persons with disabilities had been found for the applicant yet and that, while the SAMUR was providing basic assistance, it was not assisting in family matters. The report concluded that there was a significant emotional bond between the applicant and her children, and that “the problem was [the applicant’s] lack of capacity to take care of her children and to ensure adequate attention to all their needs”. It noted in that regard that I.A. could not be considered as an adequate source of support or a positive point of reference for the family.

25.  On 26 September 2018 the applicant had another meeting with an officer from the Guardianship Authority. She was informed of the grounds justifying the measures and she expressed her disagreement with the reports on which the measures had been based.

26.  In September 2018 the CPC where the children were staying sent an information request to the DGFC. According to the CPC, the applicant and I.A. had asked to visit their children since their admission to the centre, and they had been granted a weekly visit taking place on its premises, and two telephone calls per week. In addition, the CPC stated that the children’s relationship with their parents was good, and that the parents were affectionate towards the children. The CPC stressed the difficulties in establishing a working programme with the children in the absence of clear information concerning the restraining order imposed on I.A. in respect of the applicant and the alleged sexual behaviour of I.A. towards A and whether it had been reported. In reply, the DGFC informed the CPC of the criminal proceedings against I.A. (see paragraph 9 above) and that it had reported I.A.’s sexual behaviour towards A on 12 September 2018. Following the receipt of that information, the CPC suspended the joint visits by the applicant and I.A. It appears that at least for some time I.A. did not visit the children. There is no further information in the file about any criminal proceedings against I.A. in respect of a possible sexual offence against A or about any investigative or protective measures taken in that connection.

27.  In November 2018 the CPC sent a report to the DGFC providing information about the children’s situation.

Regarding A, the report noted that she had difficulties managing her emotions, had frequent arguments with other children and displayed sexualised behaviour. It stressed that she was very close to the applicant and mentioned the fondling incident involving her father.

Concerning B, the report referred to his cerebral palsy and his need for support with daily activities, noting that he was showing greater autonomy and improving his communication abilities. He was respectful and had a good relationship with other children and with his siblings. It was noted that he was attached to his father and it was hard for him to say goodbye at the end of his parents’ visits.

With regard to C, it was observed that he did not have any special needs, apart from those corresponding to his age (22 months at the relevant time). He was happy to see his siblings and was calm after the applicant’s visits. A placement with a foster family was proposed as the family situation would not improve in the short or medium term.

The CPC indicated that the guardianship measure should be confirmed by the board of the Guardianship Authority and proposed a placement with a foster family for B and C. With regard to A, it stated that it would be more appropriate for her to stay in the CPC, as an educational intervention was needed to ensure her emotional stability, given her personal circumstances.

28.  In another report of November 2018 the CPC proposed placing B and C with different foster families, as both of them required a significant level of attention, owing to B’s disability and C’s young age. It further indicated that visits between the three siblings should be maintained once they were placed in family foster care, as they had a good relationship with each other.

29.  On 11 November 2018 the applicant gave birth to her fourth child, D. A “protection file” was opened in respect of D by the DGFC, but she remained under the applicant’s care. They were both subsequently hosted by a private foundation, Fundación Madrina, which was asked to periodically report on their situation.

30.  On 20 December 2018 the applicant lodged a claim with the DGFC seeking the revocation of the decision declaring the children to be in a situation of neglect and its replacement with a voluntary custody arrangement (guarda) for a period of two years, to be extended if necessary. She argued that she had not opposed the decision within the two-month time-limit because she had been unaware of that possibility. She affirmed that the measure had been disproportionate as her disability, lack of resources and status as a victim of domestic violence were not grounds to declare the children as being in a situation of neglect. She asserted that she had never been negligent in respect of her children, and that a voluntary custody arrangement would have been more appropriate. She stated that she was staying at an NGO facility with her newborn child and that she was taking steps to address her circumstances so as to be reunited with her children. She further asked for an increase in the number of visits with her children, and for them to be allowed to spend the Christmas holiday with her. The applicant referred to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and to the Supreme Court’s case-law according to which a situation of neglect should only be declared in cases where parents neglected the protection, care and attention of the children’s basic needs, and not because of economic difficulties.

31.  On 9 January 2019 the CPC issued an updated report on the children, in which it stated that the applicant showed mistrust towards the CPC. It further noted that I.A. was visiting the children every week.

32.  In February 2019 the CPC issued another report assessing the possibility of allowing the children to visit the applicant on the weekends. The report stated that the children had been authorised to visit the applicant at the apartment where she was residing for a few hours on Sundays and that they were very happy about it. It was thus considered that weekend visits could be authorised as long as necessary support to take care of the children was ensured and the restraining order imposed on I.A. was respected.

33.  On 20 March 2019 Fundación Madrina submitted a report on the applicant’s situation. It stated that the applicant had been residing in an apartment managed by the foundation, together with other women, where there was 24-hour support provided by four caregivers. It indicated that the children could spend nights there with the applicant, as she was able to take care of them and the apartment was large enough to accommodate them. It affirmed that, with adequate support, she could take care of her children. It noted that earlier that month the applicant had asked Madrid City Council for an adapted apartment for her and her children, as well as other material assistance such as disability and maternity allowances. The report proposed increasing the time allocated to weekly visits and examining the possibility of extending the visits to holidays, as well as replacing the protection measures with custody.

34.  On 22 March 2019 the DGFC authorised the children to visit the applicant on weekends and during holidays.

35.  On 30 May 2019 the applicant had a meeting with a child protection officer from the Guardianship Authority, during which she was informed of the possibility of the children being placed with foster families, with which she disagreed.

36.  On 3 June 2019 Fundación Madrina submitted an updated report, proposing that the children moved in with the applicant in her apartment.

37.  In June 2019 the CPC submitted an updated report on the children’s situation.

Regarding A, the report noted that her emotional management had improved, and she had learnt to solve disputes in a more positive way. It also stated that she had a realistic view of the family’s situation.

In relation to B, the report stated that his mobility had improved and that he was attending primary school with the necessary adjustments. It observed that his behaviour had worsened since he started spending weekends with the applicant. His relationship with C was closer than with A, and he was managing his emotions better after his father’s visits.

Concerning C, the report noted that his development in different areas was in accordance with his age, and that he was happy with the weekend visits with the applicant. The report indicated that the proposal of foster family care was to be suspended to monitor the development of the circumstances.

The report concluded that the guardianship needed to be confirmed urgently before the board of the Guardianship Authority and that the children should remain at the CPC. It noted that the weekend visits with the applicant were positive and should continue and even be extended. It stated that an assessment of whether the children could move in with the applicant was being carried out, but the applicant was experiencing some difficulties with the other women residing in the apartment.

38.  A report by the Family Support Commission (“the CAF”) of the Madrid City Council’s Social Services of 19 September 2019 stated that the Childcare Centre no. 5 (Centro de Atención a la Infancia – hereinafter “the CAI”) had observed that the applicant had a strong bond with her children and had the emotional capacity to take care of them, but that she had physical limitations, a lack of a family support network and circumstances preventing her from adequately taking care of them. It noted that there were not enough social resources to support the children if they stayed with their mother and agreed to confirm the guardianship measure.

39.  On 25 October 2019 a social educator and a social worker of the CAI issued a report examining the possibility of maintaining, lifting or replacing the protection measure in respect of the children. It observed that the children showed stress indicators owing to the family’s past experiences, namely war, exile and conflict between their parents. The applicant’s eldest daughter, A, had particularly suffered from those situations: she had performed a parental role which had been inappropriate, and there were suspicions of sexual abuse, pending further assessment.

The report noted that the applicant’s capacity to take care of her children was affected by her mobility limitations, that she needed support and that she did not have a family support network. It stated, nevertheless, that she had good parenting abilities and that her shortcomings were based on her physical disability. However, she had difficulties acknowledging her limitations and accepting that there were no available resources that could meet her needs plus those of her children in order to allow family reunification.

The report noted the previous CAF report (see paragraph 38 above) and concluded the following:

“... the only elements preventing the lifting of the protection measure so that [the applicant] can take care of her children are her physical disability and her high socio-economic vulnerability. There are no elements justifying maintaining the protection measure besides those caused by her disability”.

Thus, the report concluded that the protection measure should be maintained, but it would be possible to apply the less restrictive measure considering that (i) the children had a strong bond with their parents; (ii) the applicant was a protective figure for the children; (iii) there was a strong bond between the siblings that should be maintained; and (iv) a more restrictive measure would result in the separation of the siblings and make intervention with the applicant more difficult, also hampering the processing of different support resources. Thus, the report proposed that the children remain at the CPC and that there be cooperation with the parents to ask for a custody measure. It further added that the CAI would inform the applicant of the proposal, “based on the idea that she would have a right to be reunited with her children if she had a family support network available to her or if public services could adequately address her dependency needs”.

40.  In November 2019 the CPC prepared a report proposing to lift the protection measure in respect of C, reuniting him with the applicant. The report stated that C was attached to the applicant and living with her would allow him to maintain his relationship with his siblings, which could be affected if he were to be placed with a foster family. It also noted that the applicant had parental skills and was able to take care of her baby, D, since her birth the year before.

41.  On 13 December 2019 Fundación Madrina issued an updated report on the applicant’s situation indicating that in six months she would be leaving the apartment where she was staying. It further noted the existence of problems coexisting with other residents, including when her children were visiting her, as she did not impose any limits or rules on the children.

42.  In December 2019 the CPC issued an updated report on the children’s situation reiterating the need for the board of the Guardianship Authority to confirm the protection measure. It noted that the applicant’s situation was uncertain, as Fundación Madrina had changed its position from being available to host the children to being unable to extend their visits. It observed that there were no indicators that the applicant had failed to provide protection for her children, apart from her disability and the lack of a support network in Spain. The report concluded that the children’s placement at the centre should be maintained.

43.  In a meeting with the child protection officer from the Guardianship Authority on 14 January 2020 the applicant reiterated her opposition to the placement of B and C with foster families.

44.  On 21 January 2020 the child protection department of the DGFC issued three separate reports on the applicant’s children proposing to confirm the guardianship measure. The three reports considered that the circumstances underlying the adoption of the protection measure were still relevant, namely:

“ – The inadequate exercise of the protection duties by [I.A.] because of the serious difficulties observed: signs of mistreatment against the children, judgment [convicting him of] gender-based violence against his wife, abuse of alcohol and criminal proceedings pending decision.

– Owing to the [applicant’s] complete inability to exercise or adequately fulfil her parental protection responsibilities (el imposible e inadecuado ejercicio de los deberes de protección). This inability stems from her personal limitations associated with her disability and her reliance on third parties to take care of her children, one of whom has a disability and two of them are very young. [The exercise of those responsibilities has also been considered] inadequate because she demonstrates limited awareness of her [circumstances], her own limitations and the risks to which she has exposed her children, while failing to cater for their needs.

– The place where [the applicant] currently lives cannot facilitate the [staff] support needed to ensure the necessary attention and care required by the children, [and the fact that] she must leave that accommodation within six months.

– The protection department has maintained the urgent [guardianship] decision for a longer period than the one provided by law in order to clarify the parents’ situation, citing the complexity of the case and the number of institutions involved, which have not yet provided an alternative form of assistance for [the applicant] and her children.

– The lack of other relatives who could take responsibility for the children.

– The measure of custody requested by [the applicant] is dismissed, based on two main grounds:

(i) The measure of custody is legally defined [as a protective measure that may only be imposed in the presence of] serious circumstances of a temporary nature. There are no indications that the protection measure will be temporary in nature, as required by law, which limits such measures to a period of less than two years. [Furthermore,] the protection measure cannot be implemented as an alternative to institutionalisation.

(ii) The parents are not legally separated and they do not have a legal agreement in respect of the children. Implementing a custody measure would mean that [I.A.] would continue to be responsible for the children, being able to visit them without supervision and even to cohabitate.”

In respect of A, the report proposed that she remain in residential care. For B and C, the reports proposed permanent family placements.

45.  On 4 February 2020 the CPC submitted an updated report on the children’s situation. The report noted that it appeared that the applicant and I.A. were in touch, despite the restraining order, as they had been seen together, and that it was possible that they could take the children away during a weekend visit. On 11 February 2020 the director of the CPC ordered the suspension of the children’s visits to the apartment where the applicant was living after observing that the applicant had met I.A. and that the children were attending some lessons on Sundays without authorisation. Weekly visits were to take place at the CPC from then on.

46.  On 4 March 2020 Fundación Madrina submitted an updated report on the applicant’s situation. It stated that her placement in its apartment was temporary and due to terminate in May 2020, so three options were under consideration: (i) the applicant returning to Türkiye with the children, where they had relatives; (ii) finding permanent alternative accommodation for the applicant and her children; and (iii) the applicant and the children moving with I.A. into an adapted apartment. The report concluded that the applicant’s relationship and bond with her children were good, but the limitations imposed by her disability prevented her from autonomously performing all the relevant tasks required to take care of her children – the support of caregivers was needed. Regarding the possibility of the children staying in the foundation’s apartment, it noted that it would require financial support to face the costs of accommodating and caring for the whole family. The report noted that the weekend visits had been cancelled by the CPC because (i) the children were attending Arabic and Koran lessons without authorisation; (ii) A was carrying out activities which were not appropriate for her age during the visits (such as washing dishes); and (iii) the applicant had met I.A. in January 2020, together with B, despite the restraining order.

47.  In March 2020 the CPC submitted an updated report. With respect to C, it noted that, in view of the uncertainty of the applicant’s situation, he should be placed with a foster family.

48.  On 8 April 2020 the CAI issued a report on the children’s situation. The report identified the following “risk indicators” in respect of the applicant: (i) her high level of disability; (ii) the lack of a family support network; (iii) her mistrust of the Spanish protection system; and (iv) the high level of attention required by her children (two young children and one with a disability requiring specialised attention). It also observed several “protection indicators”, including a strong bond and emotional relationship with her children; good capacity to activate formal and informal support resources; good management of her divorce; and capacity to carry out basic day-to-day activities despite her disability. The report concluded that the family situation was dependent on external resources and that, under section 17 of the Institutional Law on the Legal Protection of Minors (hereinafter “the LOPJM”), “material shortcomings [were] considered a risk indicator, but [could not] result in the separation of the family”. It thus suggested implementing a custody measure, with the children remaining at the CPC, and working with the applicant so she could take care of her children.

49.  In September 2020 Fundación Madrina issued an updated report, in which it stated that the applicant had to leave the apartment by mid-November. It concluded that the difficulties the applicant faced in taking care of her children could be overcome with the support of a trusted third party and that she had sufficient financial means to ensure her personal autonomy, noting that I.A. was also giving her money to help pay for the children’s expenses.

50.  On 23 October 2020 the CAI issued a new report examining whether to maintain, lift or modify the protection measure. The report indicated that the family’s main difficulty in taking care of the children was related to their housing situation. Apparently, a request for social housing was still pending and a request for emergency housing had been unsuccessful as there were no adequate options in view of the applicant’s health condition. The family was on the waiting list of a housing programme managed by the regional authorities and an NGO. It noted that there was a possibility of a housing option provided by an NGO. It noted that the applicant and I.A. had agreed that custody of the children would be granted to the applicant, and I.A. would visit the children on Fridays and Sundays. They had further agreed that I.A. would pay the applicant a child allowance of EUR 700 per month as well as a compensatory allowance of EUR 200. It was indicated in the report that the applicant had the support of a third party who could move in with her and the children to help her take care of them. According to that report, A was not receiving special support regarding child sexual abuse.

The report concluded that the applicant was cooperating with the CAI: she had followed the advice she had received to find a house and had looked for support to handle her mobility limitations. The adverse circumstances preventing her from being reunited with her children were not attributable to the applicant, as she had actively responded to all the indications made by the CAI and social services to change her situation. Both parents had a strong bond with their children and were aware of the negative impact institutionalisation was having on the children. There were no indications of a lack of protection in respect of D, who lived with the applicant, and there were no serious shortcomings in the applicant’s parental skills, although further work with both parents was appropriate.

The report reiterated that the family’s situation was determined by two circumstances: the lack of adequate housing adapted to the applicant’s needs and the need to have a support person or service complementing the deficits resulting from her dependence. In those circumstances, it was not possible for the children to be with the applicant, so the CAI recommended that the children stay at the CPC, promoting the relationship with their parents and between them. The intervention should focus on reuniting them with the applicant once she could offer a stable environment adapted to their needs.

51.  On 16 December 2020 the board of the Guardianship Authority confirmed the situation of neglect and the protection guardianship measure in respect of the children. It ruled that A would remain in residential care while B and C would be placed with foster families. The decision was based on the following facts:

“1. The children are under the guardianship [of the child protection authorities] and were provisionally accommodated in a SAMUR facility. [The applicant] was pregnant at that time, with a disability and was a victim of gender-based violence by [I.A.] She was scarcely aware of her difficulties, rejecting both medical assistance and the support of professionals taking care of the children. Lack of a family support network.

[I.A.] was expelled from the facility without the possibility of being readmitted owing to a restraining order. There is a report against him for gender-based violence ... Alcohol abuse. Whereabouts unknown at the time when the measure was adopted.

2. The family’s situation, as reported by the CAI, currently defined by the functional limitations of [the applicant] on account of her disability and, as a result, her need to have the support of a third party to take care of the children, and not having a stable house adapted to her personal needs for her and the children, as she will soon have to leave the place where she is currently living.

[Account should also be taken of] her attitude and inadequate use of the resources made available to her and the ages of the children, one of them with a recognised disability of 80% [and] with a need for constant supervision.

Currently, as reported by the CAI, the parents are involved in separation proceedings, and an agreement is foreseen.

3. [I.A.] was convicted of gender-based violence; the restraining order and prohibition to communicate with [the applicant] has been terminated. He is cooperating with the intervention and acknowledges part of his responsibility concerning the protection measure, but he [is not yet treating] his alcohol consumption.

4. The children currently go out [of the CPC] with [the applicant] without staying for the night and receive visits from the father in the CPC. There is a strong bond between them. Contact had to be adapted owing to the breach of the restraining order imposed on [I.A.]”

The decision was taken considering (i) that the circumstances on which the measure had been based had been confirmed; (ii) that the family’s situation had become chronic and the time spent by the children in residential care; (iii) the lack of family alternatives for the children’s care; (iv) and that a family environment, providing them safety, stability and covering their needs, would favour their development. It made reference to the relevant provisions of the Civil Code (see paragraph 70 below) and of the regional regulations on child protection (see paragraphs 75 and 77 below). The decision indicated that it could be challenged within two months from its notification. It further indicated that the social services should report on the family’s situation every six months.

52.  On 19 January 2021 the applicant submitted observations before the Guardianship Authority. It appears that at that point she had not yet been informed of the decision of 16 December 2020. She argued that the reasons behind the provisional decision to deprive her of her children’s guardianship were questionable, as they should have resulted in a provisional removal of custody and the provision of solutions from the administration so mother and children could stay together. The decision had been taken in breach of the prohibition to declare a situation of neglect based on reasons of poverty or disability, the obligation to prioritise the family unit, and the obligation to protect and assist people with disabilities and victims of gender-based violence. She argued that the authorities were not working to reunite her with her children, despite her good parental skills, her strong bond with her children, and the fact that the only reason not to return them to her was that she lacked the material means and that there were no available public resources allowing for family reunification. Furthermore, some of the circumstances had changed as she was divorced from I.A., she was receiving several allowances and had someone available to assist her. The applicant thus asked for: (i) the measure of provisional guardianship to be replaced by voluntary custody; (ii) a family intervention plan to be adopted to ensure the relationship between the applicant and her children and the one between siblings; and (iii) the protection measure to be lifted and the family to be reunited once material conditions allowed.

53.  On 26 January 2021 the applicant submitted further allegations before the DGFC supplementing her observations of 19 January 2021. She asked that, in the event that placement with a foster family was considered in the best interests of the children, that was only indicated temporarily and the children were placed together.

the judicial proceedings confirming the situation of neglect and the family’s circumstances during that period (january 2021 - november 2023).

54.  On 25 March 2021 the applicant lodged a claim (escrito de oposición) challenging the decision of the Guardianship Authority of 16 December 2020, which was supplemented with further observations lodged on 6 July 2021 (demanda de oposición). She argued that the decision had been based on her disability and her lack of economic means, that her maternal skills had not been disputed by any report and that the improvements in her situation had not been considered. In addition, she argued that no measures had been taken to support the family so that they could stay together or to reunite her with her children. Lastly, she complained that the decision would result in the separation of the siblings. She asked for the annulment of the decision, seeking measures to facilitate family reunification or, in the alternative, the changes in her circumstances to be taken into consideration, lifting the protection measure and reuniting her with her children. She further asked for interim measures aimed at suspending the decision in respect of the placement of B and C with foster families.

55.  On 21 October 2021 the Madrid Court of First Instance no. 75 dismissed the applicant’s claim and upheld the decision of 16 December 2020. It held that the decision had been adopted in conformity with relevant rules. Referring to the different reports issued concerning the situation of the applicant and the children, namely the reports of the DGFC of January 2020 and the CAI reports of April and October 2020 (see paragraphs 44, 48 and 50 above), it stated:

“Based on the proceedings and a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence ... it must be concluded that, given the current situation, the confirmation of the guardianship and custody measures should be upheld, for while it is true that progress is being made and the situation regarding the [applicant] is evolving positively – taking into account her previous attitudes, in which she did not cooperate or acknowledge the problem – and regarding the relationship, work is being done toward the possibility of the minors returning to their mother, beginning, if appropriate, with overnight stays, it is not considered that the conditions currently exist for the minors to return to their mother. [A] is doing well at the [CPC], where she should remain, so that she is not the one responsible for her siblings and her mother as she was previously.

It is true that this is an evolving situation, but it must be considered that the necessary circumstances do not exist to terminate this measure.”

56.  The court referred to section 17(1) of the LOPJM, as amended by Law no. 26/2015 of 28 July (see paragraph 70 below) and concluded that the protection measure should be maintained, considering that “the children would be at risk should they return to be with their mother” and that there were “risk indicators that required further work”.

57.  The applicant appealed against the court’s judgment. She argued that the judgment had been issued in breach of legal provisions preventing the declaration of a situation of neglect based on reasons of poverty and disability and of those provisions imposing an obligation on the administration to take measures in support of families in those situations. In addition, the judgment had wrongly assessed the evidence, namely in regard to the applicant’s attitude and to C’s situation, in respect of whom the administration had proposed to lift the protection measure.

58.  On 19 May 2022 the Madrid Audiencia Provincial dismissed the applicant’s appeal, considering that there had not been an incorrect assessment of the evidence and no rules had been breached. It held as follows:

“The [administrative] decision ... duly sets out the difficulties faced by [the applicant] in exercising her parental responsibilities towards her minor children, her refusal or limited use of support services to assist with the care of her minor children, [I.A.’s] use of violence against his children and [the applicant], [I.A.’s] alcohol abuse, as well as the abuse and family burdens borne by the minor daughter, A.

...[t]he administrative file itself takes into account the CAI file, which emphasises that the [applicant] currently faces functional limitations on account of her disability and ... the need for a third party to look after and care for her children, and the lack of permanent accommodation adapted to her personal needs and those of the children, as she will also have to leave the Fundación Madrina accommodation where she currently resides in the near future. Added to this are her attitude and the inappropriate use of the resources made available to her, as well as the ages of the children, one of whom has a recognised disability of 80% and requires constant supervision. The file states that, according to the information provided by the CAI, the parents are currently in the process of separating.

...

At the moment when the administrative decision was issued, neither of the parents could take care of the children for the following reasons.

...

(b) [The applicant] cannot take care of the children on account of the functional limitations caused by her disability and her need for a third party to look after and care for her children, one of whom has a disability; [the applicant] has difficulty accepting her current situation, coupled with her inappropriate use of the resources made available to her, as well as the ages of the children – three, nine and ten years old (at the time the administrative decision was issued, she was pregnant with a fourth child), one of whom, as indicated, has a disability and requires constant supervision, with the risk that the responsibility for their care and supervision will once again fall on the ten-year-old girl.

(c) [The applicant] must leave the accommodation where she is currently staying in the near future, thus there is no stable housing alternative available either for her alone or for her together with the children.

(d) This family’s difficulties in providing for and caring for their children have become chronic, both owing to the level of support the [applicant] requires and owing to the passivity of [I.A.] who, during the two years he has been working, has neither sought suitable accommodation to provide for and care for the children, nor followed the professionals’ advice to begin treatment for alcoholism.

(e) The need to develop a long-term plan for these children based on a stable protective measure, and, building on that stability, to assess any requests to amend the measure on the basis of realistic plans that are guaranteed to be stable and better for the children than the protective measure itself.

(f) That it is not in the best interests of C, aged almost four, and B, who has special needs, to continue growing up in a care institution.

(g) The absence of other family members who could take on responsibility for the children.”

59.  Referring to section 17 of the LOPJM (see paragraph 70 below), the Audiencia Provincial further held as follows:

“In the light of the above legislation, the court considers that, in the present case, the children are at risk and that it would not be in their best interests to return to their mother. It must be borne in mind that the evidence ... shows that [the applicant], together with her children, has been entitled to various forms of social assistance while living with them, as was the case with the Fundación Madrina; she has also received financial support from various associations and organisations, and even [social housing].

In sum, the children’s situation of neglect is not caused by [the applicant’s] disability, as noted in the CAI’s report following its assessment of the minors, which indicates that the [applicant] has a poor awareness of her own difficulties – refusing medical care and professional support in looking after her children – in addition to her lack of family support. [I.A.], as recorded in the case file, reportedly continues to suffer from alcohol addiction and therefore does not constitute a figure capable of protecting the children either.

... Consequently, the measure taken is justified, as it cannot be considered that the risk of a situation of neglect has ceased ... This entails the dismissal of the appeal lodged by [the applicant] on the grounds that there are risk indicators which must be monitored and addressed as far as possible so that this situation is resolved.”

60.  The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law arguing that the courts had assessed the evidence in an arbitrary fashion and had breached several legal provisions (namely Article 172 § 2 of the Civil Code, sections 17 and 18 of the LOPJM, Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and Article 8 of the Convention) and ignored related case-law.

61.  On 12 April 2023 the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible, stating that its only role in the framework of the appeal on points of law was to examine whether the courts had duly applied the principle of the best interests of the child. Since the lower court’s judgment had considered that the lack of protection of the children had been demonstrated, the best interests of the child called for the confirmation of the decision.

62.  The applicant lodged an amparo appeal, arguing a violation of her right to judicial protection (Article 24 of the Constitution), in connection to the rights to family life and not to be discriminated against (Articles 18 and 14 of the Constitution), as well as to the protection of children and the protection of their best interests (Article 39 of the Constitution) and the protection of persons with disabilities (Article 49 and Article 9 § 2 of the Constitution).

63.  On 16 November 2023 the Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal inadmissible, considering that it lacked constitutional significance.

the family’s circumstances after the termination of the ADMINISTRATIVE proceedings (DECEMBER 2020 – JANUARY 2026)

64.  On 28 December 2020 the Alcobendas Court of First Instance granted the divorce of the applicant and I.A. and approved their settlement agreement (convenio regulador), awarding custody of the children to the applicant, establishing I.A.’s visitation rights, and ordering I.A. to pay maintenance of EUR 200 per month for the applicant and EUR 700 per month for the children.
