65.  On 20 March 2021 the Families, Equality and Social Well-being Department of the Madrid City Council issued a decree declaring the applicant and her family in an “exceptional and urgent situation” within the meaning of the regulations to have access to social housing, noting that an immediate housing alternative was needed to enable the resumption of family cohabitation and the revocation of the protection measures. In July 2021 she signed a contract for an apartment and in August 2021 she moved there. Several NGOs committed to support her, namely through financial allowances to ensure the assistance of a third party.

66.  On 7 September 2021 the applicant had a meeting with the child protection officer from the Guardianship Authority and asked for her children to be allowed to visit her and spend the night with her; reiterating her wish to be reunited with them and, more urgently, with C because of his age. As from December 2021 the children were allowed to visit the applicant at her apartment and spend the night there. C spent the summer of 2021, or part of it, with the applicant.

67.  On 14 December 2022 the Guardianship Authority declared the termination of the protection measure in respect of C. It noted that both the CAI and the CPC considered that the applicant demonstrated sufficient capacity to take care of him at her place and was accepting the relevant support.

68.  According to the latest information submitted by the parties, by January 2026 A and B were still under the guardianship and custody of the child protection authorities. A had been transferred to a specialised protection centre, as she was suffering from a depressive disorder. B was living at the CPC. A and B were visiting the applicant and spending some nights at the family home. C and D were living with the applicant. A DGFC report of January 2026 indicated that the applicant had been receiving home assistance and that an intervention was taking place with the applicant and A to ensure that A did not take on the role of carer. The report also stated that the applicant still required the assistance of a carer to look after her children. The report recommended maintaining A and B’s visits to the applicant’s home.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

domestic law

69.  The relevant Articles of the Civil Code read as follows:

Article 172

“1. Where the public body responsible for the protection of minors in the relevant territory establishes that a minor is in a situation of neglect, it shall, by operation of law, assume guardianship of the minor and must take the necessary protective measures for his or her custody, notifying the public prosecutor’s office and, where appropriate, the judge who granted ordinary guardianship. The administrative decision declaring the situation of neglect and the measures taken shall be notified in due form to the parents, guardians or carers and to the child concerned if he or she is sufficiently mature and, in any event, if he or she is over 12 years of age, immediately and within a maximum period of 48 hours. The information shall be clear, understandable and in an accessible format, including the reasons for the administration’s intervention and the effects of the decision taken, and, in the case of the child, adapted to his or her level of maturity. Whenever possible, and particularly in the case of the child, this information shall be provided in person.

A situation of neglect is considered to be that which occurs in fact owing to the non-compliance or the impossible or inadequate exercise of the duties of protection established by law for the custody of minors, when they are deprived of the necessary moral or material assistance.

The assumption of guardianship by the public authority entails the suspension of parental authority or ordinary guardianship ...

2. Within two years of being notified of the administrative decision declaring the child to be in a situation of neglect, parents who continue to hold parental authority but whose authority has been suspended in accordance with paragraph 1 ... may ask the public authority to lift the suspension and revoke the declaration of the child’s situation of neglect if, owing to a change in the circumstances that led to it, they consider themselves able to resume parental authority or guardianship.

Likewise, within the same period, they may object to decisions taken regarding the child’s protection.

Once this period has elapsed, the right of the parents or guardians to request or object to the decisions or measures adopted for the protection of the child shall cease. However, they may provide information to the public authority and the public prosecutor’s office regarding any change in the circumstances that led to the declaration that the child was in a situation of neglect ...

3. The public authority may, on its own initiative or at the request of the public prosecutor’s office or any interested person or body, revoke the declaration of a situation of neglect and decide to return the child to his or her family, provided that this is deemed to be in the child’s best interests. The public prosecutor’s office shall be notified of this decision.

4. In fulfilment of the obligation to provide immediate care, the public authority may assume temporary custody of a child by means of an administrative decision, and shall notify the public prosecutor’s office thereof, while simultaneously taking the necessary steps to identify the child, investigate his or her circumstances and verify, where appropriate, the actual situation of neglect.

Such procedures shall be carried out as quickly as possible, during which time, where appropriate, a declaration of the situation of neglect shall be made and guardianship assumed, or the appropriate protective measure shall be implemented ...

5. The public authority shall cease to exercise guardianship over minors declared to be in a situation of neglect when it establishes, through the relevant reports, that the grounds for assuming guardianship have ceased to exist ...

Provisional custody shall cease for the same reasons as guardianship.”

Article 172 bis

“1. Where parents or guardians, owing to serious and temporary circumstances that have been duly certified, are unable to care for their child, they may request that the public authority assume custody of the child for such time as is necessary, which may not exceed a maximum period of two years for the temporary care of that child, unless his or her best interests exceptionally warrant an extension of the measures. Once the period or extension, where applicable, has elapsed, the child must return to his or her parents or guardians or, if the circumstances are not suitable for this, be declared in a legal situation of neglect.”

Article 172 ter

“1. Custody shall be arranged through foster care and, where this is not possible or in the child’s best interests, through residential care. Foster care shall be provided by the person or persons designated by the public authority. Residential care shall be provided by the director or person in charge of the centre where the child is placed, in accordance with the provisions of child protection legislation.

...

2. The child’s best interests shall always be sought and, where this is not contrary to those interests, priority shall be given to reintegration into his or her own family and to entrusting custody of siblings to the same institution or person so that they may remain together.”

Article 173 bis

“2. Family foster care may take the following forms, depending on its duration and objectives:

...

(c) Permanent family foster care, which shall be established either at the end of the two-year period of temporary foster care where family reunification is not possible, or directly in cases involving children with special needs or where the circumstances of the child and his or her family so warrant ...”

70.  The relevant sections of the Institutional Law on the Legal Protection of Minors (Ley Orgánica de Protección Jurídica del Menor – “the LOPJM”), provide as follows:

Section 11. Guiding principles of administrative action

“1. Public authorities shall provide children with adequate assistance to enable them to exercise their rights, including the support resources they require.

...

Compensatory policies aimed at correcting social inequalities shall be promoted. In no case shall the essential content of children’s rights be affected by a lack of basic social resources. Children with disabilities and their families shall be guaranteed the specialised social services required by their disability.

2. The following shall be the guiding principles for the actions of public authorities in relation to minors:

(a) The primacy of the child’s best interests;

(b) The child’s continued placement within his or her family of origin, unless this is not in his or her best interests, in which case family-based and stable protective measures shall be ensured, giving priority in such cases to family foster care over institutional care;

...

(k) Universal accessibility and reasonable accommodation for children with disabilities, as well as their full and effective inclusion and participation.”

Section 12. Protective measures

“1. The protection of minors by the public authorities shall be achieved through the prevention, detection and remedy of situations of risk, by establishing appropriate services and resources for this purpose, by exercising custody and, in cases where a child is declared to be in a situation of neglect, by assuming guardianship by operation of law. In protective measures, priority shall always be given to family-based measures over residential ones, stable arrangements over temporary ones and mutually agreed arrangements over imposed ones.

2. The public authorities shall ensure that parents, guardians, custodians or foster carers fulfil their responsibilities appropriately and shall provide them with accessible services for prevention, advice and support in all areas affecting the development of minors.

3. Where children are under the parental authority, guardianship, custody or foster care of a victim of gender-based or domestic violence, the actions of the public authorities shall be aimed at ensuring the necessary support to enable the children, regardless of their age, to remain with that person, as well as their protection, specialised care and recovery.

7. [8. in the version in force since June 2021] Public authorities shall guarantee the rights and obligations of children with disabilities in relation to their custody, guardianship, adoption or similar arrangements, ensuring that the best interests of the child are always paramount. They shall also ensure that children with disabilities have the same rights with regard to family life. To give effect to these rights and to prevent their concealment, abandonment, neglect or segregation, they shall ensure that general information, services and support are provided in advance to children with disabilities and their families.”

Section 14. Immediate assistance

“Public authorities and services shall be obliged to provide any minor with the immediate assistance required, to take action where this falls within their area of competence or, otherwise, to refer the matter to the competent body and to bring the facts to the attention of the minor’s legal representatives or, where necessary, of the public authority and the public prosecutor’s office.

In the fulfilment of the obligation to provide immediate care, the public authority may assume the temporary custody of a child as provided for in Article 172.4 of the Civil Code, which shall be notified to the public prosecutor’s office, while simultaneously taking the necessary steps to identify the child, investigate their circumstances and verify, where applicable, the actual situation of neglect.”

71.  With regards in particular to situations of risk, section 17(1) of the LOPJM, as amended by Law no. 26/2015 of 28 July, stated as follows:

Section 17. Action to be taken in situations of risk

“1. A situation of risk shall be deemed to exist where, owing to family, social or educational circumstances, deficiencies or conflicts, the child’s personal, family, social or educational development, or his or her rights or well-being are impaired, in such a way that, while not reaching the level, intensity or persistence that would justify a declaration of a situation of neglect and the assumption of guardianship ... the intervention of the competent public authority is necessary to eliminate, reduce or compensate for the difficulties or adverse circumstances affecting [the child] and to prevent his or her neglect and social exclusion, without having to be separated from his or her family environment. To this end, having a sibling declared to be in such a situation shall be considered an indicator of risk, amongst other factors, unless family circumstances have clearly changed. The concurrence of material circumstances or deprivations shall be considered an indicator of risk, but shall never result in separation from the family environment.

...

4. The assessment of the situation of risk shall involve the development and implementation of a social and educational intervention plan for the family, which must set out the objectives, actions, resources and expected timelines, while promoting factors that protect the child and ensuring that the child remains within his or her family environment.”

72.  An amendment that entered into force in June 2021 eliminated the last two sentences of paragraph 1 and included specific risk indicators, including, inter alia, the lack of physical or psychological care, resulting in minor harm to the child’s health; negligence in care; negative development of the intervention programmes; discriminatory practices; and being exposed to situations of domestic or gender-based violence, or any other circumstance implying violence against the child that could lead to a situation of neglect, if it were to persist.

73.  Concerning situations of neglect, section 18 of the LOPJM establishes the following:

Section 18. Measures to be taken in cases of neglect

“1. Where a public authority establishes that a child is in a situation of neglect, it shall act in accordance with Article 172 et seq. of the Civil Code, assuming guardianship of the child by operation of law, taking the appropriate protective measures and notifying the public prosecutor’s office and, where applicable, the judge who granted ordinary guardianship.

2. In accordance with the provisions of Article 172 et seq. of the Civil Code, a situation of neglect shall be deemed to exist where it arises in fact owing to the failure to fulfil, or the impossible or inadequate exercise of, the duties of protection established by law for the care of minors, when they are deprived of the necessary moral or material assistance.

The financial hardship of the parents, guardians or carers shall not be taken into account when assessing a situation of neglect. Furthermore, under no circumstances shall a child be separated from his or her parents on the grounds of a disability affecting the child, both parents or one of them.

...

In particular, a situation of neglect shall be deemed to exist where one or more of the following circumstances arise with sufficient gravity that, when assessed and weighed in accordance with the principles of necessity and proportionality, they pose a threat to the child’s physical or mental well-being.

(a) The abandonment of the child, either because the persons legally responsible for the child’s care are absent, or because they are unwilling or unable to provide such care.

(b) The expiry of the period of voluntary care, either when the child’s legal guardians are in a position to take on the custody of the child but are unwilling to do so, or when, whilst wishing to take on custody, they are not in a position to do so, save in exceptional cases where voluntary care may be extended beyond the two-year period.

(c) The risk to the child’s life, health and physical well-being. In particular, where there is serious physical mistreatment, sexual abuse or serious neglect in the fulfilment of nutritional and health obligations on the part of members of the family unit or third parties acting with their consent ...

(d) The risk to the child’s mental health, moral integrity and personality development arising from continuous psychological mistreatment or serious and chronic neglect of his or her emotional or educational needs by their parents, guardians or carers ...

(e) Non-compliance with or the inability or failure to adequately fulfil custodial duties as a result of a serious deterioration in the family environment or living conditions, where this gives rise to circumstances or behaviour that is detrimental to the child’s development or mental health.

(f) Incitement to begging, crime or prostitution, or any other exploitation of the child of a similar nature or severity.

(g) Failure to enrol a child in school, repeated unjustified absences from an educational institution, or the continued allowance or encouragement of school absenteeism during the period of compulsory education.

(h) Any other situation seriously detrimental to the child arising from the failure to exercise, or the impossible or inadequate exercise of, parental authority, guardianship or custody, the consequences of which cannot be avoided while the child remains in his or her current living environment.”

74.  Other relevant provisions of the LOPJM read:

Section 19. Child custody

“1. In addition to taking custody of children placed under guardianship because they are in a situation of neglect, the public authority shall assume custody in accordance with the provisions of Article 172 bis of the Civil Code, where the parents or guardians are unable to care for a child owing to serious circumstances of a temporary nature, or where the judge so orders in cases where this is legally appropriate.

2. Voluntary custody shall have a maximum duration of two years, unless the best interests of the child exceptionally warrant an extension of the measure owing to the foreseeable reunification of the family within a short period of time.

In such cases of voluntary custody, the family must undertake to submit, where appropriate, to professional intervention.”

Section 19 bis. Provisions common to custody and guardianship

“1. When the public authority assumes guardianship or custody of a child, it shall draw up an individualised protection plan setting out the objectives, prospects and duration of the intervention measures to be adopted with regard to the child’s family of origin, including, where appropriate, a family reintegration programme.

In the case of a child with a disability, the public authority shall ensure the continuity of the support the child has been receiving or the provision of other support more suited to his or her needs.

2. Where the assessment indicates the possibility of a return to the family of origin, the public authority shall implement a family reintegration programme ...

3. In order to agree to the return of the neglected child to their family of origin, it is essential that there is evidence of positive progress within the family, objectively sufficient to re-establish family life; that family ties have been maintained; that there is a genuine intention to fulfil parental responsibilities appropriately; and that an expert report confirms that his or her return will not pose any significant risks to the child ...”

75.  As regards regional regulations, Decree no. 121/1988 of 23 November 1988 regulates child guardianship and custody proceedings in the Madrid Autonomous Community. It states that such measures are to be guided by the best interests of the child; that preventive measures, addressing the causes that may lead to the neglect of minors, will be encouraged; and that care of the child within the family shall be favoured where possible.

76.  The relevant parts of the General Act on the rights of persons with disabilities and their social inclusion (Royal Legislative Decree no. 1/2013 of 29 November 2013) provide as follows:

Section 7. Right to equality

“1. Persons with disabilities have the same rights as other citizens under our legal system.

2. To give effect to this right to equality, public authorities shall promote the necessary measures to ensure that persons with disabilities can exercise their rights on an equal footing in a genuine and effective manner in all areas of life.

3. Public authorities shall provide particularly robust protection for the rights of persons with disabilities in relation to gender equality, health, employment, social protection ... in accordance with the provisions of this Title and other applicable legislation.

4. Furthermore, public authorities shall provide particularly enhanced protection to those individuals or groups of individuals who are especially vulnerable to multiple discrimination, such as children and women with disabilities, older persons with disabilities, women with disabilities who are victims of gender-based violence, persons with multiple disabilities, or other persons with disabilities who are members of minority groups.”

Section 50. Scope of the right to social protection

“1. Persons with disabilities and their families are entitled to social services providing family support, measures for the prevention and mitigation of disabilities and their progression, measures to promote personal autonomy, information and guidance, home and residential care, community support and residential services, and cultural, sports, leisure and recreational activities.”

Section 63. Violation of the right to equal opportunities

“The right to equal opportunities of persons with disabilities ... shall be deemed to have been infringed where, on the grounds of or by reason of disability, there is direct or indirect discrimination, discrimination by association, harassment, failure to comply with accessibility requirements and to make reasonable adjustments, as well as failure to comply with legally established positive action measures.”

Section 67. Positive action measures

“1. Public authorities shall adopt positive action measures for the benefit of persons with disabilities who are likely to face a higher degree of discrimination, including multiple discrimination, or a lower degree of equal opportunities, such as women and children, who require greater support to exercise their autonomy or make independent decisions, and those suffering from more severe social exclusion ...

2. Furthermore, within the framework of the official policy for the protection of the family, public authorities shall adopt positive action measures with regard to families where any of their members is a person with a disability.”

Section 68. Scope of positive action and equal opportunities measures

“1. Positive action measures may consist of supplementary support and more favourable rules, criteria and practices. Equal opportunities measures may include financial assistance, practical assistance, personal assistance, specialised services, and communication aids and support services.

These measures shall constitute minimum requirements, without prejudice to any measures that may be established by the autonomous communities within the scope of their powers.”

international law material

77.  The relevant Articles of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted on 20 November 1989, read as follows:

Article 3

“1. In all actions concerning children, whether undertaken by public or private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities or legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration.

2. States Parties undertake to ensure the child such protection and care as is necessary for his or her well-being, taking into account the rights and duties of his or her parents, legal guardians, or other individuals legally responsible for him or her, and, to this end, shall take all appropriate legislative and administrative measures.

3. States Parties shall ensure that the institutions, services and facilities responsible for the care or protection of children shall conform with the standards established by competent authorities, particularly in the areas of safety, health, in the number and suitability of their staff, as well as competent supervision.”

Article 8

“1. States Parties undertake to respect the right of the child to preserve his or her identity, including nationality, name and family relations as recognized by law without unlawful interference ...”

Article 9

“1. States Parties shall ensure that a child shall not be separated from his or her parents against their will, except when competent authorities subject to judicial review determine, in accordance with applicable law and procedures, that such separation is necessary for the best interests of the child. Such determination may be necessary in a particular case such as one involving abuse or neglect of the child by the parents, or one where the parents are living separately and a decision must be made as to the child’s place of residence.

2. In any proceedings pursuant to paragraph 1 of the present article, all interested parties shall be given an opportunity to participate in the proceedings and make their views known.

3. States Parties shall respect the right of the child who is separated from one or both parents to maintain personal relations and direct contact with both parents on a regular basis, except if it is contrary to the child’s best interests ...”

Article 18

“1. States Parties shall use their best efforts to ensure recognition of the principle that both parents have common responsibilities for the upbringing and development of the child. Parents or, as the case may be, legal guardians, have the primary responsibility for the upbringing and development of the child. The best interests of the child will be their basic concern.

2. For the purpose of guaranteeing and promoting the rights set forth in the present Convention, States Parties shall render appropriate assistance to parents and legal guardians in the performance of their child-rearing responsibilities and shall ensure the development of institutions, facilities and services for the care of children ...”

Article 20

“1. A child temporarily or permanently deprived of his or her family environment, or in whose own best interests cannot be allowed to remain in that environment, shall be entitled to special protection and assistance provided by the State.

2. States Parties shall in accordance with their national laws ensure alternative care for such a child.

3. Such care could include, inter alia, foster placement, kafalah of Islamic law, adoption or if necessary placement in suitable institutions for the care of children. When considering solutions, due regard shall be paid to the desirability of continuity in a child’s upbringing and to the child’s ethnic, religious, cultural and linguistic background.”

Article 23

“1. States Parties recognize that a mentally or physically disabled child should enjoy a full and decent life, in conditions which ensure dignity, promote self-reliance and facilitate the child’s active participation in the community.

2. States Parties recognize the right of the disabled child to special care and shall encourage and ensure the extension, subject to available resources, to the eligible child and those responsible for his or her care, of assistance for which application is made and which is appropriate to the child’s condition and to the circumstances of the parents or others caring for the child.

3. Recognizing the special needs of a disabled child, assistance extended in accordance with paragraph 2 of the present article shall be provided free of charge, whenever possible, taking into account the financial resources of the parents or others caring for the child, and shall be designed to ensure that the disabled child has effective access to and receives education, training, health care services, rehabilitation services, preparation for employment and recreation opportunities in a manner conducive to the child’s achieving the fullest possible social integration and individual development, including his or her cultural and spiritual development.”

78.  The United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child General Comment no. 14 (2013) on the right of the child to have his or her best interests taken as a primary consideration (art. 3, para. 1), UN Doc. CRC/C/GC/14, adopted on 29 May 2013, states as follows:

“60. Preventing family separation and preserving family unity are important components of the child protection system, and are based on the right provided for in article 9 ...

61. Given the gravity of the impact on the child of separation from his or her parents, such separation should only occur as a last resort measure, as when the child is in danger of experiencing imminent harm or when otherwise necessary; separation should not take place if less intrusive measures could protect the child. Before resorting to separation, the State should provide support to the parents in assuming their parental responsibilities, and restore or enhance the family’s capacity to take care of the child, unless separation is necessary to protect the child. Economic reasons cannot be a justification for separating a child from his or her parents.

...

63. Likewise, a child may not be separated from his or her parents on the grounds of a disability of either the child or his or her parents. Separation may be considered only in cases where the necessary assistance to the family to preserve the family unit is not effective enough to avoid a risk of neglect or abandonment of the child or a risk to the child’s safety.”

79.  The relevant Articles of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), adopted on 12 December 2006, read as follows:

Article 23 – Respect for home and the family

“1. States Parties shall take effective and appropriate measures to eliminate discrimination against persons with disabilities in all matters relating to marriage, family, parenthood and relationships, on an equal basis with others, so as to ensure that:

(a) The right of all persons with disabilities who are of marriageable age to marry and to found a family on the basis of free and full consent of the intending spouses is recognized;

(b) The rights of persons with disabilities to decide freely and responsibly on the number and spacing of their children and to have access to age-appropriate information, reproductive and family planning education are recognized, and the means necessary to enable them to exercise these rights are provided;

(c) Persons with disabilities, including children, retain their fertility on an equal basis with others.

2. States Parties shall ensure the rights and responsibilities of persons with disabilities, with regard to guardianship, wardship, trusteeship, adoption of children or similar institutions, where these concepts exist in national legislation; in all cases the best interests of the child shall be paramount. States Parties shall render appropriate assistance to persons with disabilities in the performance of their child-rearing responsibilities.

3. States Parties shall ensure that children with disabilities have equal rights with respect to family life. With a view to realizing these rights, and to prevent concealment, abandonment, neglect and segregation of children with disabilities, States Parties shall undertake to provide early and comprehensive information, services and support to children with disabilities and their families.

4. States Parties shall ensure that a child shall not be separated from his or her parents against their will, except when competent authorities subject to judicial review determine, in accordance with applicable law and procedures, that such separation is necessary for the best interests of the child. In no case shall a child be separated from parents on the basis of a disability of either the child or one or both of the parents.

5. States Parties shall, where the immediate family is unable to care for a child with disabilities, undertake every effort to provide alternative care within the wider family, and failing that, within the community in a family setting.”

Article 28 – Adequate standard of living and social protection

“1. States Parties recognize the right of persons with disabilities to an adequate standard of living for themselves and their families, including adequate food, clothing and housing, and to the continuous improvement of living conditions, and shall take appropriate steps to safeguard and promote the realization of this right without discrimination on the basis of disability.

2. States Parties recognize the right of persons with disabilities to social protection and to the enjoyment of that right without discrimination on the basis of disability, and shall take appropriate steps to safeguard and promote the realization of this right, including measures:

(a) To ensure equal access by persons with disabilities to clean water services, and to ensure access to appropriate and affordable services, devices and other assistance for disability-related needs;

(b) To ensure access by persons with disabilities, in particular women and girls with disabilities and older persons with disabilities, to social protection programmes and poverty reduction programmes;

(c) To ensure access by persons with disabilities and their families living in situations of poverty to assistance from the State with disability-related expenses, including adequate training, counselling, financial assistance and respite care;

(d) To ensure access by persons with disabilities to public housing programmes;

(e) To ensure equal access by persons with disabilities to retirement benefits and programmes.”

case_name: CASE OF A.M. v. BULGARIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF A.M. v. BULGARIA

(Application no. 23441/25)













JUDGMENT



STRASBOURG

5 November 2026



This judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of A.M. v. Bulgaria,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

María Elósegui, President,
Gilberto Felici,
Diana Sârcu, judges,
and Sophie Piquet, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 23441/25) against the Republic of Bulgaria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 1 August 2025 by an Uzbek national, A.M. (“the applicant”), who was born in 1981 and was represented by Mr V. Petkov, a lawyer practising in Sofia;

the decisions to indicate an interim measure to the Bulgarian Government (“the Government”) and to refuse to lift that measure;

the decision not to have the applicant’s full name disclosed;

the decision to give priority to the application;

the decision to give notice of the application to the Government, represented by their Agents, Ms M. Kotseva and Ms S. Sobadzhieva of the Ministry of Justice;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 15 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The applicant arrived in Bulgaria in August 2022 and applied for international protection in October 2022. The State Agency for Refugees (“the SAR”) interviewed him and, under an accelerated procedure, rejected his application as manifestly unfounded. The Sofia City Administrative Court (“the SCAC”) upheld that decision following a claim for judicial review lodged by the applicant.

2.  In December 2022 the applicant lodged a subsequent application for international protection, enclosing an opinion by a psychologist whom he had consulted. The SAR rejected that application without an examination on the merits. The applicant again sought judicial review, and the SCAC again upheld the SAR’s decision.

3.  In April 2023 the applicant lodged a second subsequent application for international protection, enclosing a report by two forensic medical experts who had examined him and four documents he described as having been issued by the Uzbek authorities. The SAR rejected that application without an examination on the merits, but the SCAC set that decision aside after the applicant lodged a claim for judicial review. After interviewing the applicant, the SAR dismissed the application. The SCAC upheld that decision, and the Supreme Administrative Court (“the SAC”) in turn upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal.

4.  In June 2025 the applicant lodged a third subsequent application for international protection. The SAR rejected it without considering it on the merits. The applicant sought judicial review of that decision, but subsequently withdrew his claim, whereupon the SCAC discontinued the relevant proceedings. He later stated that he wished to retract the withdrawal, and the SCAC directed him to clarify whether that statement was intended as an appeal against the discontinuance. The applicant took no steps to comply with that direction, and the discontinuance became final.

5.  Meanwhile, in February 2023, the migration authorities had ordered the applicant’s return to Uzbekistan. He sought judicial review of that order but the order was upheld by the SCAC. The SAC upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal. The applicant subsequently sought to have the proceedings before the SAC reopened but later abandoned that attempt.

6.  In July 2025 the applicant was placed in immigration detention. Separately, having twice attempted to cross the border into Romania illegally in March and April 2025, in October 2025 he was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment.

7.  The applicant remained in prison, serving that sentence, until June 2026. He was then placed in immigration detention.

8.  The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the Bulgarian authorities and courts had not properly assessed whether he would be at a risk of ill-treatment if removed to Uzbekistan, and that, since that risk was real, such removal would be in breach of that Article.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Bulgaria of Article 3 (Prohibition of torture) concerning Expulsion; Conditional; Uzbekistan in this case
